u1l1.h: **Hallo, ek is Hettie!** Yes, I’m a hadeda, and yes, I’m already loud. Let’s start with the words you’ll use every single day.
u1l1.c: You’ll say **hallo** when you walk into a shop, pick up the phone or meet someone’s family. **Totsiens** is the last thing you say as you leave, and it works from a taxi rank to a boardroom.
u1l1.t: Four little words: **hallo** (hello), **totsiens** (goodbye), **goeiemôre** (good morning) and **goeienag** (good night). Use **goeiemôre** in the morning and keep **goeienag** for when someone is heading to bed. That’s the only trap.
u1l1.a: Greet someone, say goodbye, and wish them a good morning or a good night in Afrikaans.
u1l1.n: Greetings matter a lot in South Africa. Walk into a shop and fire off your question, and it can come across as brusque. A quick **hallo** first is simply good manners.

u1l2.h: Two words that open every door: please and thank you. Hettie approves of manners, especially from people who want a snack.
u1l2.c: Ordering a coffee, asking a stranger for directions, passing the salt at a braai: every one of these goes better with a **dankie** or an **asseblief**.
u1l2.t: **Dankie** means thank you and **asseblief** means please. Then the two small answers you’ll need all the time: **ja** (yes) and **nee** (no). Put them together and you can say yes please or no thanks: **ja, asseblief** and **nee, dankie**.
u1l2.a: Ask for something politely, thank people, and answer yes or no without switching to English.
u1l2.n: **Asseblief** is a long one with a lovely rhythm. Say it in four beats and put the stress on the last: ah-suh-BLEEF.

u1l3.h: Family first! In Afrikaans homes the family words come out in the first five minutes of any conversation.
u1l3.c: Meeting a friend’s family, filling in a form, chatting to a colleague on a Monday morning: people ask about your family, and you’ll want to answer.
u1l3.t: Three words today: **ma** (mum or mom), **pa** (dad) and **baba** (baby). They’re short and they sound the way they look, so they’re a gentle start. Say each one out loud and listen to the pronunciation.
u1l3.a: Name your parents and a baby in the family, and recognise these words when you hear them.

u1l4.h: Now for the people who spoil you rotten: ouma and oupa. Then the ones who borrow your things: broer and suster.
u1l4.c: Sunday lunch at your grandparents', a photo on your phone, a story about your siblings. This is the vocabulary that makes small talk personal.
u1l4.t: **Ouma** (grandma) and **oupa** (grandpa) are what most Afrikaans families call their grandparents. Then **broer** (brother) and **suster** (sister). You’ll notice that **ouma** is simply **ma** with **ou** (old) in front. Nice shortcut.
u1l4.a: Talk about your grandparents, brothers and sisters, and understand when someone mentions theirs.
u1l4.n: Families often add **-tjie** to make things small and cute, so a little brother becomes **boetie** and a little sister **sussie**. You’ll meet those later.

u1l5.h: Time to stop collecting words and start chatting! These are whole sentences you can use today.
u1l5.c: At the start of nearly every conversation you’ll hear **Hoe gaan dit?** and you’ll want to have an answer ready. The others are for friends, family and bedtime.
u1l5.t: **Hoe gaan dit?** means how are you, and a good reply is **Goed dankie, en jy?** (good thanks, and you?). Then two warm ones: **Ek is lief vir jou.** (I love you) and **Lekker slaap!** (sleep well). Whole phrases are easier to remember than single words, because they come with a ready-made rhythm.
u1l5.a: Ask how someone is, answer, and say a friendly goodnight, all in full Afrikaans sentences.
u1l5.n: **Lekker** is one of the most useful words in the language. It means nice, tasty or enjoyable, and you can stick it on the front of almost anything.

u1l6.h: Grammar, but the friendly kind. The best news first: the little verb **is** never changes.
u1l6.c: Introducing yourself, pointing out your family in a photo, asking a stranger a polite question: you’ll use these small words in nearly every sentence you ever speak.
u1l6.t: The word for I, you, he, she, we and they is **ek, jy, hy, sy, ons, hulle**, and the verb stays **is** every time: **Ek is Anna.** and **Sy is my ouma.** For a yes-or-no question, flip them round: **Is jy Pieter?** Use **u** with older people and strangers, as in **Hoe gaan dit met u?**
u1l6.a: Say who someone is, ask a simple yes-or-no question, and pick the right polite form for the person you’re talking to.
u1l6.n: **Jy** is for one person you know well. For more than one, say **julle**. If you’re not sure whether to use **u** or **jy**, **u** is the safe choice with someone much older.

u1l7.h: Your first proper reading. It’s a short text message, and I promise it’s friendlier than most of the ones you get.
u1l7.c: Texting a grandparent, answering a family WhatsApp, reading a note on the fridge: short, warm messages are the first Afrikaans most people actually read.
u1l7.t: You’ll read a message from Anna to her grandma. You already know most of the words: **Hallo Ouma! Hoe gaan dit?** and **Lekker slaap!** There are two new ones in there, **kuier** (to visit) and **melktert**, a South African favourite, and you can work them out from the context. Read it once for the gist, then answer the questions.
u1l7.a: Read a short message in Afrikaans and answer questions about who wrote it, who it’s for and what’s planned.

u1l8.h: Unit check time! No pressure. Wrong answers just come back around so they stick.
u1l8.c: A quick check keeps the words fresh before you move on, the same way you’d revise before a visit to the family you just learned to talk about.
u1l8.t: Expect the words and sentences from this unit: greetings, family, and the **is** sentences. You’ll listen, pick, fill in gaps and put sentences in order. Anything you miss goes into your review, so nothing is wasted.
u1l8.a: See which words from this unit are solid, and which ones need another round.

u2l1.h: Welcome to the bush! My cousins are out here somewhere, and so are the big ones.
u2l1.c: On a game drive, at the zoo, in a children’s book or when someone tells you about their weekend at a game reserve, these four animals are some of the first names you’ll hear.
u2l1.t: **Olifant** (elephant), **leeu** (lion), **renoster** (rhino) and **seekoei** (hippo). The last one is a fun one: **seekoei** is literally sea cow. The words are short enough to say with a hadeda-sized shout.
u2l1.a: Name four of South Africa’s big animals and understand them when someone talks about a safari.

u2l2.h: Tall, striped and cheeky. Excellent animals for learning Afrikaans, and none of them are as noisy as me.
u2l2.c: Anywhere you’d talk about wildlife: on holiday, at a road sign, in a documentary, or when somebody points at the roadside and shouts.
u2l2.t: **Kameelperd** (giraffe), **sebra** (zebra), **volstruis** (ostrich) and **bobbejaan** (baboon). The “oe” and “ui” sounds are new for English speakers, so listen for them and copy the voice.
u2l2.a: Name four more animals and pick them out of a list, even when you only hear them.

u2l3.c: Meerkats at a wildlife park, a tortoise in a garden, a frog after rain and a bird on your stoep: these are the small things you’ll actually see in South Africa.
u2l3.t: **Stokstert** (meerkat), **skilpad** (tortoise), **padda** (frog) and **voël** (bird). The word **stokstert** is a lovely one, because it’s stick plus tail, and meerkats stand upright to keep watch, with that tail helping them balance.
u2l3.a: Name four small creatures and describe a garden or a game park a little more precisely.

u2l4.h: Now for the animals who don’t need a safari: the ones on the farm, or on your sofa.
u2l4.c: Describing a pet, chatting about a farm visit, reading a children’s story, or telling a friend that the neighbour’s dog was barking all night.
u2l4.t: **Hond** (dog), **kat** (cat), **koei** (cow), **hoender** (chicken) and **skaap** (sheep). These are everyday words, and they all have a plural that you’ll learn two lessons from now.
u2l4.a: Talk about pets and farm animals and say which one is yours.

u2l5.h: Big and small. Now we’re building sentences, not just lists. Hettie is very proud of you.
u2l5.c: Pointing at something and saying what it’s like is one of the most useful sentences in any language, from a shop (a big one or a small one?) to a zoo.
u2l5.t: **Groot** (big) and **klein** (small), used in sentences with **is**: **Die olifant is groot.** and **Die stokstert is klein.** Notice how **die** (the) comes before the animal and **is** sits in the middle. There’s also an action sentence: **Die hond blaf.**
u2l5.a: Say whether something is big or small, and build a short sentence with **die** and **is**.

u2l6.h: One dog, two dogs: the plural lesson. English adds an s. Afrikaans has more than one trick, but they’re easy.
u2l6.c: Counting your pets, talking about a farm or a flock, describing what’s on the road ahead: as soon as you talk about more than one of anything, you need the plural.
u2l6.t: Most nouns add **-e** (**hond** becomes **honde**) or **-s** (**hoender** becomes **hoenders**). The word **die** stays exactly the same for one or many. Watch the spelling, because a short vowel doubles the consonant (**kat** becomes **katte**) and a long one drops a letter (**skaap** becomes **skape**).
u2l6.a: Make most plural nouns correctly and spot the spelling change when it happens.
u2l6.n: Afrikaans nouns have no gender and no different **die** for plural. It really is simpler than English plurals, once you’ve seen the four patterns.

u2l7.h: A real-life notice, the kind you’d find on a farm gate. Read it properly, because the gate really will be left open if you don’t.
u2l7.c: Signs on gates, farm stalls and farm stays are some of the first Afrikaans you’ll actually need to read, whether it’s a warning, a welcome or a polite request.
u2l7.t: This notice says who lives on the farm and gives two instructions. You’ll recognise **koeie**, **hoenders** and **honde**, and meet **moenie** (don’t) and **maak … toe** (close). That’s a lot of real language in a few short lines.
u2l7.a: Read a simple notice, work out what you’re allowed to do, and answer questions about it.

u2l8.h: Animal unit check! If you can name them all, I’ll let you off one wing-flap of shouting.
u2l8.c: This is a quick look back at the whole unit before you move on to food: the animals, **groot** and **klein**, and the plural rule.
u2l8.t: You’ll hear and match animal names, fill the gaps in sentences and rebuild plurals like **honde** and **katte**. Anything that trips you up comes back later.
u2l8.a: Know which animal words and plural forms you’ve got, and which need another go.

u3l1.h: Breakfast! Hadedas wake up early and so does every South African with a kitchen.
u3l1.c: Ordering at a café, reading a menu, or asking what’s for breakfast at your host’s table. These are the four words you’ll see first.
u3l1.t: **Brood** (bread), **melk** (milk), **eier** (egg) and **pap**, the maize porridge that many South Africans grow up on. The word **pap** is the same in English when people talk about South African food, so it’s a very easy one.
u3l1.a: Name four breakfast foods and understand a short breakfast order.
u3l1.n: **Pap** can be soft and creamy at breakfast, or firm and served with meat at a braai. Same word either way.

u3l2.h: Fruit time! I’m very fond of a piesang, but I will not be sharing.
u3l2.c: At the market, in a supermarket aisle or in a lunch box: fruit is something you name, choose and ask for constantly.
u3l2.t: **Appel** (apple), **piesang** (banana), **lemoen** (orange) and **druiwe** (grapes). Look at the last one: **druiwe** is plural already, because you never really eat one grape. The word **lemoen** is a juicy one. It comes up everywhere, from the juice in the fridge to the orchard.
u3l2.a: Name four fruits and ask for them at a stall or a shop.

u3l3.h: Pudding lesson! These are the foods that make South Africans misty-eyed.
u3l3.c: Tea with someone’s gran, a church bazaar, a bake sale or a coffee shop display: this is the sweet corner of any Afrikaans table.
u3l3.t: **Koeksister** (a plaited, syrupy fried pastry), **melktert** (milk tart with a dusting of cinnamon), **beskuit** (rusks, made for dunking in your coffee) and **roomys** (ice cream, literally cream ice). Most of these have no English equivalent, so you simply need to taste them.
u3l3.a: Name four sweet treats and order them with confidence.
u3l3.n: A Cape Malay **koesister** is a different treat from the Afrikaner **koeksister**: it’s spiced and rolled in coconut. Ask which one before you order.

u3l4.h: This is the best lesson of the unit and I will not be taking questions. **Kom ons braai!**
u3l4.c: A braai is the heart of a South African weekend: friends, family, a fire, and far too much meat. You’ll hear these four words at nearly every one.
u3l4.t: **Braai** (barbecue, but much more than that), **boerewors** (the coiled farmers' sausage), **mielie** (corn on the cob) and **braaibroodjie** (a toasted sandwich cooked over the coals). Notice that **braai** is both a noun and a verb: you have a braai, and you braai the meat.
u3l4.a: Talk about a braai and name what’s on the grid.
u3l4.n: Heritage Day on 24 September is nicknamed Braai Day, and many South Africans really do mark it with a braai.

u3l5.h: Hungry? Thirsty? Say so! It’s the fastest way to get fed in any language.
u3l5.c: At a restaurant, at a friend’s house, or at the end of a long afternoon: these four short sentences get you fed and watered.
u3l5.t: **Ek is honger.** (I’m hungry) and **Ek is dors.** (I’m thirsty). When something tastes good, say **Dis lekker!** (It’s delicious!), and when you’d like another helping, **Nog, asseblief!** (More, please!). Remember that **dis** is a short form of **dit is**.
u3l5.a: Tell someone you’re hungry or thirsty, praise the food, and ask for seconds.

u3l6.h: How to say what you like, and how to say what you don’t. This lesson has Hettie’s favourite word: nie.
u3l6.c: Telling a host what you eat, talking about food you like, and politely turning something down: these sentences come up constantly at the table.
u3l6.t: **Ek hou van koeksisters.** is I like koeksisters. Verbs have one form for every person in the present, so it’s **ek eet, jy eet, sy eet**. To say not, put **nie** after the verb, and close the sentence with a second **nie** if more words follow: **Ek eet nie.** but **Ek hou nie van pap nie.**
u3l6.a: Say what you like and don’t like, and use the two-**nie** pattern in a negative sentence.
u3l6.n: The double **nie** is the hardest habit for English speakers, so go slowly. Listen for it in every negative sentence you hear.

u3l7.h: A recipe! Real Afrikaans, cooked over real coals. Follow the steps and nobody goes hungry.
u3l7.c: Recipes, packet instructions and braai tips are where you read Afrikaans in kitchens, in cookbooks and on food blogs.
u3l7.t: This short recipe is for a braaibroodjie. You’ll see a list of what you need and three steps, each starting with a verb: **smeer** (spread), **sit** (put) and **braai**. Recipes always use the instruction form of the verb, so they’re a great first read.
u3l7.a: Read a short recipe, follow the steps in order, and answer questions about it.

u3l8.h: Food unit check! **Kom ons kyk wat jy onthou.**
u3l8.c: A short look back at food, likes and dislikes before the next unit, just like glancing at the menu before you order.
u3l8.t: You’ll see the foods, the **hou van** sentences and the double **nie** again. Listen, pick, fill gaps, and put sentences in order. Anything you miss comes back for another try.
u3l8.a: See which food words and sentences are solid.

u4l1.h: Colours! Three of them first, because I’m a hadeda and I like to keep things simple.
u4l1.c: Describing a shirt, choosing paint, giving directions by a house, or reading a traffic light: colours turn a bare description into a vivid one.
u4l1.t: **Rooi** (red), **blou** (blue) and **geel** (yellow). Three of the colours you see on every South African taxi, shop sign and flag.
u4l1.a: Name red, blue and yellow, and hear them in sentences.

u4l2.h: More colours, and here’s one that looks like a fruit: oranje.
u4l2.c: Describing food, clothes and nature: the green of a hillside, the orange of a sunset, a purple jacket that someone’s very proud of.
u4l2.t: **Groen** (green), **oranje** (orange) and **pers** (purple). Notice that **oranje** is the colour, while **lemoen** is the fruit, even though English uses one word for both.
u4l2.a: Name green, orange and purple and tell a fruit from a colour.

u4l3.h: Pienk and bruin: bubblegum and braai-coal, if you ask me.
u4l3.c: Describing your hair, a shirt, a puppy or a plate of food. Brown especially comes up more than you’d think.
u4l3.t: **Pienk** (pink) and **bruin** (brown). Both words sound a lot like the English, so you won’t forget them. Say **bruin** with the Afrikaans “ui” sound, and copy the voice.
u4l3.a: Name pink and brown and use them to describe everyday things.

u4l4.h: Swart en wit: the colours of a zebra, and the first two colours I ever learned.
u4l4.c: Describing a pet, a photograph, a football team or a cow in a field. Black and white show up on road signs too.
u4l4.t: **Swart** (black) and **wit** (white). Remember that in Afrikaans “w” sounds like an English “v”, so **wit** is close to “vit”.
u4l4.a: Name black and white and recognise them quickly.

u4l5.h: Now put those colours to work. Whole sentences, no hiding.
u4l5.c: Pointing at things and describing them: a ripe banana at the market, a zebra in a picture book, an apple in a lunch box.
u4l5.t: Follow the pattern **Die piesang is geel.** and **Die appel is rooi.** Once you know the pattern (die + noun + is + colour), you can describe almost anything. There’s a nice one with two colours: **Die sebra is swart en wit.**
u4l5.a: Say what colour something is in a full sentence.

u4l6.h: Bigger, biggest, best. Comparing is one of life’s great pleasures, and Afrikaans does it neatly.
u4l6.c: Choosing between two jerseys, saying who is taller, naming the best coffee shop in town: comparing is how you give opinions.
u4l6.t: To compare, add **-er** and use **as** for than: **Die olifant is groter as die renoster.** For the most, use **die** and **-ste**: **die langste dier**. One word breaks the rules: **goed** becomes **beter** and **die beste**. Colours can also go before the noun, as in **Ek soek 'n blou hemp.**
u4l6.a: Compare two things, name the biggest or the best, and use a colour before a noun.
u4l6.n: Watch the spelling: **lank** becomes **langer** and **die langste**, not "lankker". Just listen to the examples and copy the sound.

u4l7.h: Somebody has lost a cat! Time to be a detective. Mielie is orange, and she’s friendly.
u4l7.c: A lost-pet notice on a lamp post or in a community group is a very South African text. It’s short, practical and full of useful detail.
u4l7.t: This notice describes the cat using colours and sizes you know: **klein**, **oranje** and **wit**. It also gives a name, a day and an address. Look for **sedert** (since) and **Bring haar asseblief** (please bring her).
u4l7.a: Read a lost-pet notice and pick out who, what and where.

u4l8.h: Last one for this unit! Show me those colours and comparisons.
u4l8.c: One more round of colours and comparing before you carry on to numbers, the way a quick glance back helps you remember where the shop was.
u4l8.t: You’ll listen, match and rebuild sentences with the colours, **groter as**, **die langste** and **die beste**. The ones that go wrong come back later.
u4l8.a: Know which colours and comparisons you have down.

u5l1.h: Een, twee, drie! Hettie can count to three in her sleep. She often does.
u5l1.c: Counting people for a table, asking for two coffees, reading a house number: numbers are some of the first words you’ll use.
u5l1.t: **Een** (one), **twee** (two) and **drie** (three). The “ee” in **een** and **twee** is a long one, like the “ay” in “say”. Listen to all three before you try them.
u5l1.a: Count to three and recognise the numbers when you hear them.

u5l2.h: Four, five, six. The middle bit. Keep going, and don’t skip any.
u5l2.c: Telling someone your age, ordering a round of drinks, reading a time or a bus number: you’ll need the middle numbers a lot.
u5l2.t: **Vier** (four), **vyf** (five) and **ses** (six). Remember that “v” sounds like an English “f”, so **vyf** sounds like “fayf” and **vier** is a bit like “feer”.
u5l2.a: Count from four to six and use these numbers in short sentences.

u5l3.h: Sewe tot tien! The end of the line, and then you can count to ten.
u5l3.c: Saying a phone number, asking for the price of something or telling a friend you’ll be there in ten minutes.
u5l3.t: **Sewe** (seven), **agt** (eight), **nege** (nine) and **tien** (ten). With these you can count all the way to ten. The word **nege** has a throaty “g” that comes from right at the back of your throat.
u5l3.a: Count to ten and recognise each number by ear.
u5l3.n: The Afrikaans “g” is a scratchy sound from the back of the throat, a bit like the end of “loch”. It takes practice, so be patient with it.

u5l4.h: **Kom ons tel!** Counting out loud is the best way to make numbers stick.
u5l4.c: Counting up the family, a pile of braai wood or the steps to the front door: counting out loud is where numbers become automatic.
u5l4.t: You’ll practise the numbers in no particular order: **een, twee, vyf, ses** and **tien**. Say each one aloud as you hear it, and try to answer before the audio finishes.
u5l4.a: Recognise and say the numbers one to ten quickly, in any order.

u5l5.h: How old are you? How many do you have? Two questions that make Afrikaans real.
u5l5.c: Getting to know somebody: how old they are, how many brothers they have, how big the family is. This is classic small talk, and it’s the next step after greetings.
u5l5.t: **Hoe oud is jy?** means how old are you, and you answer with **Ek is …** and a number. **Ek het drie broers.** says I have three brothers. Look at **hoeveel** (how many) and **het** (have). The word **het** is important, and we’ll use it a lot.
u5l5.a: Ask someone’s age, say your own, and say how many of something you have.

u5l6.h: Question words: the pocket tools for asking anything you like. This is the grammar that makes you a real conversationalist.
u5l6.c: Asking where someone lives, when their birthday is, how many kids they have or why they’re laughing: these are the questions that turn a hello into a conversation.
u5l6.t: Put the question word first, then the verb, then the person: **Waar woon jy?** and **Wanneer verjaar jy?** The words you need are **wat, wie, waar, wanneer, hoe, hoeveel, watter** and **hoekom**. Yes-or-no questions simply start with the verb: **Het jy 'n hond?**
u5l6.a: Ask who, what, where, when, how and why in Afrikaans, in the right word order.
u5l6.n: Afrikaans never says "do you" the way English does. **Het jy 'n hond?** is simply have you a dog, and that’s the whole question.

u5l7.h: A short conversation between two friends. Listen in, nosy is fine.
u5l7.c: Overhearing and joining a dialogue is how most language really happens. Here Thandi and Pieter chat about brothers, sisters and dogs.
u5l7.t: You’ll read a dialogue with questions and answers: **Hoe oud is jou sussie?** and **Hoeveel honde het julle?** Spot the numbers, the question words and the **is** sentences, which you now know well.
u5l7.a: Read a short dialogue, follow who says what and answer questions about it.

u5l8.h: The last check of the Beginner level! You’ve come a long way, and I’m not even crying. Much.
u5l8.c: This unit check covers numbers and questions, and it’s the last stop before Graad 1.
u5l8.t: Expect the numbers, **hoeveel** and **waar** questions, and **Het jy 'n hond?**-type questions. Listen, match, fill gaps and order sentences. Take your time.
u5l8.a: Check that you can count to ten and ask the basic questions in Afrikaans.

g00u01l01.h: Rise and shine, or at least rise and shout. Mornings are my favourite time to be loud, so let’s learn how to talk about the day.
g00u01l01.c: Talking about your day is one of the first real conversations you’ll have: with a colleague over coffee, a new neighbour, or the person you share a kitchen with.
g00u01l01.t: Three parts of the day: **die oggend** (the morning), **die middag** (the afternoon) and **die aand** (the evening). Then three meals and a room: **die ontbyt** (breakfast), **die aandete** (dinner, supper) and **die kombuis** (the kitchen). Each starts with **die**, which means the.
g00u01l01.a: Name the parts of the day and two meals, and say where in the house the food happens.
g00u01l01.n: Afrikaans has a separate word for the evening meal, **aandete**, which is literally evening-eat. It’s a very practical language.

g00u01l02.h: Now for what you do with the day. This is where Afrikaans starts to feel like a real, living language.
g00u01l02.c: At the office, at a gym, in a group chat: everyone asks what your day is like. You’ll use these verbs to give a quick, natural answer.
g00u01l02.t: Four everyday sentences: **Ek word om sesuur wakker.** (I wake up at six), **Ek stort elke oggend.** (I shower every morning), **Ek eet ontbyt in die kombuis.** and **Ek gaan om agtuur werk toe.** Notice that the verbs sit in the same place each time: right after **ek**.
g00u01l02.a: Describe a few things you do in a day, in a full sentence each.

g00u01l03.h: What time is it? Hettie asks a lot. Mostly about snack time.
g00u01l03.c: Making plans, catching a bus, confirming a meeting or a dinner: time is part of nearly every plan you’ll ever make.
g00u01l03.t: **Hoe laat is dit?** asks what time it is, and **Dit is sewe-uur.** answers it. Then two more sentences with times in them: **Ek kom om vyfuur tuis.** and **Ek gaan om tienuur slaap.** Notice **om**, which means at.
g00u01l03.a: Ask what time it is, tell someone the hour, and say when you do something.

g00u01l04.h: Grammar time, and there’s a small trick with hyphens that catches everyone out once. Now you’ll know it in advance.
g00u01l04.c: Reading a timetable, arranging a meeting or a lunch, or catching a bus: you’ll use these patterns in every plan you make.
g00u01l04.t: To say at eight, use **om agtuur**. The number and **uur** are written together (**vieruur, sesuur**), but when two vowels meet you add a hyphen: **twee-uur, drie-uur, sewe-uur**. The time usually follows the verb, as in **Die winkel maak om agtuur oop.** If you start with the time, the verb jumps in second: **Om sewe-uur eet ons aandete.**
g00u01l04.a: Say at what time something happens, write the hour correctly and put the time at the front of a sentence.
g00u01l04.n: That second pattern, where the verb always sits second, is one of the big rules of Afrikaans word order. You’ll meet it again and again.

g00u01l05.h: Here’s Mia’s message to Sipho. Listen first, read second, then tell me about your own day. I’ll pretend I’m not nosy.
g00u01l05.c: A friendly message with an invitation in it is the kind of text you’ll get from friends and colleagues, and this one has times, plans and a dinner invitation.
g00u01l05.t: Mia tells Sipho when she wakes up, when she goes to work and when she gets home, then invites him to dinner. Look for the times (**om sesuur**, **om sewe-uur**, **om vyfuur**) and for **Kom eet vanaand saam met ons.** (Come and eat with us tonight.) After the questions, you’ll tell us about your own day in three sentences.
g00u01l05.a: Understand a short message with times and an invitation, and tell someone about your own day.

g00u01l06.h: Day-and-time check! Let’s see how well you’ve got the clock.
g00u01l06.c: A quick check on telling the time before you move on to the days of the week.
g00u01l06.t: Expect to hear and rebuild sentences with **om**, the hours and the daily verbs, such as **Ek word om sesuur wakker.** and **Die bus kom om drie-uur.** Take your time with the spelling of the hours.
g00u01l06.a: See which time sentences you’ve got, and which need another go.

g00u02l01.h: Monday to Thursday! Days of the week are the first thing everybody wants in any language.
g00u02l01.c: Booking a table, agreeing on a meeting, arranging a lift: nothing happens without a day to hang it on.
g00u02l01.t: **Maandag** (Monday), **Dinsdag** (Tuesday), **Woensdag** (Wednesday) and **Donderdag** (Thursday). In Afrikaans the days always start with a capital letter. Listen to **Woensdag** carefully: the “w” sounds like a “v”.
g00u02l01.a: Name Monday to Thursday and recognise each when you hear it.

g00u02l02.h: The best days of the week! Friday through Sunday, and I have strong opinions about all three.
g00u02l02.c: Making weekend plans: a braai on Saturday, a lazy Sunday, a lift home on Friday. This is the vocabulary of weekends.
g00u02l02.t: **Vrydag** (Friday), **Saterdag** (Saturday), **Sondag** (Sunday) and **die naweek** (the weekend). Then two sentences: **Ek werk van Maandag tot Vrydag.** (I work from Monday to Friday) and **Op Saterdag speel ek sokker.** (On Saturday I play soccer).
g00u02l02.a: Name the weekend days and say what you do from Monday to Friday and on a Saturday.

g00u02l03.h: Yesterday, today, tomorrow. Time is a lot easier when you can pin it to a day.
g00u02l03.c: Telling a friend what happened yesterday, what’s on today, or what you’ll do tomorrow is the heart of everyday conversation.
g00u02l03.t: **Gister was Sondag.** (Yesterday was Sunday) and **Môre is Dinsdag.** (Tomorrow is Tuesday). Then two questions and plans: **Wat doen jy die naweek?** and **Ons kuier Sondag by Ouma.** The little word **was** is just the past of **is**.
g00u02l03.a: Talk about yesterday, today and tomorrow, and ask someone what they’re doing this weekend.

g00u02l04.h: Grammar for days. Simple, but very handy, because every plan you make has a day in it.
g00u02l04.c: Arranging a meeting, telling someone your shop is closed on Sunday, talking about next week’s leave: all of these use the day patterns.
g00u02l04.t: "On Monday" is **op Maandag**, or just **Maandag**, as in **Ons het Woensdag 'n vergadering.** "From … to …" is **van … tot …**. For the past, use **was**: **Gister was Sondag.** And **Die winkel is Sondag toe.** means that the shop is closed on Sunday.
g00u02l04.a: Say on which day something happens, give a range of days and talk about yesterday.

g00u02l05.h: Lindi has written to Ben. Listen, read, then tell me about your own week. I love a good week report.
g00u02l05.c: Friendly messages with an invitation, like this one, are what you’ll get from colleagues and friends all the time.
g00u02l05.t: Lindi says when she works, when she plays soccer and when she’s free, then asks Ben for coffee: **Kom ons drink Sondag koffie?** Notice **Lekker naweek!** at the end, which is how many South Africans sign off on a Friday. After the questions, tell us about your own week in three sentences.
g00u02l05.a: Read a short message about someone’s week and tell someone about yours.

g00u02l06.h: Week check! Seven days, plus a couple of sentences. You’ve got this.
g00u02l06.c: One last check on the days of the week before you move on to the next level.
g00u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences about days, such as **Ek werk van Maandag tot Vrydag.** and **Gister was Sondag.** The ones you miss come back later.
g00u02l06.a: See which days and week sentences you’ve got.

g01u01l01.h: Feathers are my entire wardrobe, so I’ve had to learn about clothes from you lot. Let’s get dressed in Afrikaans!
g01u01l01.c: Packing a bag, shopping for something to wear, getting ready for work or answering "what are you wearing?" in a message: clothes come up in everyday life far more than you expect.
g01u01l01.t: Six pieces of clothing, each with **die** in front: **die hemp** (shirt), **die broek** (trousers), **die rok** (dress), **die trui** (jersey), **die baadjie** (jacket) and **die hoed** (hat). Learn the word together with **die**, because that’s the way you’ll hear it.
g01u01l01.a: Name six items of clothing and understand them in a shop or a message.
g01u01l01.n: South Africans say **trui** for a jumper or jersey, and you’ll hear it a lot in winter, especially on the Highveld, when mornings are cold.

g01u01l02.h: Put it on, take it off, and where on earth is my jersey? Short commands and short questions.
g01u01l02.c: Getting ready in the morning, telling a child to put a coat on, or asking a housemate where something went: these are everyday sentences.
g01u01l02.t: **Trek … aan** means put on and **trek … uit** means take off, with the thing in the middle: **Trek jou baadjie aan, dis koud.** and **Trek asseblief jou skoene uit.** Then **Waar is my trui?** and **Wat is dit? Dis 'n hoed.** Two more clothes words come along: **die skoene** (shoes) and **die sokkies** (socks).
g01u01l02.a: Tell someone to put on or take off an item of clothing, and ask where something is.

g01u01l03.h: Grammar: more than one, and whose is it? You’ll need both every single day.
g01u01l03.c: Counting what’s in your wardrobe, saying whose hat is on the table, telling someone that the shoes are too small: you can’t get through a day without plurals and "whose".
g01u01l03.t: Plurals: most short words add **-e** (**skoen** becomes **skoene**) and words ending in **-ie** add **-s** (**sokkie** becomes **sokkies**). After a short vowel the last letter doubles: **rok** becomes **rokke**. For whose, use **my, jou, sy, haar, ons**, and for a name use **se**: **Pa se hoed is op die tafel.**
g01u01l03.a: Make plurals of everyday words and say whose something is.
g01u01l03.n: The little word **se** is a lovely shortcut. It does the job of the English 's, so **Mia se trui** is simply Mia’s jersey.

g01u01l04.h: A message from Ma, and she’s packing a bag for the sea. Read it like you’re the one going on holiday.
g01u01l04.c: Packing lists, holiday plans and a mother with strong views about warm jackets: this is a message you could actually receive.
g01u01l04.t: Sam’s mum tells him what to pack for the seaside, how many of each thing, and what not to forget. Look for **Pak asseblief jou tas** (please pack your bag), **Moenie … vergeet nie** (don’t forget …) and the numbers before each clothing word. After the questions, you’ll say what you’re wearing today.
g01u01l04.a: Read a short message with instructions, and say three sentences about what you’re wearing.

g01u01l05.h: Your turn to write. Three sentences, three bits of clothing, no pressure from me. I’m only a hadeda with an opinion.
g01u01l05.c: Describing what you’re wearing is useful when you’re meeting someone you’ve never met, or when you’re sending a photo and want to caption it.
g01u01l05.t: Write three sentences about what you’re wearing today. You can borrow the shapes you’ve seen: **Ek het 'n … aan.** or **My hemp is …**. After you write, you’ll see a model answer, and you can tick off a checklist to see how yours compares.
g01u01l05.a: Write a few short sentences about your clothes and check your own work against a model.

g01u01l06.h: Clothes check! Dress for success, as they say. Wait, that’s in English. Let’s find out.
g01u01l06.c: A quick look back at clothes, instructions and plurals before the next unit.
g01u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with the plurals (**hemde**, **rokke**, **sokkies**), the **trek aan / trek uit** instructions and the whose-pattern **Pa se hoed**. Take your time.
g01u01l06.a: See which clothes words and patterns you’ve got, and which are worth another round.

g01u02l01.h: Everybody loses keys. Even birds, because we lose the plot. Let’s learn the words for where it all goes.
g01u02l01.c: Moving in, talking about your home or describing a room: these household nouns are the ones you’ll use when you tell someone where something is.
g01u02l01.t: Six things around the house: **die tafel** (table), **die bank** (couch), **die kas** (cupboard), **die laai** (drawer), **die sak** (bag) and **die deur** (door). Notice that **die kas** can also be a wardrobe, so the context tells you which.
g01u02l01.a: Name six everyday things in a home and understand them in a sentence.

g01u02l02.h: Waar is my sleutels? It’s the question that sums up most mornings. Today we learn to ask it and answer it.
g01u02l02.c: Asking a housemate where your keys are, helping someone find a phone, or telling a guest where to put their bag: this is practical Afrikaans.
g01u02l02.t: **Waar is …?** asks where something is, and you answer with a place word: **Hulle is op die tafel.** (on), **Is dit onder die bank?** (under), **Die sak is agter die deur.** (behind) and **My foon lê langs die bed.** (next to). Add **die bed** (bed) to your list, and the polite request **Sit dit asseblief in die laai.**
g01u02l02.a: Ask where something is and say where it is with in, op, onder, agter and langs.

g01u02l03.h: Grammar with a surprise: in Afrikaans, things don’t just "be" somewhere. They lie, stand and hang.
g01u02l03.c: Describing a room, giving directions to the thing you left behind, writing a note for a guest: you’ll want to say exactly how something is placed.
g01u02l03.t: Flat things **lê** (lie): **Die boek lê op die tafel.** Upright things **staan** (stand): **Die bottel staan in die kas.** Things on a hanger **hang**: **Die hemp hang in die kas.** People and cats usually **sit**. If you’re unsure, **is** is always correct. Add place words like **in, op, onder, langs, agter, voor** and **tussen**.
g01u02l03.a: Describe where things are using lê, staan, hang and sit, and a place word.
g01u02l03.n: Don’t panic about picking the "right" verb. Native speakers will understand **is** every time, and the others will come naturally as you hear them.

g01u02l04.h: A note left on the table by Thandi. In Afrikaans, of course. Read it like you’re the one coming home.
g01u02l04.c: Notes about keys, food and where to find things are the most real Afrikaans at home. You’ll see them on fridges, tables and WhatsApp groups.
g01u02l04.t: Thandi tells a visitor where the key is and where the food is. Watch for the place words **onder, in, op** and the verbs **staan** and **lê**, which you’ve just seen. After the questions, look round your room and say where three things are.
g01u02l04.a: Follow a note that tells you where things are, and say where things are in your own room.

g01u02l05.h: Now you leave the note! Be a good host. Tell your visitor where the key is and where the food is.
g01u02l05.c: When a friend or a family member is coming to your home and you’re out, a short written note is the most polite way to help them.
g01u02l05.t: Write a short message saying where the key is and where the food is. Use the place words (**onder, in, op**) and **lê** or **staan**, and don’t forget **asseblief** and a friendly sign-off. After you write, compare your note to the model.
g01u02l05.a: Write a short, friendly note that tells someone where things are.

g01u02l06.h: Where-is-it check! Let’s see whether you know where everything lives.
g01u02l06.c: One more round on the house, the place words and the way things lie, stand and hang before the next unit.
g01u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **onder, agter, op, tussen** and the verbs **lê, staan** and **hang**. If you miss a few, they’ll come back in your review.
g01u02l06.a: See whether you can say where things are, and which sentences need another go.

g01u03l01.h: Head, shoulders, knees and… feet. A hadeda knows her body parts. Here are six of yours in Afrikaans.
g01u03l01.c: At the doctor, at the gym, in a yoga class or when you’re telling someone that your back hurts: body words are among the most useful you’ll learn.
g01u03l01.t: **Die kop** (head), **die arm** (arm), **die been** (leg), **die hand** (hand), **die voet** (foot) and **die rug** (back). Note that **die been** is a leg, not a bone in this lesson. The plurals are slightly irregular, so listen carefully.
g01u03l01.a: Name six parts of the body and understand them in a sentence about a sore spot.

g01u03l02.h: Can you swim? I can fly, but I’m hopeless at swimming. Let’s talk about what you can do.
g01u03l02.c: Signing up for a class, answering at a doctor’s surgery, telling friends what hurts: sentences about what you can do and what hurts come up in real life.
g01u03l02.t: **Kan jy swem?** asks if you can swim, and **Ja, ek kan swem.** says you can. To say you can’t, use two **nie**: **Ek kan nie sing nie.** Other sentences are about health: **My rug is seer.** (My back is sore), **Hy het sy been gebreek.** and **Was jou hande.** Add **die oë** (eyes) and **die ore** (ears) to your list.
g01u03l02.a: Say what you can and can’t do, and tell someone something hurts.

g01u03l03.h: Grammar: can and can’t. The little word **kan** changes where the other verb sits.
g01u03l03.c: Asking for help, saying what you’re able to do, explaining why you can’t come: **kan** is one of the most useful verbs you’ll ever learn.
g01u03l03.t: With **kan**, the other verb goes to the end: **Sy kan baie vinnig hardloop.** For a question, start with **kan**: **Kan jy my help?** For can’t, use two **nie**: **Ons kan nie vandag kom nie.** and **Ek kan nie my bril kry nie.**
g01u03l03.a: Say what you can and can’t do, ask someone for help and use the double **nie** with **kan**.
g01u03l03.n: Pushing the second verb to the end is a classic Afrikaans habit. It feels odd at first and then feels perfectly natural.

g01u03l04.h: A notice for a yoga class in the park. If you can’t touch your toes, don’t worry. I can’t either.
g01u03l04.c: Community notices on a lamp post, a gym board or a neighbourhood group are the kind of text where you’ll practise everyday Afrikaans.
g01u03l04.t: The notice invites you to a yoga class: when, what to bring and who to ask. You’ll meet **elke Saterdag** (every Saturday), **gratis** (free) and **Geen probleem nie!** (No problem!). After the questions, you’ll say what you can and can’t do.
g01u03l04.a: Read a short notice for an activity and say what you can and can’t do.

g01u03l05.h: Write what you can do. Two sentences about yes, two about no, and no excuses from anybody.
g01u03l05.c: Describing your abilities is useful when you’re filling in a form, joining a club or chatting to someone new.
g01u03l05.t: Write four sentences: two things you can do (**Ek kan …**) and two things you can’t (**Ek kan nie … nie**). Remember the double **nie** at the end, and the verb that goes to the end after **kan**.
g01u03l05.a: Write sentences about what you can and can’t do, using **kan** and the double **nie**.

g01u03l06.h: Body-and-abilities check! Show me what you’ve got, and watch the double nie.
g01u03l06.c: A final run through the body, the "can" sentences and the "sore" sentences before the next unit.
g01u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **kan**, **kan nie … nie**, and the body words. Listen for the verb at the end.
g01u03l06.a: See which can/can’t sentences are solid and which need another round.

g01u04l01.h: Tall, short, old, new, fast, slow: the describing words that let you say what something is actually like.
g01u04l01.c: Describing a person, a car, a train or a coffee queue: these six words give your sentences colour.
g01u04l01.t: **Lank** (tall or long), **kort** (short), **oud** (old), **nuut** (new), **vinnig** (fast) and **stadig** (slow, slowly). They go together in pairs, and each pair is a pair of opposites, so they’re easier to remember.
g01u04l01.a: Describe people and things with six pairs of everyday adjectives.

g01u04l02.h: My car’s old, the train’s new and the bus is slow. Let’s put the describing words into sentences.
g01u04l02.c: Describing your car, your friend, your commute or the bus that always runs late. Describing words are a daily habit.
g01u04l02.t: After **is**, the word stays as it is: **My kar is oud.** Before a noun, it can change: **Ek het 'n ou kar.** and **Die nuwe trein is baie vinnig.** Notice **Die lang man is my oom.**, with **lank** becoming **lang**. Also: **Die bus ry stadig.**
g01u04l02.a: Say what something is like in a sentence and use the describing word before a noun.

g01u04l03.h: Grammar: the describing word that changes shape. It’s like a hadeda in a hat. Same bird, slightly different look.
g01u04l03.c: Whenever you describe something, you choose between "the car is old" and "the old car". Knowing both forms means your sentences sound natural.
g01u04l03.t: After **is**, the basic form: **Die kos is koud.** Before a noun, many change: **koue kos, 'n goeie idee, die ou kar, die nuwe trein**. Short, common words such as **groot** and **klein** don’t change. Learn the changes in pairs: **oud** becomes **ou**, **lank** becomes **lang**, **nuut** becomes **nuwe**, **goed** becomes **goeie**, **koud** becomes **koue**.
g01u04l03.a: Choose the right form of a describing word before a noun and after **is**.
g01u04l03.n: Many of these changes just add an **-e** at the end. You’ll get a feel for it quickly once you’ve seen a handful of pairs.

g01u04l04.h: Riddles! Raai, raai! I’ll give you the clues. You work out whether it’s me.
g01u04l04.c: Riddles are a classic children’s game, and they’re also a clever way to practise describing things, because the clues have to be precise.
g01u04l04.t: Three riddles, each describing a thing with a few short sentences and ending with **Wat is ek?** (What am I?). Look for describing words such as **groot, grys, klein, vinnig** and **lang**. After the questions, you’ll make up your own riddle.
g01u04l04.a: Solve simple riddles and make one up yourself, in three short sentences.

g01u04l05.h: Describe someone in your family. Be kind. They might read it.
g01u04l05.c: Describing a person is something you’ll do all the time: introducing a friend, talking about a relative, or helping someone spot a person in a crowd.
g01u04l05.t: Write three or four sentences about someone in your family. Use describing words from this unit: **lank, kort, oud, jonk** or **vinnig**. Remember that the word changes before a noun, as in **my lang broer**.
g01u04l05.a: Write a short description of a person, using describing words correctly.

g01u04l06.h: Describing check! Is it oud or ou? Let’s find out.
g01u04l06.c: A last look at describing words before the next unit: the pairs, the two forms and the sentences.
g01u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die lang man is my oom.** and **Ek hou nie van koue kos nie.** Pay attention to which form you need.
g01u04l06.a: See whether you can choose the right form of a describing word.

g01u05l01.h: Laying the table: the nicest bit of any meal is when everyone finally sits down. Words for the table.
g01u05l01.c: Setting a table, asking for a fork at a restaurant, or helping at a family braai: you’ll use these table words at any meal.
g01u05l01.t: **Die glas** (glass), **die koppie** (cup), **die bord** (plate), **die suiker** (sugar), **die servet** (napkin) and **die vurk** (fork). Notice that **koppie** is a little cup, because **-ie** means small.
g01u05l01.a: Name six things on a table and ask for one of them.

g01u05l02.h: Another cup of tea? Of course. This is the Afrikaans that gets you fed and watered, politely.
g01u05l02.c: At a café, at a family lunch, at work when someone’s making the tea: a polite request is the easiest way to start a friendly chat.
g01u05l02.t: **Mag ek asseblief 'n glas water kry?** (May I please have a glass of water?) and **Kan ek nog 'n koppie tee kry?** (Can I have another cup of tea?) are your two polite starters. Add **Hoeveel koppies is daar?** and **Daar is vyf borde op die tafel.** to count what’s on the table, and **Gee my asseblief die suiker aan.** to ask for something to be passed.
g01u05l02.a: Ask politely for something to eat or drink, and ask how many of something there are.

g01u05l03.h: Grammar: asking nicely. Hettie believes manners make the world go round, and also get you extra seeds.
g01u05l03.c: Ordering in a restaurant, asking a favour at work, asking permission in someone’s home: asking nicely opens doors.
g01u05l03.t: **Mag ek …?** asks permission: **Mag ek die venster toemaak?** **Kan ek … kry?** asks for something, and **Ek wil graag … hê** says what you’d like: **Ons wil graag 'n tafel vir vier hê.** To ask someone to do something, use **Kan jy asseblief …?** and put the action word last. After **mag, kan** and **wil**, you use **hê**.
g01u05l03.a: Ask for things, ask permission and ask someone to do something, politely.
g01u05l03.n: Notice how many polite openers there are. Afrikaans is a warm language, and people usually soften a request.

g01u05l04.h: A menu from a little café. Reading a menu is the most useful kind of reading, because it ends in food.
g01u05l04.c: A menu is one of the first Afrikaans texts you’ll truly need: at a café, a rest stop on a road trip or a family restaurant.
g01u05l04.t: The Fynbos Kafee menu lists drinks and food with prices in rand (the R). You’ll see **koffie, tee** and **rooibostee**, **roosterbrood** (toast) and **pannekoek** (pancake). The last line, **Vra gerus vir 'n glas water.**, means you’re welcome to ask for water. After the questions, order something yourself.
g01u05l04.a: Read a simple menu, find the price of something, and order food and a drink.

g01u05l05.h: You’re ill, the flatmate’s heading to the shop, and you need three things. Write the message. Be polite. I’ll wait.
g01u05l05.c: Asking for help in writing is a very real everyday task: to a flatmate, a neighbour or a family member who’s on their way to the shops.
g01u05l05.t: Write a short message that asks for three things. Use **asseblief** and one of the polite openers you’ve learned: **Kan jy asseblief … vir my bring?** or **Ek wil graag … hê.** Finish with **dankie**.
g01u05l05.a: Write a short, polite message asking for three things.

g01u05l06.h: Please-and-thank-you check! Let’s see whether your manners survived.
g01u05l06.c: A last practice of table words and polite requests before you meet the weather.
g01u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild polite sentences such as **Mag ek die venster toemaak?** and **Ons wil graag 'n tafel vir vier hê.** and the table words. Take your time with word order.
g01u05l06.a: See whether your polite requests are in good shape.

g01u06l01.h: Sun, rain, wind, clouds, and one umbrella. Let’s talk about the weather, the most universal small talk there is.
g01u06l01.c: Small talk with a neighbour, planning a braai, deciding what to wear: weather is the first thing people mention.
g01u06l01.t: **Die weer** (the weather), **die son** (sun), **die reën** (rain), **die wind** (wind), **die wolke** (clouds) and **die sambreel** (umbrella). The word **reën** has two dots over the **e**, because the two **e**s are pronounced separately.
g01u06l01.a: Name six weather words and understand a short comment about the weather.

g01u06l02.h: Dit reën! Let’s learn how to complain about it, and how to be cheerful about it too.
g01u06l02.c: Greeting a neighbour, choosing a jacket, checking in with a friend: a few words about the weather are a perfect opener.
g01u06l02.t: **Hoe is die weer vandag?** asks about today. **Dit reën en dis koud.**, **Die son skyn.** and **Die wind waai baie sterk.** describe it. For advice, **Vat jou sambreel saam.**, and for tomorrow, **Môre gaan dit warm wees.** Notice **dis**, the short form of **dit is**.
g01u06l02.a: Ask about the weather, describe today’s weather and say what it’s going to do tomorrow.

g01u06l03.h: Grammar: weather and seasons. Warning: in the southern hemisphere, summer is in December.
g01u06l03.c: Weather and seasons come up when you plan a holiday, talk about the climate or chat to someone in another country.
g01u06l03.t: Weather sentences begin with **dit**: **Dit reën.** For later, use **gaan** with the action word at the end: **Dit gaan die hele week reën.** The seasons are **somer, herfs, winter** and **lente**, as in **In Desember is dit somer.** and **Die lente begin in September.**
g01u06l03.a: Talk about the weather now and later and name the four seasons.
g01u06l03.n: South Africa and Australia are both in the southern hemisphere, so the seasons are the reverse of Europe’s. Summer starts in December.

g01u06l04.h: A weather report for four cities. Pack your umbrella. Or don’t, and see.
g01u06l04.c: Weather reports in the news, on the radio and on weather apps use this kind of short, clear language.
g01u06l04.t: The report covers Cape Town, Durban, Johannesburg and Perth, with the weather and the temperature for each. Look for **koud en nat** (cold and wet), **sonnig** (sunny), **koel** (cool), **warm** and **grade** (degrees). After the questions, tell us about the weather where you are.
g01u06l04.a: Read a short weather report and say what the weather is like where you are.

g01u06l05.h: Write a note to a friend about the weather where you are. Throw in what you’re doing, too.
g01u06l05.c: A quick message about the weather and your plans is a classic, friendly thing to send: to a friend, a cousin or a colleague on another continent.
g01u06l05.t: Write a short message saying what the weather is like and what you’re doing today. Use weather sentences such as **Dit reën.** or **Die son skyn.**, then add a plan with **gaan**: **Ons gaan …**.
g01u06l05.a: Write a short message about the weather and your plans.

g01u06l06.h: The final check in Graad 1! Weather and seasons, and a whole unit’s worth of practice.
g01u06l06.c: One last look at the weather before you move on to Graad 2.
g01u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die son skyn.** and **Die lente begin in September.** and the **dit gaan** pattern. Pay attention to the verbs at the end.
g01u06l06.a: See which weather sentences you’ve got, and which are worth another round.

g02u01l01.h: So far you’ve lived in the present. Time to go back in time! Six verbs that let you say what you did.
g02u01l01.c: Monday morning at the office, a catch-up with a friend, a message to your gran: "What did you do at the weekend?" is one of the most common questions in any language.
g02u01l01.t: Each verb comes with its past form: **werk** becomes **het gewerk**, **kook** becomes **het gekook**, **lees** becomes **het gelees**, **stap** becomes **het gestap**, **speel** becomes **het gespeel** and **koop** becomes **het gekoop**. The pattern is **het** plus the verb with **ge-** in front.
g02u01l01.a: Say six everyday verbs in the past tense.

g02u01l02.h: Wat het jy gedoen? Now you can answer, with full sentences. Be honest. I won’t judge. Much.
g02u01l02.c: Chatting with a colleague on a Monday or telling a friend about your Saturday: you’ll hear and say sentences like these all the time.
g02u01l02.t: Listen to how the **ge-** word sits at the end of the sentence: **Ek het gister tot laat gewerk.** and **Ons het pasta gekook.** **Sy het die hele boek gelees.** and **Hulle het op die strand gestap.** For a question, **het** moves to the front: **Het jy Saterdag tennis gespeel?**
g02u01l02.a: Tell someone what you did yesterday or at the weekend, and ask them the same.

g02u01l03.h: Grammar: the past tense. One easy rule, one small exception, and a very useful word: was.
g02u01l03.c: Telling a story, explaining why you’re late, giving a quick update on your weekend: the past tense is the way you talk about everything that has already happened.
g02u01l03.t: For the past, use **het** and put **ge-** in front of the verb, which goes to the end: **Ek het gewerk.** Verbs starting with **be-, ver-, her-** or **ont-** don’t take **ge-**: **Ek het my ouma besoek.** and **Ek het my sleutels vergeet.** **Is** becomes **was**: **Ek was baie moeg.** And to say you didn’t, use **nie … nie**: **Ek het gister nie gewerk nie.**
g02u01l03.a: Say what you did, what you didn’t do and how you were, in the past tense.
g02u01l03.n: The **het … ge-** pattern is the same for every person, so there’s no table of endings to memorise. It’s a very friendly past tense.

g02u01l04.h: Nadia asks about a weekend, then tells you hers. Mountains, pasta and a very lazy Sunday. Count me in.
g02u01l04.c: Messages that start with "How was your weekend?" are the most common friendly texts at work and among friends on a Monday.
g02u01l04.t: Nadia’s message uses the past tense throughout: **Saterdag het ons in die berge gestap.** and **Sondag het ek net gelees en geslaap.** Look for **Hoe was jou naweek?** at the start and **Wat het jy gedoen?** at the end. After the questions, tell us what you did yesterday.
g02u01l04.a: Read a short message about a weekend and say what you did yesterday.

g02u01l05.h: Your weekend, in your own words. Four sentences. Tell the truth, the hadeda won’t tell anyone.
g02u01l05.c: Writing about your weekend is classic practice, and it’s exactly what you’d send to a friend or colleague who asks.
g02u01l05.t: Write four sentences. Use **het … ge-** for each thing you did, and if you want to say what you didn’t do, **nie … nie**. Add a time such as **Saterdag** or **gister**, and the **ge-** word goes at the end.
g02u01l05.a: Write a few sentences about your weekend in the past tense.

g02u01l06.h: Past-tense check! Let’s see whether you’ve got het and ge- under control.
g02u01l06.c: A final practice of the past tense before you move into the house.
g02u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **het … ge-**, with the verbs that don’t take **ge-**, and with **was** and **nie … nie**. Look carefully at where the verb sits.
g02u01l06.a: See which past-tense patterns are solid.

g02u02l01.h: Come in! The front door is open, mind the hadeda on the roof. Let me show you around.
g02u02l01.c: Describing your home, asking about a flat to rent, or hearing a friend describe where they live: room names are the first thing you need.
g02u02l01.t: **Die sitkamer** (lounge), **die slaapkamer** (bedroom), **die badkamer** (bathroom), **die tuin** (garden), **die stoep** (veranda) and **die motorhuis** (garage). Many of these are compound words, so **slaapkamer** is simply sleep plus room.
g02u02l01.a: Name six parts of a house or flat and understand a simple description of one.
g02u02l01.n: The **stoep** is the heart of many South African homes: a raised veranda where you drink coffee, watch the rain and greet the neighbours.

g02u02l02.h: Daar is 'n tuin! Now to say what’s in the house, how many rooms it has and what it costs.
g02u02l02.c: Looking at a flat, chatting to an estate agent or telling a friend about your new place: you’ll want to describe rooms, numbers and prices.
g02u02l02.t: **Die huis het drie slaapkamers.** says how many, and **Daar is 'n groot tuin agter die huis.** says what’s there. Use **staan** or **is** for where things are: **Die bank staan in die sitkamer.** And for rent, **Die huur is agtduisend rand per maand.**
g02u02l02.a: Describe a home: how many rooms, what’s there and what it costs to rent.

g02u02l03.h: There is, there isn’t. Grammar for house-hunters.
g02u02l03.c: Reading an advert, asking a landlord a question or describing your own place: you need to say what is there and what isn’t.
g02u02l03.t: **Daar is** means there is or there are: **Daar is drie slaapkamers.** **Het** means has: **Die badkamer het 'n bad en 'n stort.** For no, use **geen … nie**: **Daar is geen motorhuis nie.** If you start a sentence with a time or place, the verb comes next: **Saans sit ons op die stoep.**
g02u02l03.a: Say what a place has and doesn’t have, and ask how many rooms there are.
g02u02l03.n: If you start a sentence with something other than the subject, the verb takes second place. It’s one of the most important word-order rules in Afrikaans.

g02u02l04.h: A flat to let. Read it like a would-be tenant: what’s in, what’s out and what do you do next?
g02u02l04.c: Adverts for flats and rooms are an everyday text in South Africa, and the vocabulary you need to read one is exactly what you’ve been learning.
g02u02l04.t: The advert is for a flat in Melville with two bedrooms and a small stoep. Look for **een badkamer met 'n stort**, **geen tuin nie**, **water ingesluit** (water included) and **Geen troeteldiere nie** (no pets). It ends with how to get in touch. After the questions, describe your own home.
g02u02l04.a: Read a flat-to-let advert and pick out the details, then describe your own home.

g02u02l05.h: Describe your own home, in four sentences. Is there a stoep? There should be a stoep.
g02u02l05.c: Describing your home is useful when you write to a host, chat to a neighbour or fill in an accommodation form.
g02u02l05.t: Write four sentences about your house or flat. Use **Daar is** for what’s there, **het** for how many rooms, and **geen … nie** for what’s missing. Add where things are: **in, op, agter**.
g02u02l05.a: Write a short description of your home using daar is, het and geen … nie.

g02u02l06.h: House check! Is everything in its place?
g02u02l06.c: A final look at rooms, **daar is** and **geen … nie** before you move on to work.
g02u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences about homes, such as **Daar is geen motorhuis nie.** and **Hoeveel kamers het die woonstel?** Watch the word order after **Saans**.
g02u02l06.a: See which house sentences are in good order.

g02u03l01.h: What do you do for a living? Everyone asks, and now you can answer. Hettie’s job? Professional shouting.
g02u03l01.c: Meeting new people, talking at a braai or filling in a form: "What do you do?" is a standard question in South Africa, usually within the first three minutes.
g02u03l01.t: **Die onderwyser** (teacher), **die verpleegkundige** (nurse), **die boer** (farmer), **die kok** (cook, chef), **die bestuurder** (manager or driver) and **die werktuigkundige** (mechanic). **Bestuurder** has two meanings, so the context tells you which one.
g02u03l01.a: Name six jobs and understand what people do for a living.

g02u03l02.h: Ek is 'n kok! Well, you might not be. Let’s work out how to say what you do and where.
g02u03l02.c: Introducing yourself at a new job, answering a stranger’s question or describing a friend’s work: these sentences are the standard set.
g02u03l02.t: Ask **Watter werk doen jy?** and answer with **Ek is 'n kok by 'n hotel.** or say where you work: **Sy werk in die hospitaal.** and **Ek werk in 'n kantoor in die stad.** You’ll also learn **die kantoor** (office) and a teacher’s sentence: **Hy gee Engels by 'n hoërskool.**
g02u03l02.a: Ask and say what you do for a living and where you work.

g02u03l03.h: Grammar: one farmer, two farmers. Job words and their plurals.
g02u03l03.c: Talking about a team, counting the teachers at a school or describing the people you work with: you’ll want job words in the plural.
g02u03l03.t: Say what you do with **Ek is 'n …**. Job words ending in **-er** or **-e** add **-s**: **onderwyser** becomes **onderwysers**. Short ones add **-e**, and double after a short vowel: **boer** becomes **boere** and **kok** becomes **kokke**. The verb stays the same for everyone: **ek werk, sy werk, hulle werk.**
g02u03l03.a: Say your job, name a job in the plural and describe where someone works.

g02u03l04.h: A staff newsletter, with new colleagues, a pizza-making chef and a manager with a Knysna past. Read it like the new office gossip.
g02u03l04.c: Staff newsletters, company intranets and welcome emails are how workplaces introduce new people, and you’ll see this kind of text in any office.
g02u03l04.t: The newsletter introduces three new colleagues at a hotel: a manager, a chef and an office worker. Look for **nuwe kollegas**, **vroeër** (earlier) and **van die huis af** (from home). The last line, **Sê gerus hallo**, means feel free to say hello. After the questions, you’ll tell us about your own work.
g02u03l04.a: Read a short workplace newsletter and say what work you do.

g02u03l05.h: Introduce yourself to a new colleague. Four sentences, and a smile. They can’t see the smile in writing, but they can feel it.
g02u03l05.c: A friendly introduction to a new workmate is a very real writing task: in an email, in a group chat or in a welcome note.
g02u03l05.t: Write four sentences: who you are, what you do, where you work and something about your day. You can use **Ek is …**, **Ek werk in …** and **Ek begin om … **.
g02u03l05.a: Write a short introduction of yourself for a new colleague.

g02u03l06.h: Work-and-jobs check! Time for the interview.
g02u03l06.c: One more round on jobs, workplaces and plurals before you move on to numbers.
g02u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences about work, such as **Watter werk doen jy?** and **Ek werk twee dae per week van die huis af.** Listen for the plurals, too.
g02u03l06.a: See which job and workplace sentences are solid.

g02u04l01.h: Dertig, veertig, vyftig… counting in tens gets you to a hundred in no time. I can count to six. Mostly.
g02u04l01.c: Saying your age, reading a price, giving a distance or a phone number: you’ll need your tens all the time.
g02u04l01.t: **Dertig** (thirty), **veertig** (forty), **sestig** (sixty), **sewentig** (seventy), **tagtig** (eighty) and **negentig** (ninety). **Twintig** and **vyftig** you may have met already. Notice that each ends in **-tig**.
g02u04l01.a: Count in tens to a hundred and recognise each number when you hear it.

g02u04l02.h: Een-en-twintig! In Afrikaans you say the small number first, like a very old nursery rhyme.
g02u04l02.c: Telling someone your age, ordering a round, quoting a price or reading out a number: numbers between the tens come up constantly.
g02u04l02.t: **Sy is een-en-twintig.** and **Die brood kos vyf-en-dertig rand.** show how to say the ones before the tens, joined by **-en-**. You’ll also meet **honderd** in **Daar is honderd mense in die saal.** and the question **Wat is jou selfoonnommer?**
g02u04l02.a: Say any number up to a hundred, give your age and read out a price.

g02u04l03.h: Grammar: numbers to a hundred. Two sneaky spellings, one hyphen rule.
g02u04l03.c: Giving your age, reading a house number, saying how far the next town is: numbers are part of daily life.
g02u04l03.t: The tens all end in **-tig**: **twintig, dertig, veertig, vyftig, sestig, sewentig, tagtig, negentig**. Watch two: **veertig** (not viertig) and **tagtig** (not agtig). In between, say the ones first, with **-en-**: **drie-en-sestig**. Write them as one hyphenated word.
g02u04l03.a: Spell and say any number up to a hundred correctly.
g02u04l03.n: English says "twenty-one"; Afrikaans says "one-and-twenty". If you’ve ever heard "four and twenty blackbirds", it’s the same idea.

g02u04l04.h: A "for sale" sheet, with prices. Perfect practice for numbers that matter: the ones with rand signs.
g02u04l04.c: Garage-sale posters, community notice boards and online groups are where you’ll meet prices in Afrikaans.
g02u04l04.t: The advert lists things for sale with a price for each: a children’s bike, a dining table with chairs, two lamps and some books. Look for **so goed as nuut** (as good as new), **elk** (each) and the opening hours. After the questions, say three sentences with numbers.
g02u04l04.a: Read a short advert, work out prices and say sentences with numbers up to a hundred.

g02u04l05.h: Now you sell something. Three things, three prices, and a persuasive tone. Hettie would buy it.
g02u04l05.c: Writing a short advert is useful for selling something online or putting a notice up at work, and it’s a good use of numbers.
g02u04l05.t: Write a short advert selling three things with prices. Start with **Te koop**, list the items with **R** and the price, and say when and where people can come. Use **elk** for the price of each one.
g02u04l05.a: Write a short advert with items and prices.

g02u04l06.h: Numbers check! How are those tens?
g02u04l06.c: A last look at numbers to a hundred before you meet the pets.
g02u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with numbers such as **Sy is een-en-twintig.** and **Die huis is nommer drie-en-sestig.** Watch the **-en-** and the spelling of **veertig** and **tagtig**.

g02u05l01.h: Pets! Hettie is nobody’s pet, but I respect a good dog. Here are the words for pet life.
g02u05l01.c: Talking about your pet, buying supplies, going to the vet or asking a neighbour to look after the dog: pet words come up everywhere.
g02u05l01.t: **Die troeteldier** (pet), **die voerbak** (food bowl), **die leiband** (lead), **die veearts** (vet), **die halsband** (collar) and **die pote** (paws). Notice **die veearts** is literally the cattle doctor, and it’s used for any animal.
g02u05l01.a: Name six pet-related words and understand them in a conversation.

g02u05l02.h: 'n Klein hondjie! In Afrikaans, little things get a little ending. And everyone gets rather soft about it.
g02u05l02.c: Talking about your dog’s morning walk, feeding the cat or telling a friend about your kitten: pet owners always have something to say.
g02u05l02.t: **Ons het 'n klein hondjie.** and **Die katjie slaap in die mandjie.** show the small endings **-jie**. For routines, use **elke oggend** and **saans**: **Ek voer die kat elke oggend.** and **Ek gaan saans met die hond stap.**
g02u05l02.a: Describe your pet, say how you look after it and use the small form.

g02u05l03.h: Grammar: making words small. In Afrikaans, being small is a friendly thing. Hettie is not small, she’s compact.
g02u05l03.c: Afrikaans speakers use the small form constantly, to sound friendly, affectionate or polite: a little cup, a little moment, a little bird.
g02u05l03.t: Most words add **-ie**: **huis** becomes **huisie**. After **d** or **t**, add **-jie**: **hond** becomes **hondjie**. After **m**, add **-pie**: **boom** becomes **boompie**. After a long vowel or **l, n, r**, add **-tjie**: **stoel** becomes **stoeltjie**. And after a short vowel, double up: **bal** becomes **balletjie**.
g02u05l03.a: Make a small form of most everyday nouns and hear why Afrikaans sounds so friendly.
g02u05l03.n: Small forms are everywhere in friendly speech. People say **'n bietjie** (a little bit) or **'n koppietjie koffie** (a nice little coffee) without any intention of being tiny.

g02u05l04.h: A poster for a lost dog. Little Koko is missing! Read it carefully. Help find her.
g02u05l04.c: Missing-pet posters are everywhere in South African neighbourhoods and online groups, and they’re a good example of real, useful Afrikaans.
g02u05l04.t: The poster gives a name, a description, when and where the dog went missing, and how to get in touch. Look for **bruin hondjie**, **wit pote**, **rooi halsband**, **weggeraak** (went missing) and **beloning** (reward). After the questions, describe a pet.
g02u05l04.a: Read a lost-pet poster, pick out the details and describe a pet.

g02u05l05.h: Describe a pet, yours or somebody else’s. Hettie has a favourite subject too: Hettie.
g02u05l05.c: Describing a pet is useful when you’re writing to a pet-sitter, a vet or a neighbour, or making a poster for a missing one.
g02u05l05.t: Write four sentences about a pet. Say what it is, how big, what colour, and what it likes to do. Use the small forms from this unit, like **hondjie** and **katjie**.
g02u05l05.a: Write a short description of a pet using describing words and small forms.

g02u05l06.h: Pet check! Even small things matter.
g02u05l06.c: A final practice of pets and small forms before you head into hobbies.
g02u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die voëltjie sit in die boompie.** and **Is dit 'n mannetjie of 'n wyfie?** Watch the endings. Check each small ending as you go: the little forms are the point of this unit.
g02u05l06.a: See which small forms you’ve got.

g02u06l01.h: What do you do when nobody’s making you work? Hobbies! Mine is flying around being loud.
g02u06l01.c: Meeting someone new, joining a club or chatting at a braai: "What do you do in your free time?" is very easy to answer if you’ve got the words.
g02u06l01.t: **Tuinmaak** (gardening), **brei** (knit), **fietsry** (cycle), **skilder** (paint), **die klub** (the club) and **die vrye tyd** (free time). **Tuinmaak** and **fietsry** are single words in Afrikaans, where English needs two.
g02u06l01.a: Name six hobbies and talk about your free time.

g02u06l02.h: Ek lees graag! The magic word is graag. It means gladly, and it’s how Afrikaans says "I like doing".
g02u06l02.c: Talking about your hobbies, joining a book club or saying what you do at the weekend: this is how you talk about the things you enjoy.
g02u06l02.t: **Ek lees graag.** says you like to read, and **Ons ry graag fiets.** says you like to cycle. Add details with **Saans hardloop ek vyf kilometer.** and **Ek is lid van 'n boekklub.** The weekend sentence starts with a time: **Die naweek werk ons in die tuin.**
g02u06l02.a: Say what you like doing and tell someone about a club or a routine.

g02u06l03.h: Grammar: graag, and the three little words that join ideas: en, maar and of.
g02u06l03.c: Telling someone what you like and don’t like, offering a choice, or joining two ideas into one sentence: you’ll use these words in nearly every conversation.
g02u06l03.t: **Graag** goes straight after the verb: **Ek lees graag.** To say you don’t like something, wrap it in **nie … nie**: **Ek kook nie graag nie.** Join ideas with **en** (and), **maar** (but) and **of** (or), without changing the word order: **Sy brei graag, maar sy skilder nie.**
g02u06l03.a: Say what you like and don’t like doing and join two ideas with **en, maar** and **of**.
g02u06l03.n: Another way is **Ek hou daarvan om te skilder.** It’s a little longer and a little more formal, but just as natural.

g02u06l04.h: A community centre’s timetable, with a painting class, a knitting club and a walking group. Pick yours.
g02u06l04.c: Timetables and noticeboards at community centres, gyms and libraries are the most practical Afrikaans you’ll read every week.
g02u06l04.t: The timetable lists the days, times and activities at the Rivierpark centre. Look for **Skilderklas, Breiklub, Boekklub** and **Stapgroep**, and the phrase **Alles is gratis** (everything is free). After the questions, say what you like doing in your free time.
g02u06l04.a: Read a timetable, find a day and time and say what you like doing.

g02u06l05.h: Write a message and invite a friend to one of the clubs. Your friend will say yes if you make it sound fun.
g02u06l05.c: Inviting a friend to something is one of the nicest reasons to write a message, and it’s a very natural thing to do in Afrikaans.
g02u06l05.t: Write a short message to a friend and invite them to one of the clubs at the centre. Use **Kom ons …** or **Wil jy saam kom?**, say which day and time, and use **graag** to say why you like it.
g02u06l05.a: Write a short, friendly invitation with a day and a time.

g02u06l06.h: Last check in Graad 2! Hobbies, **graag**, and all those little joining words.
g02u06l06.c: One more look at hobbies before you move up to Graad 3.
g02u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek kook nie graag nie.** and **Speel jy tennis of sokker?** Watch where **graag** and **nie** go.
g02u06l06.a: See which hobby sentences are solid.

g03u01l01.h: Big, bigger, biggest. I’m the loudest bird on this page, but I’ll let the grammar speak for itself.
g03u01l01.c: Choosing between two things is something you do all day: which route is quicker, which shop is cheaper, which coffee is the best. You need comparing words for every one of those.
g03u01l01.t: Each word comes in three steps: **groot → groter → grootste**, **goed → beter → beste**, **duur → duurder → duurste** and **ver → verder → verste**. After **r** you add a **d** before **-er**, which is why it’s **duurder** and **verder**. **Goed** is the odd one out, with **beter** and **beste**.
g03u01l01.a: Compare two things and say which one is the biggest, best or most expensive.

g03u01l02.h: The bus is cheaper than the train. Now to turn those comparing words into sentences you’d actually say.
g03u01l02.c: Planning a trip, picking a restaurant, saying you feel better today: you’ll use these sentences when you give opinions and make choices.
g03u01l02.t: **Die bus is goedkoper as die trein.** compares two things with **-er** and **as**. **Dit is die duurste restaurant in die stad.** says it’s the most expensive, with **die … -ste**. Then two to learn as they stand: **Vandag voel ek baie beter.** and **Wie maak die beste koffie?**
g03u01l02.a: Compare two things in a sentence and name the best or most expensive one.

g03u01l03.h: Grammar: comparing. Add -er to compare, -ste to crown a winner, and learn the oddballs.
g03u01l03.c: Shopping, travelling, choosing a flat, talking about films: every time you say something is better, cheaper or longer, you’re comparing.
g03u01l03.t: Add **-er** to compare two things and use **as** for than: **Die tweede fliek was langer as die eerste.** Add **-ste** for the most. For "as … as", use **so … soos**: **My kamer is so groot soos joune.** Learn the odd ones: **goed → beter → beste** and **baie → meer → meeste**. **Ek soek 'n kleiner grootte** is how you ask for a smaller size.
g03u01l03.a: Compare things in three ways: bigger than, the biggest, and as big as.
g03u01l03.n: **Soos** means like or as, and you’ll hear it everywhere. **So … soos** is the pair that says "as … as".

g03u01l04.h: Two holiday cottages by the sea, one cheaper and one bigger. Which would you book? Read the advert and decide.
g03u01l04.c: Adverts that compare places, prices and distances are exactly what you read when you’re choosing where to stay on a South African holiday.
g03u01l04.t: The advert describes two cottages: Bloublommetjie and Seemeeu. You’ll compare price, size and distance to the beach with sentences such as **Dit is groter en nuwer as …**. Look for **per nag** (per night), **swembad** and the numbers in rand. After the questions, you’ll compare two places you know.
g03u01l04.a: Read an advert, compare two options and say which you’d choose.

g03u01l05.h: You compare two things in a short paragraph. Two phones, two cafés, two cars. I’d compare two perches, but that’s me.
g03u01l05.c: Comparing is one of the best ways to explain your opinion in writing, whether it’s a review, a message to a friend or a note for a flatmate.
g03u01l05.t: Write a short paragraph that compares two things. Use **-er … as**, **die -ste** and **so … soos**, and give a reason for your choice. Keep to simple sentences and check each verb.
g03u01l05.a: Write a short, clear comparison using the comparing words.

g03u01l06.h: Comparing check! Which is better, you before the check or you after?
g03u01l06.c: One more look at comparing before you start making plans.
g03u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **-er … as**, **die -ste**, **so … soos** and the odd ones, **beter** and **beste**. Say each comparison aloud, because the ear often catches a wrong ending before the eye does.
g03u01l06.a: See which comparing sentences are solid.

g03u02l01.h: January to June, the first half of the year. In the southern hemisphere, that’s summer sliding into winter.
g03u02l01.c: Booking a trip, arranging a meeting, writing a date on a form: you’ll use the months in almost any plan you make.
g03u02l01.t: **Januarie, Februarie, Maart, April, Mei** and **Junie**. In Afrikaans months start with a capital letter, and **Januarie** and **Februarie** have an extra **-ie** at the end. **Maart** is the one to listen for, with its long “aa” sound.
g03u02l01.a: Name the first six months and recognise them when you hear them.

g03u02l02.h: July to December, and a promise: Ek sal jou bel. The second half of the year, and a future to talk about.
g03u02l02.c: Planning a holiday, setting a date for a wedding, telling a friend when your birthday is: you’ll mention months and the future all the time.
