g03u02l02.t: **Julie, Augustus, September, Oktober, November** and **Desember** finish the list. Then two future sentences: **Ek sal jou môre bel.** (I’ll call you tomorrow) and **Hulle gaan in Maart trou.** (They’re getting married in March). You’ll also hear a birthday date with **op**.
g03u02l02.a: Name all twelve months and say what you’ll do or what’s going to happen.

g03u02l03.h: Grammar: the future. Two little words, sal and gaan, and a verb that likes to be at the end.
g03u02l03.c: Making plans, promising to call someone, saying when a course begins or what the weather will do: you’ll use the future constantly.
g03u02l03.t: Use **sal** (will) or **gaan** (going to) and put the action word at the end: **Ek sal jou môre bel.** and **Hulle gaan in Maart trou.** For won’t, use **sal nie … nie**: **Ek sal nie kan kom nie.** Dates use **op** and the normal number: **Die kursus begin op een Junie.** **Wanneer gaan julle met vakansie?** is a handy question to ask a friend.
g03u02l03.a: Talk about future plans with **sal** and **gaan**, give a date, and say what won’t happen.
g03u02l03.n: You can use either word for the future, and they overlap a lot. **Gaan** often sounds like a plan, while **sal** often sounds like a promise or a prediction.

g03u02l04.h: You’re invited! A birthday braai in Stellenbosch. Read the invitation, and then reply.
g03u02l04.c: Invitations by message, email or on a card are some of the friendliest texts in the language, and they follow a clear pattern: who, when, where and what to bring.
g03u02l04.t: Thabo is turning forty, and the invitation gives the date, time, place and what to bring. Look for **Wanneer** and **Waar**, **Ons sal braai** and **Bring net jouself, en 'n trui.** The last line asks you to let them know, and the next lesson has you write your reply. After the questions, say what you’ll do next month.
g03u02l04.a: Read an invitation, find the date, place and what to bring, and say your own plans.

g03u02l05.h: Reply to Lerato’s invitation. Say yes or no, and ask whether you can bring something. Hettie always brings something. Usually opinions.
g03u02l05.c: Replying to an invitation is a polite thing to do in any language, and in Afrikaans you do it in two or three friendly sentences.
g03u02l05.t: Write a short reply: say whether you can come (**Ek sal graag kom.** or **Ek sal nie kan kom nie.**), thank them (**Dankie vir die uitnodiging.**) and ask if you can bring something (**Kan ek iets saambring?**). Use the future, **sal**, and a friendly sign-off.
g03u02l05.a: Write a polite reply to an invitation.

g03u02l06.h: Plans-and-dates check! No excuses for forgetting the date.
g03u02l06.c: A final practice of months, dates and the future before you start giving reasons.
g03u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **sal**, **gaan**, **sal nie … nie**, months and dates. Check each date and watch where the verb goes. It’s also a good moment to say your own birthday and one plan for next week aloud.
g03u02l06.a: See which future sentences are solid.

g03u03l01.h: Laat en vroeg: late and early. I’m usually early, because the birds start at dawn.
g03u03l01.c: Being late is a universal problem, and so is apologising for it. In traffic, at the office or on a train platform, you’ll want these words.
g03u03l01.t: **Laat** (late), **vroeg** (early), **die verkeer** (traffic), **die vergadering** (meeting), **die verskoning** (excuse or apology) and **jammer** (sorry). **Verskoning** is also what you say when you want to get past someone in a crowd.
g03u03l01.a: Talk about being late or early and say sorry in Afrikaans.

g03u03l02.h: Giving reasons. Because! That one word makes you sound a lot more convincing.
g03u03l02.c: Explaining why you’re late, why you’re staying home, what you do when it’s sunny: reasons turn a statement into a conversation.
g03u03l02.t: **Ek is laat omdat die verkeer so swaar is.** gives a reason with **omdat**. **As die son skyn, eet ons buite.** sets up a condition with **as**. **Bel my wanneer jy klaar is.** uses **wanneer**. The pattern in all of them: the verb moves to the end of its part.
g03u03l02.a: Give a reason with **omdat**, set a condition with **as** and talk about a time with **wanneer**.

g03u03l03.h: Grammar: the verb that runs to the end. It’s the trickiest and most Afrikaans habit of all.
g03u03l03.c: Explaining yourself, making a promise, or telling someone when to call you back: these sentence types come up in every real conversation.
g03u03l03.t: After **omdat** (because), **as** (if), **wanneer** (when) and **dat** (that), the verb goes to the end of its part: **Ons het die trein gemis omdat ons laat was.** and **Jammer dat ek so laat is.** If the sentence starts with an **as** part, the next verb comes straight after the comma: **As die son skyn, eet ons buite.** **Want** also means because, but keeps the normal order.
g03u03l03.a: Join two ideas with **omdat, as** and **wanneer**, with the verb in the right place.
g03u03l03.n: Many English speakers find this the hardest rule. Don’t try to understand it, just say lots of examples aloud until the end-of-sentence verb feels natural.

g03u03l04.h: An apology email to a colleague. It has a good reason, a clear sorry and a polite request. Learn from it.
g03u03l04.c: Writing a short, polite apology email is one of the most useful things you can do in any workplace. Here’s how it looks in Afrikaans.
g03u03l04.t: The email says sorry for missing a meeting, gives the reason with **omdat** and asks for the notes. Look for **Onderwerp** (subject), **Jammer dat ek …**, **Ek het nie gebel nie omdat …** and **Kan jy asseblief …?** After the questions, tell about a time you were late.
g03u03l04.a: Read an apology email, find the reason and the request, and tell about a time you were late.

g03u03l05.h: Write your own apology, with a reason and a better time. A good apology always offers a new plan.
g03u03l05.c: When you can’t make an appointment, a short message with a reason and a new suggestion is polite, and it’s the sort of thing you’ll write often.
g03u03l05.t: Write a short message saying you can’t make it. Give the reason with **omdat**, say you’re sorry, and suggest another time. Remember the verb goes to the end after **omdat**, and finish with **Dankie vir jou begrip.**
g03u03l05.a: Write a short apology with a reason and a new suggestion.

g03u03l06.h: Reasons check! Because, if and when. Let’s see where those verbs end up.
g03u03l06.c: One more look at giving reasons and conditions before you start telling stories.
g03u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **omdat**, **as**, **wanneer** and **dat**, so watch where the verb goes. Try finishing each reason in your own words, so that the verb has to land in the right place.
g03u03l06.a: See which reason sentences are solid.

g03u04l01.h: First, then, after that, finally. These four little words are how every set of instructions in any language is built.
g03u04l01.c: Following a recipe, putting together a flat-pack cupboard, explaining the way to someone: you need the order words for any task with steps.
g03u04l01.t: **Eers** (first), **dan** (then), **daarna** (after that) and **laastens** (finally), plus two kitchen words: **meng** (mix) and **die oond** (the oven). Say the order words in a row until they feel like a rhythm.
g03u04l01.a: Put steps in order and understand instructions that use first, then, after that and finally.

g03u04l02.h: Mix the flour! We’re in the kitchen now, and I’m only allowed to supervise.
g03u04l02.c: Recipes, packet instructions and a family member shouting instructions across the kitchen: this is the language of cooking.
g03u04l02.t: **Was eers jou hande.** and **Meng die meel en die suiker in 'n bak.** show the instruction form, with the verb at the front. **Voeg dan die eiers by.** adds the next step, and **Sit die pan vir twintig minute in die oond.** gives a time. Instructions start with the verb, with no **jy** needed.
g03u04l02.a: Follow and give a short set of cooking instructions in order.

g03u04l03.h: Grammar: instructions in order. Verbs first, order words second, and a very useful word called tot.
g03u04l03.c: Following a recipe, assembling furniture, or giving someone directions: instructions follow a pattern, and once you know it you can follow any set.
g03u04l03.t: Instructions start with the verb: **Meng die meel.** The order words go after it: **Was eers jou hande.** and **Voeg dan die eiers by.** (a verb that splits sends its small part to the end). **Tot** means until, and the verb goes to the end after it: **Bak die koekies tot hulle goudbruin is.** To say what you need, use **Jy het … nodig.**
g03u04l03.a: Give instructions in order and say how long something should take or until when.
g03u04l03.n: You can use the same pattern for all sorts of instructions, not just recipes: a route, a game, a craft or a how-to message.

g03u04l04.h: Pampoenkoekies! A South African classic, and the recipe is yours to follow. Read it carefully and don’t burn it.
g03u04l04.c: Recipes in cookbooks, on food blogs and on the backs of packets are some of the best everyday texts to read in Afrikaans.
g03u04l04.t: The recipe for pumpkin fritters lists what you need and then numbers the steps. Look for **Jy het nodig:** and the list, then verbs such as **druk, meng** and **bak**, and measures such as **koppies, teelepels** and **'n knippie sout**. After the questions, explain how you make a cup of tea or coffee in three steps.
g03u04l04.a: Read a recipe, follow its steps in order and explain a simple task in three steps.
g03u04l04.n: **Pampoenkoekies** are fritters made from cooked pumpkin and often served with cinnamon sugar. They’re a staple of South African tables.

g03u04l05.h: Write instructions for something simple: toast, a sandwich, a smoothie. Four steps, no skipping.
g03u04l05.c: Writing clear instructions is a real-life skill: to a flatmate, in a note on the fridge or in a message to someone who’s cooking for the first time.
g03u04l05.t: Write four steps for a simple task. Start each step with the verb, use **eers, dan, daarna** and **laastens**, and add a time or an amount where it helps, such as **vir twee minute**.
g03u04l05.a: Write clear instructions in four steps.

g03u04l06.h: Recipe check! Let’s see whether you can follow the steps.
g03u04l06.c: A final look at instructions and order words before you tell your first story.
g03u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **eers, dan, daarna, laastens** and **tot**, and the kitchen words. Imagine reading a recipe to a friend in the kitchen, and put each step in order.
g03u04l06.a: See which instruction sentences are solid.

g03u05l01.h: Skielik! Suddenly! Every good story has one, and I’m going to teach you the words for it.
g03u05l01.c: Telling a friend what happened, writing a short story or explaining how you lost your keys: story words move a tale along.
g03u05l01.t: **Toe** (then, when), **skielik** (suddenly), **gelukkig** (luckily), **ongelukkig** (unfortunately), **die beursie** (purse, wallet) and **verloor** (lose). Notice that **gelukkig** can also mean happy, so the context tells you which.
g03u05l01.a: Use story words such as suddenly, luckily and unfortunately.

g03u05l02.h: Toe lui my foon: then my phone rang. Little sentences that turn into a story.
g03u05l02.c: Telling a friend about your commute, an accident, a lucky escape or an unlucky day: stories are the best part of any conversation.
g03u05l02.t: **Toe lui my foon.** (Then my phone rang) and **Skielik het die trein gestop.** (Suddenly the train stopped) move a story along. **Gelukkig het niemand seergekry nie.** (Luckily nobody got hurt) and **Ongelukkig was die winkel al toe.** (Unfortunately the shop was already closed) add the mood. Notice the verb comes straight after **toe** and **skielik**.
g03u05l02.a: Tell a short story of what happened, with time words and a bit of mood.

g03u05l03.h: Grammar: telling a story in the past. One small word, toe, does a lot of work.
g03u05l03.c: Stories, anecdotes and "you won’t believe what happened" messages are all told in the past, and **toe** helps you tell them well.
g03u05l03.t: Stories use the past: **het** plus **ge-** at the end. **Toe** moves the story on, with the verb straight after: **Toe lui my foon.** **Toe** can also mean when, in the past, and then the verb goes to the end: **Toe ek jonk was, het ek in Durban gewoon.** Add **eers, skielik, gelukkig, ongelukkig** and **uiteindelik** to colour the tale.
g03u05l03.a: Tell a story in the past using **toe**, the order words and the mood words.
g03u05l03.n: **Toe** is a lovely little word. It means then or when, and it has a close cousin, **toe maar**, which means something like "never mind" or "it’s okay".

g03u05l04.h: A story about a lost wallet, a sleepy train ride and a very bad evening. Don’t worry, there’s a happy ending.
g03u05l04.c: Short stories and anecdotes are the heart of reading in a language, and a good one makes the vocabulary stick.
g03u05l04.t: The narrator falls asleep on the train, jumps off at the last moment and only later finds the wallet is missing. Look for **Verlede Vrydag**, **skielik**, **eers by die huis** and the past tense with **het … ge-**. After the questions, retell the story in three sentences.
g03u05l04.a: Read a short story, put the events in order and retell it in three sentences.

g03u05l05.h: Write your own story about something you once lost or forgot. A little drama is allowed. I’ll pretend to be shocked.
g03u05l05.c: Writing a short story is the best way to practise the past tense, and it’s something people do on blogs, in messages and around a braai.
g03u05l05.t: Write a short story about something you lost or forgot. Use the past (**het … ge-**), the order words (**eers, toe, uiteindelik**) and at least one of **skielik, gelukkig** or **ongelukkig**.
g03u05l05.a: Write a short story in the past tense with order words and mood words.

g03u05l06.h: Story check! And then what happened? Let’s find out.
g03u05l06.c: A final look at the story words and the past tense before you meet the penguins.
g03u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **toe, skielik, gelukkig, ongelukkig** and **uiteindelik**, and put events in order. Think of a small story from your own week, and see if you can tell it with the right order words.
g03u05l06.a: See which story sentences are solid.

g03u06l01.h: Penguins! Not my relatives, but I respect their commitment to formal dress. Let’s look at the coast.
g03u06l01.c: South Africa’s coast is home to a famous penguin colony, and talking about wildlife and conservation is something you’ll want to do if you ever visit.
g03u06l01.t: **Die pikkewyn** (penguin), **die kus** (coast), **die nes** (nest), **die vlerke** (wings), **bedreig** (endangered, threatened) and **die toeris** (tourist). **Bedreig** is the one for conservation: you’ll hear it about animals whose numbers are shrinking.
g03u06l01.a: Talk about wildlife and the coast, and understand the word for endangered.

g03u06l02.h: Hulle swem baie goed. Penguins can’t fly, but they’re brilliant in the water. Let’s say it in Afrikaans.
g03u06l02.c: Describing an animal’s habits, chatting at a nature reserve or helping a child with a school project: facts about animals are a classic use of simple sentences.
g03u06l02.t: **Pikkewyne kan nie vlieg nie.** and **Hulle swem baie goed.** state facts. **Die wyfie lê gewoonlik twee eiers.** and **Hulle eet klein vissies soos sardyne.** add detail. Notice **kan nie … nie** again, the same double **nie** you learned for can’t.
g03u06l02.a: State simple facts about an animal using **kan nie … nie**, **gewoonlik** and **soos**.

g03u06l03.h: Grammar: more ways to say no. You’ve got nie … nie. Now meet geen, niks, nooit and niemand.
g03u06l03.c: Describing what an animal can’t do, saying you’ve never seen something or telling someone nobody is allowed in: negatives are part of everyday speech.
g03u06l03.t: **Geen** (no), **niks** (nothing), **nooit** (never) and **niemand** (nobody) all keep **nie** at the end: **Voëls het geen tande nie.** and **Ons het niks gesien nie.** **Nog nooit … nie** means never ever: **Ek het nog nooit 'n pikkewyn gesien nie.** **Niemand mag die pikkewyne voer nie.**
g03u06l03.a: Say no in more ways: no, nothing, never and nobody.
g03u06l03.n: **Niks** is stronger than a simple **nie**. **Ons het niks gesien nie.** means we saw nothing at all, whereas **Ons het dit nie gesien nie.** means we didn’t see that one thing.

g03u06l04.h: An information text about the African penguin. It’s a real animal, real facts and a real conservation problem.
g03u06l04.c: Information texts about animals appear in school books, on websites and on signs at nature reserves, and they’re a useful way to read facts.
g03u06l04.t: The text says where the African penguin lives, what it looks like, what it eats and why it needs protection. Look for **brilpikkewyn**, **broei** (breed), **Namibië** and **die enigste** (the only). After the questions, tell three facts about an animal you know.
g03u06l04.a: Read an information text, find the facts and tell three facts about an animal.

g03u06l05.h: Write a short information paragraph about an animal from your own country. Only write what you’re sure of. I’m a stickler.
g03u06l05.c: Information writing is a real skill: for a school project, a nature blog or a note on a reserve. The golden rule is to say only what you know.
g03u06l05.t: Write a short paragraph about an animal. Say where it lives, what it looks like, what it eats and one thing it can’t do. Use **nie … nie** or **geen** once, and write only facts you’re sure of.
g03u06l05.a: Write a short information paragraph about an animal, using only facts you know.

g03u06l06.h: Last check of Graad 3! Penguins, negatives and a whole year’s work behind you.
g03u06l06.c: This is the final check of Graad 3, and it covers the facts, the negatives and the animal words before you move up.
g03u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **geen, niks, nooit** and **niemand**, and the penguin words. Fact-finding, saying what isn’t there and animal words all come round again, so take your time.
g03u06l06.a: See which negative sentences are solid, and which are worth another go.

i1l1.h: **Goeiemiddag! Kan ek help?** That’s the sentence you’ll hear in every shop in the country. Time to learn what to say back.
i1l1.c: Walking into a corner café, asking a shop assistant where something is, or being greeted at a till: this is real, everyday Afrikaans that you will need on your first day in a South African town.
i1l1.t: Staff greet you with **Goeiemiddag! Kan ek help?** and you can answer **Ja, ek soek melk en brood.** (Yes, I’m looking for milk and bread). To find something, ask **Waar is die brood?** and expect an answer such as **Dis langs die melk.** The pattern is short and polite, and you can swap in any item you like.
i1l1.a: Greet a shop assistant, say what you’re looking for, ask where it is and understand the answer.
i1l1.n: Many shop assistants will switch to English the moment they hear an accent. Keep answering in Afrikaans, and they will usually follow your lead.

i1l2.h: How much? It’s the question that saves you money. Let’s get you asking it, and paying for the answer.
i1l2.c: At a till, at a market stall, or at a petrol station with a card machine: you’ll ask about prices and payment in nearly every shop you visit.
i1l2.t: **Hoeveel kos dit?** asks the price, and **Dit kos vyftig rand.** answers it. To pay, ask **Kan ek met my kaart betaal?** At the till the cashier may ask **Het jy 'n sak nodig?**, because many shops now charge for plastic bags. Notice that **rand** doesn’t take an **-s** when it follows a number.
i1l2.a: Ask the price, understand the answer in rand, and pay by card or by cash.
i1l2.n: In South Africa you pay in rand, and the amount is often said as a single number: **vyftig rand**, not "fifty rands".

i1l3.h: A coffee, a cheeky bit of cake and the bill, please. This lesson is where Afrikaans meets your stomach.
i1l3.c: Ordering at a café, a bakery or a roadside restaurant is one of the first things you’ll want to do in Afrikaans, especially in the Cape and the Karoo.
i1l3.t: Order with **Ek wil graag 'n koffie hê, asseblief.** The waiter might ask **Nog iets?** and you can answer **Nee dankie, dis al.** When you’re ready to leave, say **Kan ons die rekening kry, asseblief?** If you want to leave a tip, say **Hou maar die kleingeld.** (Keep the change.)
i1l3.a: Order food and drink, say that’s all, ask for the bill and leave a tip.
i1l3.n: In South African restaurants it is customary to tip roughly a tenth of the bill, and a polite **Hou maar die kleingeld** goes down well in cafés too.

i1l4.h: Grammar: want, can, must and may. Four little verbs that run most of your daily life.
i1l4.c: Asking permission, saying what you must do, and making polite requests: these four verbs are behind a huge number of the things you say in a day.
i1l4.t: After **wil** (want), **kan** (can), **moet** (must) and **mag** (may), the second verb goes to the very end: **Jy moet by die toonbank betaal.** and **Ek kan dit nie kry nie.** In questions the helper verb goes first: **Mag ek dit aanpas?** The polite way to ask for something is **Ek wil graag … hê.**
i1l4.a: Ask permission, say what you must do or can do, and make a polite request.
i1l4.n: Putting the second verb at the very end is the most important word-order habit in Afrikaans. Say the examples out loud until it feels natural.

i1l5.h: A real shop notice. It tells you when the bread is fresh and when the shop is shut. Read it like a local.
i1l5.c: Notices in shop windows, on doors and by tills are everywhere in South Africa, and they’re often your first real reading in Afrikaans.
i1l5.t: This notice is from Die Hoek-kafee. You’ll find the opening time for fresh bread (**Vars brood elke oggend om sewe-uur!**), prices for milk and bread, and the opening days. The last line, **Ons is Sondae toe.**, says the shop is closed on Sundays. Look for the numbers, the days and the times.
i1l5.a: Read a shop notice, find prices and opening hours, and answer questions about it.

i1l6.h: Shop check! Let’s see if you can find your way round a shop, a café and a till.
i1l6.c: A short look back at asking, paying and ordering before you move on to a braai.
i1l6.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences from this unit, such as **Kan ek met my kaart betaal?** and **Jy moet by die toonbank betaal.**, and sort out the helper verbs. Anything you miss comes back in your review.
i1l6.a: See which shop sentences you can say with confidence.

i2l1.h: **Kom binne, kom binne!** You’ve just arrived at a braai, and the host is already waving you in. Let’s learn what to say.
i2l1.c: Arriving at someone’s home for a braai, a birthday or a Sunday lunch: you’ll be welcomed warmly, offered a drink, and expected to say something friendly back.
i2l1.t: Your host will say **Kom binne, kom binne!** and **Sit gerus!** (the **gerus** means feel free). They’ll ask **Wat drink jy?** and you can answer **'n Koeldrank, asseblief.** **Koeldrank** is the word for a soft drink or cold drink in South Africa.
i2l1.a: Greet a host, accept a seat and ask for a drink.
i2l1.n: **Kuier** is the word for visiting and socialising, and you’ll hear it at every gathering. A good **kuier** can last a whole afternoon.

i2l2.h: Now we’re by the fire. This is where the real conversations happen, and where I try to steal a bit of boerewors.
i2l2.c: Standing near the grid, chatting while the meat cooks, complimenting the cook: this is the heart of a braai and the best place to practise.
i2l2.t: Comment on the food: **Die vleis is amper gaar.** (The meat is almost done) and **Dit ruik heerlik!** (It smells delicious). Ask **Wie het die slaai gemaak?** and say **Dankie vir die lekker kuier!** when you leave. **Bring jou eie vleis.** is a very common instruction on an invitation.
i2l2.a: Chat by the fire, compliment the food and say thank you for a lovely visit.
i2l2.n: At many braais the guests bring their own meat and the host provides the fire and the salads. It’s a very normal arrangement, not rude at all.

i2l3.h: Seconds, polite refusals and goodbye. Leaving a braai takes longer than arriving at one, and that’s a good thing.
i2l3.c: Being offered more food, saying you’re full, helping with the dishes and finally leaving: these are the polite moves that make you a popular guest.
i2l3.t: Your host might ask **Wil jy nog wors hê?** and you can say **Nee dankie, ek is vol.** Offer to help with **Kan ek met die skottelgoed help?** When it’s time to go, say **Ons moet nou ry.** Notice **moet** again, with **ry** at the end.
i2l3.a: Accept or politely refuse food, offer to help and say goodbye gracefully.

i2l4.h: Grammar: telling people what to do, nicely. At a braai there’s a lot of "Don’t let the meat burn!"
i2l4.c: Giving instructions to guests, asking a friend to bring something, or telling someone not to touch the grid: you need commands, and you need softeners.
i2l4.t: To tell someone to do something, start with the verb: **Kom binne!** and **Bring 'n stoel saam.** To say don’t, use **Moenie … nie**: **Moenie die vleis laat brand nie!** To soften a command, add **asseblief** or use **Moet asseblief nie … nie**, as in **Moet asseblief nie die hond kos gee nie.** And **gerus** makes it friendly.
i2l4.a: Give friendly instructions and say don’t politely.
i2l4.n: **Gerus** is a lovely little word. **Sit gerus** means feel free to sit, and the same word makes almost any command sound warm.

i2l5.h: An invitation to a braai in Stellenbosch. It’s got the date, the place and what to bring. Read it, then say yes.
i2l5.c: A braai invitation is one of the most common texts in South African social life, by message, card or WhatsApp, and it has a clear, practical shape.
i2l5.t: Marike and Johan invite you with **Kom braai saam met ons!** and give the date, place and what to bring. Look for **Wanneer**, **Waar** and **Bring jou eie vleis en 'n stoel.** The last line asks you to let them know, with **Laat weet asseblief voor Donderdag of jy kom.**
i2l5.a: Read a braai invitation, find the date, place and what to bring, and know when to reply.

i2l6.h: Braai check! Fire’s lit, let’s see how you do.
i2l6.c: A short look back at welcoming guests, offering food and giving friendly instructions before you start making phone calls.
i2l6.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Moenie die vleis laat brand nie!** and **Nee dankie, ek is vol.**, and the polite requests. Look carefully at where **nie** goes.
i2l6.a: See which braai sentences you’ve got.

i3l1.h: Family visits! Afrikaans families **kuier** a lot, and this lesson teaches you what to say when you arrive.
i3l1.c: Visiting grandparents, checking in on someone who’s been ill, or welcoming a relative: family conversations start with asking after people, and that’s what this lesson is for.
i3l1.t: Ask after someone with **Hoe gaan dit met Ouma?** and answer **Sy is baie beter, dankie.** Announce a visit with **Ons kom Sondag kuier.** and invite someone to stay with **Bly vir ete!** To show you care, say **Ek het jou gemis.**
i3l1.a: Ask after family, announce a visit, invite someone to stay and say you missed them.
i3l1.n: **Kuier** is hard to translate. It means to visit, but also to chat, to hang out and to stay a while. You’ll use it all the time.

i3l2.h: On the phone, there’s no face to read. All the more reason to know exactly what to say.
i3l2.c: Calling someone at home, asking for a colleague, leaving a message or asking to be called back: phone etiquette in Afrikaans has a small set of phrases that you use over and over.
i3l2.t: Start a call with **Hallo, dis Anna hier.** and ask for someone with **Kan ek met Pieter praat, asseblief?** If they’re out, you’ll hear **Hy is nie nou hier nie.** Ask **Kan jy my later terugbel?** and close with **Ek bel jou môre.**
i3l2.a: Answer or make a phone call, ask for someone and leave a message.

i3l3.h: Making plans, the Afrikaans way. When, where and who’s bringing the pudding.
i3l3.c: Arranging to meet a friend, confirming a time with family, or telling someone you’re running late: plans are made, changed and apologised for in every WhatsApp chat.
i3l3.t: Ask **Hoe laat kom julle?** and answer **Ons kom om sewe.** Promise to follow up with **Ek stuur vir jou 'n boodskap.** If you’re late, say **Jammer, ons is 'n bietjie laat.** and sign off with **Lekker, sien jou dan!** Notice that people often use **om** plus the hour when they give a time, and that a time on its own, like **Ons kom om sewe.**, needs no word for o’clock at all.
i3l3.a: Agree a time, send a message, apologise for being late and say see you then.

i3l4.h: Grammar: whose is it? Mine, yours, hers, Pieter’s. It’s all about a tiny word called se.
i3l4.c: Asking whose keys these are, saying a phone isn’t yours or asking for someone’s number: possession comes up whenever people share a space.
i3l4.t: Before a noun use **my, jou, sy, haar, ons, julle, hulle** and polite **u**. With a name or a noun, use **se**: **Is dit Pieter se foon?** To ask whose, say **Wie se sleutels is dit?** On its own the form changes: **Nee, dis myne.** (mine), **joune**, **syne**, **hare**.
i3l4.a: Say whose something is, ask whose it is and use mine, yours and hers on their own.
i3l4.n: **Sy** is both she and his. The word that follows tells you which, so **sy motor** is his car and **sy werk** is she works.

i3l5.h: A WhatsApp chat between Lize and her mum, and it’s all about Sunday lunch. Read along, and notice how people really write.
i3l5.c: Family WhatsApp chats are where most real Afrikaans happens today, in short, friendly and slightly abbreviated lines.
i3l5.t: Lize asks if she can bring Pieter. Her mum says **Natuurlik!** and asks if they’ll stay for lunch. They agree a time (**Om twaalfuur.**) and Lize offers to bring something. Look for **Bly julle vir ete?** and **Bring sommer poeding saam.** The word **sommer** means just, or simply.
i3l5.a: Read a short chat, follow who says what and answer questions about the plans.

i3l6.h: Last check of the first Graad 4 stretch. Visits, calls, and a whole lot of plans.
i3l6.c: A look back at family visits, phone calls and whose-is-it before the next unit.
i3l6.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Kan ek met Pieter praat, asseblief?** and **Wie se sleutels is dit?**, and use mine, yours and hers correctly. Listen for the endings.
i3l6.a: See which phone and plans sentences are solid.

g04u04l01.h: A Saturday market, a long queue for coffee and a stall selling second-hand books. Perfect. Let’s learn the words.
g04u04l01.c: Community markets are a big part of South African weekends, and they’re where you’ll hear and read this kind of vocabulary in real life: on signs, in posts and in local news.
g04u04l01.t: **Die mark** (the market), **die stalletjie** (the stall), **die tou** (the queue, also a rope), **die groente** (vegetables) and **tweedehands** (second-hand). **Stalletjie** is a small form, with **-tjie** at the end, so it’s a little stall. **Tweedehands** is written as one word, and takes **-e** before a noun, as in **tweedehandse boeke**.
g04u04l01.a: Talk about a market, name what’s sold there and read local news about one.
g04u04l01.n: Weekend food and craft markets are a regular feature of many South African towns, and a favourite spot to meet neighbours.

g04u04l02.h: Neighbours, news and free parking. The kind of local report that makes you feel part of the street.
g04u04l02.c: Local newspapers, community pages and neighbourhood groups are where you read about events in your area, and this vocabulary is what you’ll meet there.
g04u04l02.t: **Gratis** (free), **reël** (to organise), **die bure** (the neighbours), **ontmoet** (to meet) and **die berig** (the report). Use them in sentences such as **Parkering is gratis.** and **Wie het die mark gereël?** For the past, **Ons het lank in die tou gestaan.** Together they let you read, and talk about, the small news stories of your own street.
g04u04l02.a: Understand and say who organised something, what was free and who you met.

g04u04l03.h: Grammar: first, second, third. Order numbers tell you which place something is in.
g04u04l03.c: Reading a news report, giving directions, talking about the first market or the third house on the left: whenever order matters, you need order numbers.
g04u04l03.t: Counting numbers say how many (**een, twee, drie**) and order numbers say which place (**eerste, tweede, derde**). Up to nineteen most add **-de**: **tweede, vierde, vyfde**. Learn the odd ones: **eerste, derde, agtste**. From twenty upwards add **-ste**: **twintigste**. In dates, Afrikaans speakers mostly use the ordinary number: **Die mark is op veertien Desember.**
g04u04l03.a: Say which place something is in, and use order numbers in sentences and dates.
g04u04l03.n: Dates are one of the places where Afrikaans is simpler than English. You don’t say "the fourteenth of December", just **veertien Desember**.

g04u04l04.h: A news report about the first Saturday market at the old railway station. It’s got the who, what, where and when.
g04u04l04.c: A short news report is the first kind of non-fiction you read in a language, and it follows a clear pattern that gets easier every time you see it.
g04u04l04.t: The report starts with the place (in capital letters) and tells you what happened, when the market opened and how many stalls there were. Look for the **who** (who organised and who came), the **what** (the market), the **where** (the old railway station) and the **when** (Saturday, eight o’clock). After the questions, retell it in three sentences.
g04u04l04.a: Read a short news report, find who, what, where and when, and retell it in three sentences.

g04u04l05.h: Now you’re the reporter. Twenty to forty words about something that happened where you live. Keep it factual, no gossip.
g04u04l05.c: Writing a short report is useful for a neighbourhood group, a workplace newsletter or just practising clear writing.
g04u04l05.t: Write a short report of 20 to 40 words. Answer the four questions: **wie** (who), **wat** (what), **waar** (where) and **wanneer** (when). Use the past tense with **het … ge-**, and start with the place or the time. Only write what really happened, and keep each sentence short. A good local report is plain and clear, never longer than it needs to be.
g04u04l05.a: Write a short factual report that answers who, what, where and when.

g04u04l06.h: Market check! Let’s see what you remember about the news, the order numbers and the stalls.
g04u04l06.c: A look back at the unit before you move on to notices.
g04u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with order numbers such as **die derde huis links**, and the market and news words from this unit.
g04u04l06.a: See which order numbers and news words are solid.

g04u05l01.h: The lift is broken, the rubbish goes out on Tuesday, and nobody read the notice. Let’s change that.
g04u05l01.c: If you live in a flat or work in a building, you’ll see notices from the management on the lift, the door and the noticeboard. Knowing the vocabulary saves a lot of confusion.
g04u05l01.t: **Die kennisgewing** (the notice), **die inwoner** (the resident), **die hysbak** (the lift), **die vullis** (the rubbish), **die herstelwerk** (repair work) and **die trappe** (the stairs). **Herstelwerk** is a compound: **herstel** means repair and **werk** means work. Afrikaans builds long words by sticking short ones together, and once you spot the parts you can often read a word you’ve never seen.
g04u05l01.a: Read the key words on a building notice.

g04u05l02.h: Buite werking: out of order. The two most feared words on any lift, and now you’ll recognise them.
g04u05l02.c: Notices that explain a problem, apologise for it and ask you to do something are a fixture of apartment blocks and offices everywhere.
g04u05l02.t: **Buite werking** (out of order), **die ongerief** (inconvenience), **onthou** (to remember) and **die bestuur** (management). In sentences: **Die hysbak is buite werking.**, **Sit asseblief die vullis Dinsdag buite.** and **Onthou om die deur te sluit.** Notices like these are written in a short, direct style, so you’ll often see the verb first and **asseblief** doing the polite work.
g04u05l02.a: Understand a notice that explains a problem and asks residents to do something.

g04u05l03.h: Grammar: me, him, her. Pronouns change shape after a verb, and Afrikaans only changes three of them.
g04u05l03.c: Asking someone to call you, saying you saw him, giving the key to her: object pronouns come up in every conversation and in every notice that tells someone what to do.
g04u05l03.t: After a verb or a preposition, **ek** becomes **my**, **hy** becomes **hom** and **sy** becomes **haar**: **Bel my.** and **Ek het hom gister by die hysbak gesien.** The others stay the same: **Ek help jou.** and **Die bestuur sal julle laat weet.** Before a noun, **sy** is his and **haar** is her.
g04u05l03.a: Use me, him and her after verbs and prepositions, and tell sy (she) from sy (his).
g04u05l03.n: Only three words change: **my, hom** and **haar**. Everything else stays the same, which makes this one of the easier pronoun systems to learn.

g04u05l04.h: A notice to all residents. Water off, lift out and a bucket needed. Read it, then tell your neighbour.
g04u05l04.c: Notices that tell residents about maintenance and what to do are everywhere in flats and complexes, and reading one correctly is a practical skill.
g04u05l04.t: The notice gives the day and the hours when there will be no water, and asks residents to fill a bucket and a bottle the night before. It also tells you the lift is out of order all day. Look for **herstelwerk**, **Van 08:00 tot 14:00**, **buite werking** and **Tap asseblief …**. After the questions, tell a neighbour what it says in three sentences.
g04u05l04.a: Read a notice to residents, find what, when and who, and pass the message on in three sentences.

g04u05l05.h: Write a short notice for your building, work or club. Keep it clear, keep it polite, and remember the apology.
g04u05l05.c: Writing a notice is a practical skill. You might need one for a workplace, a group of neighbours or a club.
g04u05l05.t: Write a short notice of 20 to 40 words. Say what is happening, when and who it affects, and ask readers to do something with **asseblief**. End with a short apology such as **Jammer vir die ongerief.** Use **my, hom** and **haar** correctly if you mention people, and keep the tone friendly: a notice that apologises gets a better response than one that just gives orders.
g04u05l05.a: Write a clear, polite notice with what, when and who.

g04u05l06.h: Notice check! Read the signs and show me what you know.
g04u05l06.c: A short look back at building words, notices and pronouns before the story unit.
g04u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **my, hom, haar** and the vocabulary of notices, such as **Die hysbak is buite werking.**
g04u05l06.a: See which notice words and pronouns are solid.

g04u06l01.h: A rainy morning, a bus stop and a stranger with an umbrella. A short story is about to start.
g04u06l01.c: Short stories are how you meet a language in its more human voice. This one is short, everyday and has a small mystery.
g04u06l01.t: **Die bushalte** (the bus stop), **sopnat** (soaking wet), **die vreemdeling** (the stranger) and **glimlag** (to smile). **Sopnat** is the sort of word that makes Afrikaans fun: **sop** means soup and **nat** means wet, so it’s soup-wet. Afrikaans is full of vivid compounds like this, and they make stories easier to remember.
g04u06l01.a: Read a short story that begins at a bus stop, with its key words in place.

g04u06l02.h: The wrong one. Everyone has taken the wrong umbrella at least once. Let’s look at the words in the story.
g04u06l02.c: Misunderstandings, mix-ups and small coincidences are the stuff of most short stories, and you’ll find them in everyday conversations too.
g04u06l02.t: **Verkeerd** (wrong), **omruil** (to swap), **herken** (to recognise), **haastig** (in a hurry) and **die handvatsel** (the handle). In sentences: **Ek ry elke oggend met die bus werk toe.** and **Sy het haastig by die deur uitgestap.** These are everyday verbs and adverbs that make a story vivid.
g04u06l02.a: Use the words you need to tell a small story of a mix-up.

g04u06l03.h: Grammar: when, how, where. In Afrikaans the order is always time, manner, place. English does it differently.
g04u06l03.c: Telling someone your plans, describing what you did or giving directions: whenever you say when, how and where together, the order matters.
g04u06l03.t: Afrikaans keeps a fixed order: **time, manner, place**. **Ek ry môre met die bus stad toe.** has **môre** (when), **met die bus** (how) and **stad toe** (where). You can also start with the time, and then the verb stays second: **Vanaand eet ons by my ma.** In the past, the **ge-** word goes to the end: **Ons het gister vinnig in die winkel ingegaan.**
g04u06l03.a: Build sentences with when, how and where in the right order.
g04u06l03.n: English tends to say the place first ("to town tomorrow"), which is why English speakers often put the words in the wrong order. Remember: **time first**.

g04u06l04.h: A short story about a wet Monday morning and an umbrella that isn’t quite right. I won’t spoil it.
g04u06l04.c: Short stories are a pleasure to read, and this one is about the kind of small mix-up that could happen on any rainy day.
g04u06l04.t: Sanele arrives at the bus stop in a hurry. There’s only one other person there, an old man with a big black umbrella. When the bus comes, Sanele grabs an umbrella from the wall. Look for **Dit was 'n nat Maandagoggend.**, **haastig** and the past tense with **het … ge-**, which tells you the story already happened. After the questions, retell the story in three sentences.
g04u06l04.a: Read a short story, put its events in order and retell it in three sentences.

g04u06l05.h: Write a new ending. Make it funny, make it kind, or make it dramatic. I’m hoping for a plot twist.
g04u06l05.c: Changing a story’s ending is a fun and low-pressure way to practise writing in a language, and it’s exactly how many writers start.
g04u06l05.t: Write a different ending of 25 to 40 words. Use the past tense, follow the time, manner, place order, and use words from the story such as **haastig, verkeerd** and **herken**. Keep the sentences short and clear. A good ending can be surprising, but it should still make sense of everything that came before.
g04u06l05.a: Write a short new ending to a story in the past tense.

g04u06l06.h: Story check! The last one in the first half of Graad 4.
g04u06l06.c: A short look at the story words and the time-manner-place order before Graad 5.
g04u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek ry môre met die bus stad toe.** and put the words in the right order.
g04u06l06.a: See whether your time-manner-place order is solid.

i4l1.h: Verbs are the engine of every sentence, and this unit gives you all three gears: now, then and later. We start with now.
i4l1.c: Telling someone what you do for a living, what you’re eating or where you live: the present tense is what you reach for first in every conversation.
i4l1.t: Afrikaans has one present-tense form for everyone: **ek werk, jy werk, sy werk, hulle werk**. There’s no separate "-ing" form either, so **Ons eet nou. Kom sit!** means both we eat now and we’re eating now. This lesson gives you four basic verbs: **eet** (eat), **drink** (drink), **slaap** (sleep) and **werk** (work), plus **Sy werk in Kaapstad.** to put them in a sentence.
i4l1.a: Say what you and other people do now, with four everyday verbs, and use one form for every person.
i4l1.n: No endings to memorise is one of the biggest gifts Afrikaans gives to learners. You can spend your energy on word order instead.

i4l2.h: Yesterday I flew, tomorrow I’ll fly. Let’s get the past and the future into your mouth.
i4l2.c: Telling a friend what you did last night, promising to do something tomorrow, or explaining that you’ve already eaten: you can’t have a real conversation in the present tense alone.
i4l2.t: The past is **het** plus **ge-** plus the verb, with the **ge-** word at the end: **Ons het gisteraand gebraai.** Verbs that already begin with **be-, ver-, ont-** or **her-** don’t take **ge-**. The future uses **sal**, as in **Ek sal dit môre doen.**, or **gaan** for a plan. Four new verbs come with it: **praat** (talk), **lees** (read), **koop** (buy) and **gaan** (go).
i4l2.a: Talk about what you did, what you’ve already done and what you’ll do tomorrow.

i4l3.h: What did you do? You’ll hear this question on every Monday morning of your life, so let’s practise the answers.
i4l3.c: Chatting to a colleague about the weekend, telling a friend what you got up to, or saying you’ve finished a book: past-tense sentences are what fill most small talk.
i4l3.t: Ask **Wat het jy die naweek gedoen?** and answer with a past-tense sentence: **Ek het die hele dag gewerk.** or **Ek het die boek klaar gelees.** Notice **klaar** (finished), which makes it clear you’ve completed the whole thing. For a plan, **Ek gaan gou winkel toe.** uses **gaan**, with **gou** meaning quickly or just.
i4l3.a: Ask someone what they did, answer in the past tense and mention a quick plan with **gaan**.

i4l4.h: Grammar: verbs that split in two. They’re a bit dramatic, but you’ll get used to them.
i4l4.c: Getting up, phoning someone back, getting off a bus: many of the most common everyday verbs have a small front part that gets separated from the rest.
i4l4.t: Verbs such as **opstaan** (get up), **afklim** (get off) and **terugbel** (call back) split in a normal sentence: **Ek staan elke oggend om sesuur op.** and **Ek bel jou later terug.** The small part goes to the end. In the past, **ge-** goes in the middle: **Ek het vanoggend laat opgestaan.** After **gaan, sal, wil, moet** or **kan**, the verb stays whole at the end: **Ek gaan hom môre opbel.**
i4l4.a: Use verbs that split, in the present, the past and after a helper verb.
i4l4.n: If a verb has a short word at the front like **op-, af-, aan-, uit-, in-** or **terug-**, there’s a good chance it splits. Watch for the little word at the end of the sentence.

i4l5.h: A diary entry. It’s Saturday, it’s a market day, there’s a braai and somebody is very tired. Sounds like a good day.
i4l5.c: Diaries, journals and personal blogs are written in a mixture of past, present and future, and reading one is a good test of everything you’ve just learned.
i4l5.t: The writer tells us what happened (**Vandag het ek vroeg opgestaan.**), what they did with Ouma (**Ek en Ouma het mark toe gegaan.**) and what’s coming (**Môre gaan ons kerk toe.**). Look for the three tenses and the verb **opstaan** splitting in the past. After the questions, write or say your own diary lines.
i4l5.a: Read a diary entry, tell the past, present and future apart, and write a short entry of your own.

i4l6.h: Tenses check! Past, present and future, all together.
i4l6.c: This check pulls together the three tenses and the split verbs before you move on to word order.
i4l6.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek het vanoggend laat opgestaan.** and **Ek sal dit môre doen.**, and choose the right tense for each. Anything you miss comes back in your review.
i4l6.a: See which tenses and split verbs you can use with confidence.

i5l1.h: The verb comes second. It’s the first rule of Afrikaans word order, and it will carry you a very long way.
i5l1.c: Starting a sentence with when, where or why instead of who is natural in everyday speech, and it’s the main reason learners end up with strange-sounding sentences.
i5l1.t: In a main sentence, the verb is always the second idea. If you start with something else, the verb jumps ahead of the person: **Vandag gaan ek werk toe.** and **Môre speel ons sokker.** After joining words such as **dat**, the verb goes to the end: **Ek weet dat hy moeg is.**
i5l1.a: Start a sentence with a time or place and keep the verb in second place, and send it to the end after **dat**.
i5l1.n: Think of it as the verb holding second place like a very polite guest: it will not go first, and it won’t go third.

i5l2.h: Nie … nie. The double negative that makes Afrikaans learners nervous. It’s actually quite logical.
i5l2.c: Saying you don’t drink coffee, that nobody’s home or that you’re not hungry: negative sentences are part of every conversation, and getting them right makes you sound natural.
i5l2.t: Afrikaans usually needs two **nie**s: one after the verb and one at the end of the sentence. **Ek drink nie koffie nie.** The words **niemand, nooit, niks** and **nêrens** also take a **nie** at the end: **Niemand is tuis nie.** and **Ek het nooit daar gewoon nie.** If the sentence ends right after the verb, one is enough: **Ek is nie honger nie.** has two, but **Ek weet nie.** has one.
i5l2.a: Make negative sentences with the double **nie** and the negative words.
i5l2.n: Listen for the second **nie** at the end of a sentence. Native speakers drop it in fast speech sometimes, but in writing it should always be there.

i5l3.h: Because, if and when: three words that make you sound like you’ve got opinions and a reason for them.
i5l3.c: Explaining why you’re staying in, what you do when it rains, or what happened when you were little: reasons and conditions are what turn short sentences into real explanations.
i5l3.t: **En, maar, of** and **want** change nothing: **Ek bly tuis, want ek is moeg.** But **omdat, dat, as, toe, terwyl** and **voordat** send the verb to the end: **Ek bly tuis omdat ek moeg is.** If the sentence starts with the **as** part, the main verb comes straight after the comma: **As dit reën, bly ons binne.** And **toe** works for the past, as in **Toe ek klein was, …**
i5l3.a: Join sentences with want, omdat, as and toe, and put the verb in the right place.

i5l4.h: Grammar: daarom and dus. Two small words that mean so, and a verb that comes straight after.
i5l4.c: Explaining a result (it rained, so we stayed in), writing an email about why you didn’t work, or giving a quick conclusion: these two words connect cause and effect.
i5l4.t: **Daarom** and **dus** both mean so or therefore. They count as the first idea, so the verb comes right after them: **Dit reën, daarom bly ons binne.** and **Ek was siek, dus het ek nie gewerk nie.** Compare the joining words: **maar** and **want** change nothing, **omdat** and **terwyl** send the verb to the end, and **daarom** and **dus** pull it forward.
i5l4.a: Say what happened as a result, using daarom and dus with the verb in second place.
i5l4.n: If you remember one thing, remember this: some joining words push the verb to the end, and some pull it forward. Listening to the examples will teach your ear which is which.

i5l5.h: An email to a manager, saying you’re ill. It’s polite, it’s clear and it has a reason. Perfect practice for the real thing.
i5l5.c: Writing to a manager to say you can’t come in is something almost everyone has to do, and the tone is formal but warm.
i5l5.t: The email has a subject line, a polite greeting (**Goeiemôre, me. Dlamini**), a reason with **want**, a plan and a closing. It uses **u** for the manager, which shows respect. Look for **Ek kan nie vandag werk toe kom nie**, **want ek het koors** and **Vriendelike groete**. After the questions, you’ll build a short message of your own.
i5l5.a: Read a polite email, see how a reason is given and write a short message of your own.

i5l6.h: Word-order check! Let’s see where those verbs end up.
i5l6.c: A look back at the verb in second place, the double nie and joining words before the unit on slang.
i5l6.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek bly tuis omdat ek moeg is.** and **Niemand is tuis nie.** Watch where the verb sits after each joining word.
i5l6.a: See which word-order patterns are solid.

i6l1.h: Jislaaik! This is how people really talk: the slang, the exclamations and the little words that textbooks leave out.
i6l1.c: Listen to any conversation on a South African street, in a taxi or at a braai, and you’ll hear these. Knowing them means you’ll follow real speech, not just the neat kind.
i6l1.t: **Jislaaik, dis warm!** is a mild exclamation of surprise. **Ag nee, man!** shows disappointment. **Ek is poegaai.** means you’re exhausted, and **Hy praat kaf.** means he’s talking nonsense. **Ek kom nou-nou.** means you’ll be there in a little while, and it’s famously vague.
i6l1.a: Recognise common slang and exclamations, and use a few of them yourself.
i6l1.n: **Nou-nou** is not "right now". It means something between in a minute and later today, which is why it’s the subject of so many South African jokes.

i6l2.h: Idioms: where Afrikaans gets creative. Translate them word for word and you’ll get a strange picture and a wrong meaning.
i6l2.c: Idioms turn up in conversation, in the news and in stories, and you’ll understand people better and sound more natural when you know the common ones.
i6l2.t: **'n Boer maak 'n plan.** means where there’s a will there’s a way: a farmer makes a plan. **Hy het die bal mis geslaan.** means he got it completely wrong. **Die aap is uit die mou.** means the cat’s out of the bag, and **Alles sal regkom.** means everything will be fine. Learn each one as a whole phrase, because the words alone won’t give you the meaning.
i6l2.a: Recognise four common idioms and use them in the right situation.
i6l2.n: Many Afrikaans idioms are quite visual: a monkey in a sleeve, a farmer with a plan. Picture the image and you’ll remember the meaning.

i6l3.h: More everyday slang. Think of it as the words that sound like Afrikaans at its most friendly.
i6l3.c: Ouch, popping a call through, loading a pickup: this is the language of the everyday, the kind you hear at home and on the road rather than in a classroom.
i6l3.t: **Eina, dis seer!** is ouch, that hurts. **Ek bel sommer net om te hoor hoe dit gaan.** shows **sommer** at work, meaning just or simply. **Gooi dit agterop die bakkie.** uses **bakkie**, the South African word for a pickup truck. **Hy is nogal slim.** means he’s actually quite clever, with **nogal** softening it.
i6l3.a: Understand and use everyday slang words such as **eina, sommer, bakkie** and **nogal**.

i6l4.h: Grammar: diminutives. In Afrikaans, small things aren’t always small. Sometimes it’s just how you say them with love.
i6l4.c: Ordering a coffee, asking for a bit of tart, giving someone a hug: the small form comes up constantly, and it makes you sound warm.
i6l4.t: Afrikaans uses the small form all the time, often to sound friendly rather than small: **'n koppie koffie, 'n drukkie, 'n stukkie melktert**. The ending depends on the sound: **-ie** (**kop** becomes **koppie**), **-jie** (**hond** becomes **hondjie**), **-tjie** (**stoel** becomes **stoeltjie**), **-etjie** (**bal** becomes **balletjie**) and **-pie** (**boom** becomes **boompie**). A short vowel doubles the consonant first.
i6l4.a: Make the small form of a noun and use it to sound friendly.
i6l4.n: If a South African offers you **'n koppietjie koffie**, they aren’t being stingy with the cup. It’s just a warm way to say a cup of coffee.

i6l5.h: A dialogue about a bakkie that won’t start. It has slang, an idiom and a very practical solution.
i6l5.c: Everyday dialogues between friends and colleagues are full of slang and idioms, and this one is a good example of how people really sound.
i6l5.t: Johan’s bakkie won’t start, Karin is worried about being late, and Johan comes up with an idiom and a plan. Look for **Jislaaik, die bakkie wil nie vat nie!**, **Ag nee, man!**, **'n Boer maak 'n plan.** and **Ons ry sommer met jou kar.** After the questions, tell the story back in your own words.
i6l5.a: Read a lively dialogue with slang and an idiom, and understand how the two friends solve their problem.

i6l6.h: Slang check! Jislaaik, you’ve come a long way.
i6l6.c: A final look at slang, idioms and diminutives before you move up to Graad 6.
i6l6.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die aap is uit die mou.** and **Kan ek 'n stukkie melktert kry?** and match the idioms to their meanings.
i6l6.a: See which slang words and idioms are solid.

g05u04l01.h: Sun, sand and a very stern lifeguard. The beach is a lovely place, so long as you know the words that keep you safe.
g05u04l01.c: South Africa has a long coastline with some beautiful, and sometimes dangerous, beaches. Signs, flags and lifeguards use this vocabulary, and a visitor who understands it is a safer swimmer.
g05u04l01.t: **Die lewensredder** (the lifeguard), **die vlae** (the flags), **die skeurstroom** (the rip current), **die gety** (the tide), **die branders** (the breakers) and **die sonskerm** (sunscreen). A **skeurstroom** is a narrow, fast current that pulls swimmers out to sea, and it’s one of the main reasons for beach warnings.
g05u04l01.a: Read and understand the key words on a beach-safety sign.
g05u04l01.n: Many South African beaches mark a safe swimming area with flags, and lifeguards watch that area. Swim between the flags, as the poster in this unit says.

g05u04l02.h: Stay safe. The most important two words at the beach, and I’m saying them in my bossiest hadeda voice.
g05u04l02.c: Warning signs, lifeguards' instructions and a friend telling you not to go in alone all use these words and phrases.
g05u04l02.t: **Veilig** (safe), **verdrink** (to drown), **alleen** (alone) and **waai** (to wave, as well as to blow) are your new words. In sentences: **Swem tussen die vlae.** and **Die lewensredder sit in die hoë stoel.** Also **Dit is gevaarlik om alleen te swem.** A very practical word list that you’ll see on signs.
g05u04l02.a: Understand safety warnings and say why something is safe or dangerous.

g05u04l03.h: Grammar: must, mustn’t and don’t have to. Three small verbs that give rules their shape.
g05u04l03.c: Rules on a poster, instructions from a lifeguard, house rules for guests: you’ll read and give rules in a gym, a pool, an office or a holiday home.
g05u04l03.t: **Moet** means must, and the other verb goes to the end: **Jy moet die reëls volg.** **Moenie … nie** means don’t: **Moenie alleen swem nie.** **Hoef nie … te … nie** means don’t have to: **Jy hoef nie 'n kaartjie te koop nie.** After **moet, kan** and **sal**, **het** becomes **hê**: **Kinders moet altyd 'n volwassene by hulle hê.**
g05u04l03.a: Give and read rules with must, don’t and don’t have to, and put the verbs in the right place.
g05u04l03.n: **Moenie** and **hoef nie** are very different. **Moenie** forbids something, while **hoef nie** just says it isn’t necessary.

g05u04l04.h: A beach-safety poster with numbered rules. Read it carefully, because a hadeda can’t rescue anyone.
g05u04l04.c: Posters and signs at beaches, pools and parks are written in short, clear rules, and they’re a very useful kind of real-life reading.
g05u04l04.t: The poster lists rules in a numbered list: swim only where there are lifeguards and between the red-and-yellow flags, never swim alone, and so on. Look for **Swem net waar daar lewensredders is**, **Moenie alleen swem nie.** and the reasons that follow each rule. After the questions, you’ll give a friend three beach rules yourself.
g05u04l04.a: Read a safety poster, understand each rule and give a friend three rules of your own.

g05u04l05.h: Write rules for a place you know: an office kitchen, a gym or a pool. Be firm, be fair, be funny if you must.
g05u04l05.c: Writing rules for a shared space is a very real task: a notice in a communal kitchen, house rules for guests or a sign at a gym.
g05u04l05.t: Write 40 to 60 words of rules for a place you know. Use **moet** for what people must do, **moenie … nie** for what they mustn’t, and **hoef nie … te … nie** for what’s optional. Number your rules and keep each one short and clear.
g05u04l05.a: Write a short, clear set of rules for a place you know.

g05u04l06.h: Safety check! Let’s see if your rules are in good order.
g05u04l06.c: A look back at beach words and rules before the hair salon.
g05u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **moet, moenie … nie** and **hoef nie … te … nie**, and the beach safety vocabulary.
g05u04l06.a: See which rule sentences and beach words you’ve got.

g05u05l01.h: A new look starts with the right words. I’m already perfect, thanks, but you may need a trim.
g05u05l01.c: Booking a haircut, explaining what you want or reading a salon’s price list: these are practical words in any town.
g05u05l01.t: **Die haarsalon** (the hair salon), **die haarkapper** (the hairdresser), **knip** (to cut hair with scissors), **die kuif** (the fringe) and **droogblaas** (to blow-dry). **Haarkapper** is hair plus cutter, and **droogblaas** is dry plus blow, so you can see the parts. You’ll need these when you describe what you want, whether that’s a trim, a new fringe or just a wash and blow-dry.
g05u05l01.a: Talk about a visit to the hairdresser and name the things you might ask for.

g05u05l02.h: Appointments: booking, moving and cancelling. The language of busy people, and of salons with full diaries.
g05u05l02.c: Phoning a salon, a doctor or a dentist to book or change an appointment is something you’ll do in any language. The sentences are short, and very repeatable.
g05u05l02.t: **Beskikbaar** (available), **verskuif** (to reschedule), **kanselleer** (to cancel) and **bevestig** (to confirm) are the key verbs. Ask **Is daar Donderdag nog plek?** (Is there still space on Thursday?) and **Kan ek my afspraak verskuif?** (Can I move my appointment?). The salon may ask you to confirm the time.
g05u05l02.a: Book, move, cancel and confirm an appointment on the phone.

g05u05l03.h: Grammar: questions. Yes-or-no questions start with the verb; the others begin with a question word.
g05u05l03.c: Phoning a salon, asking about opening times, asking how much something costs: you can only run a conversation if you can ask good questions.
g05u05l03.t: A yes-or-no question starts with the verb: **Kom jy môre?** With a question word, the order is question word, verb, subject: **Hoe laat maak julle oop?** and **Hoeveel kos 'n knipbeurt?** The useful words are **wie, wat, waar, wanneer, hoekom, hoe, hoeveel, watter** and **hoe laat**. In the past, the **ge-** word still goes to the end: **Hoekom het jy gekanselleer?**
g05u05l03.a: Ask yes-or-no questions and question-word questions in the right word order.

g05u05l04.h: A phone call to move an appointment. Listen to how polite and practical it is. That’s the model.
g05u05l04.c: Calling to change a booking is a skill you’ll use in a salon, a clinic or a restaurant, and the language is polite but short.
g05u05l04.t: Kwame phones a salon and asks to move his Thursday appointment because he has to work. The receptionist asks which day suits him best, and they agree a new time. Look for **Ek moet ongelukkig werk.**, **Kan ek dit verskuif?** and **Watter dag pas jou die beste?** After the questions, you’ll phone a salon or doctor yourself.
g05u05l04.a: Follow a phone call about moving an appointment and make a similar call yourself.

g05u05l05.h: Write a short dialogue: you book a table at a restaurant. You’re the customer, so be as polite as a hadeda at dawn. Which is to say, not very.
g05u05l05.c: Booking a table is a classic real-life dialogue, and writing one is a good way to practise questions and polite requests.
g05u05l05.t: Write a short dialogue of 40 to 60 words. Include a greeting, a request for a table, a number of people, a time, and a confirmation. Use questions such as **Hoe laat?** and **Vir hoeveel mense?** and polite phrases like **Ek wil graag … bespreek.**
g05u05l05.a: Write a short dialogue that books a table, using questions and polite requests.

g05u05l06.c: A look back at the salon words, appointments and questions before you look at how a town has changed.
g05u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild questions such as **Hoe laat maak julle oop?** and **Hoeveel kos 'n knipbeurt?**, and match appointment verbs to their meanings.
g05u05l06.a: See which questions and appointment words are solid.

g05u06l01.h: Towns change, shops open and close, and everyone has an opinion about how it used to be. Welcome to the nostalgia unit.
g05u06l01.c: Talking to a grandparent, reading a local history piece or comparing the old days to now: this vocabulary is how people talk about change.
g05u06l01.t: **Vroeër** (earlier, in the past), **destyds** (back then), **die verandering** (the change), **die winkelsentrum** (the shopping centre) and **die kleinkinders** (the grandchildren). Both **vroeër** and **destyds** point back in time, but **destyds** sounds a bit more like telling a story.
g05u06l01.a: Talk about how a place has changed, using words for earlier and back then.

g05u06l02.h: Bigger, busier and a little less quiet. That’s how most towns change, and here’s how to say it.
g05u06l02.c: Comparing your old home town with the present one, or listening to someone older describe how things used to be, uses exactly these words.
g05u06l02.t: **Groei** (to grow), **bou** (to build), **stil** (quiet) and **besig** (busy). In sentences: **Vroeër was die dorp baie stiller.**, **Destyds was daar net een winkel.** and **Die dorp het baie gegroei.** Notice **was** for the past of **is**. Pairing a then-sentence with a now-sentence, such as quieter then and busier now, is the easiest way to describe any change.
g05u06l02.a: Describe how a place was and how it has changed.

g05u06l03.h: Grammar: could, had to, wanted to. The past of the three most useful helpers.
g05u06l03.c: Talking about your childhood, explaining what you couldn’t do, or saying what you had to do: kon, moes and wou let you tell the story of your life.
g05u06l03.t: The past of **kan, moet** and **wil** is **kon, moes** and **wou**: **Ek kon nie swem nie.**, **Ons moes elke dag stap.** and **Sy wou dokter word.** You don’t need **het … ge-** with them. **Hê** in the past is **het … gehad**: **Ons het nie 'n motor gehad nie.** And **was** is the past of **is**.
g05u06l03.a: Say what you could, had to and wanted to do in the past, and use **gehad** and **was**.
g05u06l03.n: These three little words (**kon, moes, wou**) save you from building a long past tense. Just swap the helper and keep the rest of the sentence as it is.

g05u06l04.h: An interview with Ouma Sannie, who has lived in the same town all her life. She remembers when there was only one shop.
g05u06l04.c: Interviews with older people are a staple of local newspapers and community pages. They’re a good way to hear how people really tell stories.
g05u06l04.t: Sannie Ferreira is eighty-two and talks about how her town has changed. She describes what the town was like when she was young, what life was like without a car and what has changed now. Look for **Toe ek jonk was**, **kon, moes** and **wou**. After the questions, you’ll say how your own life was ten years ago.
g05u06l04.a: Read an interview about how a town has changed and talk about how your own life was ten years ago.

g05u06l05.h: Write about your life then and now. Ten years is a long time, and I’d love to hear what’s different.
g05u06l05.c: A short piece about then and now works for a blog, a social post or a letter to someone you haven’t seen in years.
g05u06l05.t: Write a paragraph of 40 to 60 words. Describe your life ten years ago using **kon, moes** or **wou**, and then describe how it is now. Use time words like **vroeër** and **nou** to make the contrast clear, and keep every sentence short. Two or three real details will be more convincing than a long list.
g05u06l05.a: Write a short paragraph that contrasts your life then and now.

g05u06l06.h: Last check of Graad 5! Then and now, and everything in between.
g05u06l06.c: A final look at the past helpers and the vocabulary of change before you move up to Graad 6.
g05u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek kon nie swem nie.** and **Ons het nie 'n motor gehad nie.** and use the past helpers correctly.
g05u06l06.a: See which past-tense patterns you’ve got.

i7l1.h: **Verskoon my, waar is die stasie?** Getting lost is how most people learn directions. Let’s make sure you don’t stay lost.
i7l1.c: Asking a stranger for the way, following a friend’s directions over the phone or reading a sign at an intersection: directions are one of the most practical things you’ll ever do in Afrikaans.
i7l1.t: Start politely with **Verskoon my** (excuse me), then ask **Waar is die stasie?** The answers use short commands: **Gaan reguit aan.** (go straight on) and **Draai links by die robot.** (turn left at the traffic light). **Dis aan jou regterkant.** says it’s on your right, and **Hoe ver is dit?** asks how far. In South Africa a traffic light is called a **robot**.
i7l1.a: Ask the way, follow simple directions and say where something is.
i7l1.n: **Robot** surprises English speakers: in South Africa it means a traffic light. When directions mention a **robot**, count the traffic lights, not the machines.

i7l2.h: Bus, train, taxi, plane: how to get from one place to another without losing your ticket or your temper.
i7l2.c: Buying a ticket, asking which taxi goes to town, hearing that the train is late or knowing when to get off: transport vocabulary is what you need on any trip.
i7l2.t: **Watter taxi gaan stad toe?** asks which minibus taxi goes to town, and **Een kaartjie Kaapstad toe, asseblief.** buys a ticket. **Die trein is laat.** is the sentence every commuter knows, and **Ek klim by die volgende halte af.** tells the driver where you’re getting off. Notice **toe** after the place when you’re going there.
i7l2.a: Ask about transport, buy a ticket and say where you’re getting off.
i7l2.n: Minibus taxis carry a large share of South Africa’s commuters, and passengers use hand signals to flag down the right one. It’s worth asking a local how it works.

i7l3.h: Grammar: in, on, under, next to. Little words that tell you exactly where something is.
i7l3.c: Describing where the pharmacy is, where you left the keys or which side of the road a shop is on: place words are what turn a vague direction into a clear one.
i7l3.t: Learn the set: **in, op, onder, langs, agter, voor, tussen, oorkant** and **by**. **Die apteek is oorkant die bank.** and **Die kafee is tussen die bank en die apteek.** show them in action. To say to a place, put **toe** after it: **Ons gaan stasie toe.** **By** means at a place or a person: **by die werk, by Ouma.**
i7l3.a: Say where things are with place words and use **toe** and **by** correctly.

i7l4.h: Directions to a house, written down. The kind you get when somebody says "you can’t miss it", and then you miss it.
i7l4.c: Written directions to a home, a farm or a venue are very common, because street numbers aren’t always easy to see and phone maps don’t always work.
i7l4.t: The text takes you step by step: straight on to the second traffic light, right into Kerkstraat, past the school, left at the petrol station. It ends with how to recognise the house: the third on the left, across from the park, with a green gate. Look for **reguit aan, draai regs, verby, oorkant** and the order numbers **tweede** and **derde**.
i7l4.a: Read written directions, follow them on a map and say where the house is.

i7l5.h: Directions check! Time to see whether you can find your way.
i7l5.c: A short look back at asking the way, using transport and place words before you go to the doctor.
i7l5.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Draai links by die robot.** and **Die kafee is tussen die bank en die apteek.** and pick the right place word. Anything you miss comes back in your review.
i7l5.a: See which direction words and place words you’ve got.

i8l1.h: Feeling ill is bad enough. Not being able to say so in Afrikaans would be worse. Let’s fix that.
i8l1.c: Phoning a doctor’s rooms, telling a colleague you’re unwell or explaining what’s wrong to a pharmacist: this is the language you need when you don’t feel great. (This unit is for language learning, not medical advice.)
i8l1.t: **Ek voel nie lekker nie.** says you don’t feel well. **My kop is seer.** says your head hurts, **Ek het koors.** says you have a fever and **Ek hoes al drie dae.** says you’ve been coughing for three days. To book, say **Ek wil graag 'n afspraak maak.** Notice **seer** is the word for sore or hurting.
i8l1.a: Say what’s wrong, how long it’s been and ask for an appointment.
i8l1.n: Note the double **nie** in **Ek voel nie lekker nie.** It’s the same pattern as every negative sentence you’ve learned.

i8l2.h: At the doctor and the pharmacy. The questions are short and the answers are practical. Let’s practise both sides.
i8l2.c: In the consulting room you’ll be asked what hurts and given simple instructions. At the pharmacy you’ll hear how to take things. This is everyday vocabulary, and it’s useful to understand. (Language practice only, not medical advice.)
i8l2.t: The doctor asks **Waar is dit seer?** and gives instructions such as **Drink twee pille per dag.** and **Jy moet rus en baie water drink.** To find a pharmacy, ask **Is daar 'n apteek naby?** Look at how **moet** sends the second verb to the end, as you learned before.
i8l2.a: Understand a doctor’s questions and simple instructions, and ask where the nearest pharmacy is.

i8l3.h: Grammar: the passive. When what happens matters more than who does it, Afrikaans has a neat trick.
i8l3.c: Medicine labels, signs, news reports and official letters all use the passive, because they’re more interested in what happens than in who does it.
i8l3.t: The passive puts the thing first. In the present, use **word** plus a **ge-** verb at the end: **Die pille word ná ete gedrink.** In the past, use **is**: **Die afspraak is vir Dinsdag gemaak.** To say who did it, add **deur**: **Die brief is deur die dokter geskryf.**
i8l3.a: Read and write simple passive sentences in the present and past, and say who did it with **deur**.
i8l3.n: You’ll meet the passive most on signs, labels and in news reports. In speech people often prefer the active form, but you need to understand both.

i8l4.h: A medicine label. Don’t worry, it’s a made-up one for language practice, so please don’t take anything based on it.
i8l4.c: Reading a label, a leaflet or a pharmacy instruction is a real-life skill, and the language is short, formal and full of commands. (This label is fictional, for learning only, and not medical advice.)
i8l4.t: The label for a cough syrup says to take it as the pharmacist or doctor prescribes, to shake the bottle before use, to keep it out of the reach of children and to consult a doctor if the cough lasts longer than a week. Look for **Neem**, **Skud die bottel voor gebruik.** and **Hou buite bereik van kinders.** Notice the commands with no **jy**.
i8l4.a: Read a short label, understand its instructions and warnings, and know that this one is for language practice only.

i8l5.h: Doctor check! Take a deep breath. And an Afrikaans one.
i8l5.c: A look back at the doctor, the pharmacy and the passive before you move on to small talk.
i8l5.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek voel nie lekker nie.** and **Die pille word ná ete gedrink.**, and tell the passive from the active. Anything you miss comes back later.
i8l5.a: See which doctor words and passive sentences are solid.

i9l1.h: **Aangename kennis!** Meeting someone new is the best reason to speak Afrikaans. Here’s what to ask, and what to say.
i9l1.c: At a braai, a work function or a first day at a new job, someone will ask where you’re from and what you do. These are the questions you’ll hear and the answers you’ll want ready.
i9l1.t: Greet with **Aangename kennis!** (pleased to meet you) and ask **Waar kom jy vandaan?** You can answer **Ek is van Durban.** Ask **Wat werk jy?** and say **Ek is 'n onderwyser.** There’s also a question about how long someone has lived somewhere, which makes for good conversation.
i9l1.a: Meet someone new, say where you’re from and what you do, and ask the same of them.
i9l1.n: Asking where somebody is from is one of the commonest openers in South Africa, and people are usually happy to tell you more than you asked.

i9l2.h: Hobbies and the weather: the two safest topics in the world. Perfect for a first conversation.
i9l2.c: Chatting to a neighbour, making conversation at a social event or filling an awkward silence in a lift: hobbies and the weather will always save you.
i9l2.t: **Wat doen jy in jou vrye tyd?** asks about hobbies, and **Ek hou van stap en lees.** answers. For the weather, **Dis 'n pragtige dag, nè?** invites agreement (the **nè** means isn’t it), and **Dit gaan vanmiddag reën.** looks ahead. A short answer and a question back keeps things going.
i9l2.a: Chat about hobbies and the weather, and keep a conversation going with a question.

i9l3.h: Grammar: reported speech. "She said she’s tired" is how you pass on news without sounding like a parrot.
i9l3.c: Telling someone what a friend said, passing on a message or asking what someone wants to know: reported speech is how a lot of real conversation works.
i9l3.t: Direct: **Sy sê: "Ek is moeg."** Indirect: **Sy sê dat sy moeg is.** Change the person and send the verb to the end after **dat**. In everyday speech **dat** is often dropped, and then the order stays normal: **Sy sê sy is moeg.** For yes-or-no questions use **of**: **Hy vra of jy Saterdag kom.** For others, keep the question word: **Sy wil weet waar jy werk.**
i9l3.a: Pass on what someone said, with or without **dat**, and report a question with **of** or a question word.
i9l3.n: Dropping **dat** is very common in speech, so you’ll hear both versions. In writing, especially formal writing, keep the **dat** and the verb at the end.

i9l4.h: An email from Johan, who wants to tell Sanet a bit about himself. It’s friendly, short and full of useful phrases.
i9l4.c: Introducing yourself by email is very common: for a new colleague, a pen friend, a flat share or an online group.
i9l4.t: Johan says where he’s from and where he lives now, what he does and what he does in his free time. He also passes on what his mother says. Look for **Dankie vir jou boodskap!**, **Ek is van Durban, maar …**, **In my vrye tyd** and **My ma sê ek lees te veel!** After the questions, you’ll pass on something someone said.
i9l4.a: Read a friendly introduction email and write a short reply about yourself.

i9l5.h: Last check of the Intermediate units! Small talk and reported speech.
i9l5.c: A short look back at meeting people, small talk and reported speech before you move into the new Graad 6 units.
i9l5.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Sy sê dat sy moeg is.** and **Hy vra of jy Saterdag kom.** and choose the right form for each.
i9l5.a: See which small-talk and reported-speech sentences are solid.

g06u04l01.h: First weeks are nerve-wracking, in any language. Here’s the vocabulary to describe the nerves, and survive them.
g06u04l01.c: Starting a new job or course, writing in a diary or telling a friend how your first week went: this is the vocabulary of new beginnings.
g06u04l01.t: **Die dagboek** (the diary), **senuweeagtig** (nervous), **die toegangskaart** (the access card), **die kollega** (the colleague) and **die opleiding** (the training). **Senuweeagtig** is a big word for something small: it’s built on the Afrikaans word for nerve. You’ll use it every time you describe a first day.
g06u04l01.a: Talk about a first week at work, with the words for nerves, colleagues and training.
