g06u04l02.h: Getting used to a new place: the wrong turns, the new faces and the first sip of satisfaction.
g06u04l02.c: Getting lost on your first day, being introduced to the team or feeling settled by Friday: these are the experiences everyone shares, and the words to describe them.
g06u04l02.t: **Verdwaal** (to get lost), **voorstel** (to introduce), **gewoond raak aan** (to get used to) and **tevrede** (satisfied). In sentences: **Ek was baie senuweeagtig.** and **Ek het twee keer in die gebou verdwaal.** Notice that **voorstel** splits in a normal sentence, like **opstaan** did.
g06u04l02.a: Describe getting lost, being introduced and getting used to something new.

g06u04l03.h: Grammar: before, after, while, as soon as, until. The joining words that put your day in order.
g06u04l03.c: Telling a story, writing a diary entry or explaining what you do before work: time words are how you show the order of events.
g06u04l03.t: **Voordat, nadat, terwyl, sodra** and **totdat** all send the verb to the end, just like **omdat**: **Ek drink koffie voordat ek begin werk.** If the sentence starts with one of them, the main verb follows the comma: **Nadat ek geëet het, het ek my e-pos gelees.** and **Terwyl ek wag, lees ek die handleiding.** With two verbs at the end, keep them together.
g06u04l03.a: Join two events in order with before, after, while, as soon as and until, with the verb in the right place.
g06u04l03.n: A diary is a perfect place to practise these words, because it’s all about the order of your day.

g06u04l04.h: A diary: a first week at a new job. Nerves, a missing breakfast and a very kind manager. I felt that.
g06u04l04.c: Diaries and personal blogs are a great way to read natural Afrikaans, because they’re written the way people think.
g06u04l04.t: The writer is so nervous on the first day that they can’t eat breakfast. After they get their access card, their manager introduces them to everyone. Look for **Liewe dagboek**, **so senuweeagtig dat …**, **Nadat ek my toegangskaart gekry het** and the past tense throughout. After the questions, tell about your own first day.
g06u04l04.a: Read a diary entry, follow the order of events and tell about your own first day.

g06u04l05.h: Write a diary entry about a day you remember. A first date? A first job? A very bad haircut? I’m all ears. Well, holes where ears are.
g06u04l05.c: Writing a short diary entry is one of the best ways to practise the past tense and your joining words, and it’s low pressure: nobody has to read it.
g06u04l05.t: Write 60 to 80 words about a day you remember. Use the past tense and at least two of **voordat, nadat, terwyl, sodra** and **totdat**. Start with the date and **Liewe dagboek**, and say how you felt, using words like **senuweeagtig** or **tevrede**.
g06u04l05.a: Write a short diary entry that shows the order of events and how you felt.

g06u04l06.h: Diary check! Let’s see how your joining words are.
g06u04l06.c: A look back at the first-week vocabulary and the time words before you write a formal letter.
g06u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **voordat, nadat, terwyl** and **sodra**, and fix the verb at the end of each.
g06u04l06.a: See which time-word sentences are solid.

g06u05l01.h: A pothole in your street, a streetlight that never works and a complaint letter waiting to be written. Welcome to civic life.
g06u05l01.c: Reporting a problem to a council, a landlord or a company is something most adults have to do, and writing a clear, polite complaint is a useful skill in any language.
g06u05l01.t: **Die munisipaliteit** (the municipality), **die slaggat** (the pothole), **die straatlig** (the streetlight), **die klagte** (the complaint) and **die verwysingsnommer** (the reference number). **Slaggat** is literally a hole made by a blow, but everyone just means a pothole. The reference number is important, because you’ll quote it if you follow up.
g06u05l01.a: Name the common problems in a street, and the words you need to report them.

g06u05l02.h: Dit is dringend: it’s urgent. Now to explain just how urgent, and why.
g06u05l02.c: When a problem is serious, such as damage to your car from a pothole or a streetlight that leaves a street dark, you need to explain it clearly and ask for action.
g06u05l02.t: **Aanmeld** (to report a problem), **die skade** (the damage), **kla** (to complain) and the phrase **Die saak is baie dringend.** (The matter is very urgent). In sentences: **Daar is 'n groot slaggat in Kerkstraat.** Describe the problem in a clear, factual way and say what you want done.
g06u05l02.a: Report a problem clearly, say how urgent it is and describe any damage.

g06u05l03.h: Grammar: formal letters. Meneer, mevrou and die uwe. You’re about to learn how to write like a diplomat.
g06u05l03.c: A formal letter to a council, a company or an official has a set layout and a polite tone. You’ll use it for complaints, applications and requests.
g06u05l03.t: Start with **Geagte** and a title and surname: **Geagte meneer Nkosi**. Use **u** for both you and your: **Kan u asseblief die slaggat herstel?** State your reason with **Ek skryf om te kla oor …** and ask politely: **Ek sou dit waardeer as u my kan laat weet.** End with **Ek sien uit na u antwoord**, then **Die uwe** and your full name.
g06u05l03.a: Write a formal letter with the right greeting, polite **u**, a clear reason and a proper closing.
g06u05l03.n: **Die uwe** literally means "yours" (yours faithfully). It’s the standard closing in a formal letter, and you’ll see it on letters from banks, councils and schools.

g06u05l04.h: A letter of complaint about a pothole and a streetlight. Formal, firm and perfectly polite: the gold standard.
g06u05l04.c: A model complaint letter is useful because it shows the exact layout, tone and phrases that you can reuse for your own letters.
g06u05l04.t: Thandi writes to the municipal manager about two problems in her street. The letter has her address, the date, the addressee, a greeting, a subject line in capitals, the reasons for writing, a polite request and a closing. Look for **Geagte heer/dame**, **KLAGTE: SLAGGAT EN STRAATLIG** and **Ek skryf om te kla oor …** After the questions, report a problem by phone.
g06u05l04.a: Read a formal complaint letter, spot its parts and report a problem in your own words.

g06u05l05.h: Write your own complaint letter. Choose a pothole, a late delivery or a noisy neighbour. I’d choose the neighbours.
g06u05l05.c: A formal complaint is a real-life task. Doing it in a second language is a challenge, and getting it right is a very satisfying achievement.
g06u05l05.t: Write the body of a formal letter, 60 to 80 words. State why you’re writing with **Ek skryf om te kla oor …**, describe the problem factually, say what you’d like done with **Kan u asseblief …?** or **Ek sou dit waardeer as …**, and use **u** throughout. Keep the tone polite, even if you’re cross.
g06u05l05.a: Write a clear, polite complaint letter in the formal style.

g06u05l06.h: Formal-letter check! Geagte student, let’s see how you do.
g06u05l06.c: A look back at the municipal vocabulary and the formal layout before you tackle the compost unit.
g06u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Kan u asseblief die slaggat herstel?** and **Ek sou dit waardeer as u my kan laat weet.**, and use **u** correctly.
g06u05l06.a: See which formal phrases are solid.

g06u06l01.h: Compost: turning scraps into gold. It’s an information text, and it’s also a very useful thing to know how to do.
g06u06l01.c: Information texts about everyday topics, such as gardening, recycling or cooking, appear on websites, leaflets and in magazines, and they’re a good way to read facts in Afrikaans.
g06u06l01.t: **Die kompos** (compost), **die afval** (waste, scraps), **die skille** (peels), **die houer** (the container) and **die wurms** (the worms). You’ll meet them in a text on how to make compost from kitchen and garden waste. **Afval** is a very useful word: it covers any scraps or rubbish you throw away.
g06u06l01.a: Understand the words for a how-to text on compost.

g06u06l02.h: Damp and patient: the two main qualities of any good compost heap, and any good Afrikaans learner.
g06u06l02.c: Reading instructions that explain how to do something over time, such as keeping a compost heap going, uses descriptive words and a few warnings.
g06u06l02.t: **Omdraai** (to turn over), **klam** (damp), **geduldig** (patient) and **die omgewing** (the environment). A good sentence to know: **Die hoop moet so klam soos 'n uitgedrukte spons wees.** (The heap must be as damp as a wrung-out sponge.) Another: **Moenie vleis of olie bysit nie.** (Don’t add meat or oil.) You’ll recognise **so … soos** from earlier.
g06u06l02.a: Understand the main instructions for a compost heap, including what to avoid.

g06u06l03.h: Grammar: linking words. Firstly, furthermore, therefore, yet. The vocabulary of every good essay.
g06u06l03.c: Information texts, essays, reports and summaries all rely on linking words to show how ideas fit together: order, adding, result and contrast.
g06u06l03.t: Linking words show how a text is built: order (**eerstens, tweedens, laastens**), adding (**verder, boonop**), result (**daarom**) and contrast (**tog, maar**). When **eerstens, verder, boonop, daarom** or **tog** starts a sentence, the verb comes next: **Daarom gooi ons minder weg.** **Maar** and **want** don’t change the order.
g06u06l03.a: Join your points with linking words for order, adding, result and contrast, and put the verb in the right place.
g06u06l03.n: Linking words are what make a summary read well. Even a few of them make your own writing feel more organised.

g06u06l04.h: An information text about making compost. It’s clear, practical and a pleasure to read. Also, I like worms.
g06u06l04.c: A short information text like this one is exactly the kind of source you’ll summarise in the next lesson.
g06u06l04.t: The text explains that a large share of household rubbish is food and garden waste, which turns into rich, dark soil within a few months if you compost it. It says compost is easy to make, yet few people do it, and then it gives the main steps. Look for the linking words **eerstens, verder** and **tog**. After the questions, explain how to make compost in three sentences.
g06u06l04.a: Read an information text, find its main points and explain how to do it in three sentences.

g06u06l05.h: Time to summarise: five tips, one paragraph, fifty to sixty words, your own words. It’s harder than it sounds, and more useful than it looks.
g06u06l05.c: Summarising is a real-life skill, whether you’re pulling the key points from an article for a colleague or condensing instructions for a friend.
g06u06l05.t: Choose the five real tips from the compost text, leaving out the introduction and the examples. Then write one paragraph of 50 to 60 words in full sentences and in your own words, using linking words such as **eerstens, verder** and **laastens**. After you write, compare with the model answer.
g06u06l05.a: Pick the main points from a text and summarise them in one clear paragraph of 50 to 60 words.

g06u06l06.h: The last check of Graad 6! Compost, linking words and a whole year behind you.
g06u06l06.c: A final look at the unit, and at everything you’ve done in Graad 6, before the next level.
g06u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences with **eerstens, verder, daarom** and **tog**, and the compost vocabulary, such as **die afval** and **die kompos**.
g06u06l06.a: See which linking words and compost words are solid.

g07u01l01.h: Everybody has an opinion, and a hadeda has several, usually at five in the morning. Let’s learn to share yours in Afrikaans, with reasons.
g07u01l01.c: In a meeting, at a family braai or in a comment thread, someone will ask what you think and why. Giving an opinion, agreeing and disagreeing politely is what turns you from a listener into a real participant in the conversation, and it’s the skill this whole unit builds, from a newspaper debate to an e-mail of your own.
g07u01l01.t: Five words to start: **die mening** (the opinion), **die rede** (the reason), **saamstem** (to agree), **verskil** (to differ or disagree) and **die voorstel** (the proposal). **Saamstem** is a separable verb, so in a sentence the small part jumps to the end: **Ek stem saam.** You’ll hear it everywhere. These are the words of every debate, from a work meeting to a family argument about where to go on holiday, so they’re worth learning properly.
g07u01l01.a: Name an opinion, give a reason, and say whether you agree or disagree.
g07u01l01.n: Afrikaans can sound very direct, but speakers usually soften a disagreement. Learn the polite forms in this unit and you’ll sound firm without sounding rude.

g07u01l02.h: Home or office? It’s the debate of our age, and a very good one for practising opinions.
g07u01l02.c: Working from home has become a normal topic of conversation, so you’ll hear people argue for and against it at work, in the news and at dinner.
g07u01l02.t: **Die kollegas** (colleagues), **eensaam** (lonely), **buigsaam** (flexible) and **indeel** (to divide up your time) set the scene. To agree, say **Ek stem saam met jou.** To disagree strongly, say **Ek stem glad nie saam nie.** (I don’t agree at all). Back up your view with a reason: **Die rede is dat ek ver van die kantoor af bly.** Notice the verb at the end after **dat**.
g07u01l02.a: Agree and disagree with someone’s view, and give a reason for your own.
g07u01l02.n: **Glad nie** is a handy phrase: it means not at all, and it makes a negative sentence much stronger.

g07u01l03.h: Grammar: giving your opinion. There are several ways, and each changes where the verb goes.
g07u01l03.c: Arguing a point in a meeting, writing a review or replying to a friend’s idea: the way you phrase an opinion decides whether you sound clear, polite or accidentally rude.
g07u01l03.t: After **Na my mening** and **Volgens my**, the verb comes next: **Na my mening is dit 'n goeie plan.** After **Ek dink dat …**, the verb goes to the end: **Ek dink dat ons meer van die huis af moet werk.** In speech people often drop **dat**, and then the order stays normal: **Ek dink die vergadering is te lank.** Weigh up both sides with **Aan die een kant … aan die ander kant …**, and give a reason with **omdat** or **want**.
g07u01l03.a: Give an opinion in three different ways, put the verb in the right place and weigh up both sides.
g07u01l03.n: If you’re unsure, **Ek dink …** with the normal word order is the safest everyday choice. Save **Ek dink dat …** for writing and more careful speech.

g07u01l04.h: Two readers, one question, opposite answers: should people work from home? Read both, then pick a side.
g07u01l04.c: Opinion columns and reader letters in newspapers and magazines follow a clear pattern: a position, reasons for it and a firm ending. Reading a pair that disagree is the quickest way to see both sides of a topic and to borrow the language they use.
g07u01l04.t: The magazine asks its readers whether people should work from home more. Nomsa Dube, an accountant, says yes: she saves two hours a day in traffic, though she has to be disciplined because **die wasgoed roep altyd!** Johan Pretorius, a designer, says no: he felt lonely, and he’d rather learn from experienced colleagues. Watch for **Aan die een kant**, **Aan die ander kant**, **Na my mening** and **Ek stem saam dat …**, and notice that Johan agrees with part of Nomsa’s argument. After the questions, you’ll give your own opinion and both sides.
g07u01l04.a: Read two opposing opinions, pick out each writer’s reasons, and give your own view with both sides.

g07u01l05.h: Time to write: a friend is thinking of a fully remote job, and you’ve got thoughts. Be kind, be clear and give two good reasons.
g07u01l05.c: Giving advice in writing is something you’ll do all the time, to a friend, a colleague or a family member who’s about to make a decision. A short e-mail with a clear opinion and reasons is exactly what people appreciate.
g07u01l05.t: Write an e-mail of 60 to 80 words. Open with a greeting, give your opinion with **Na my mening** or **Ek dink dat …**, support it with two reasons using **omdat** or **want**, and end warmly. You can borrow ideas from the two readers in the last lesson, such as the traffic you’d save or the colleagues you’d miss. Keep your sentences clear, and watch where the verb goes after **dat** and **omdat**.
g07u01l05.a: Write a short e-mail that gives an opinion with two reasons.

g07u01l06.h: Opinions check! Let’s see whether you can argue your case.
g07u01l06.c: A look back at agreeing, disagreeing and giving reasons before you open a poem.
g07u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Na my mening is dit 'n goeie plan.** and **Ek stem glad nie saam nie.** Watch where the verb goes in each, and which phrases soften or strengthen an opinion.
g07u01l06.a: See which opinion phrases and word-order patterns are solid.

g07u02l01.h: Poems! They don’t scare me. I’m a bird, and we sing all the time. Let’s learn how to talk about them.
g07u02l01.c: Poetry is part of every language’s heart, and reading a poem is a way to hear Afrikaans in a more musical register. You’ll find poems in school books, on posters in coffee shops and in literary magazines, and talking about them is a regular part of English and Afrikaans classes.
g07u02l01.t: Five words for talking about poetry: **die gedig** (the poem), **die strofe** (the stanza), **die versreël** (the line), **rym** (to rhyme) and **die beeld** (the image). A poem is made of lines grouped into stanzas, and the pictures it paints in your head are what stay with you. Not every poem rhymes, especially modern ones, so don’t expect it.
g07u02l01.a: Talk about the parts of a poem: lines, stanzas, rhyme and images.

g07u02l02.h: The city wakes up like a tired giant. That’s not just a pretty line, it’s a technique, and you’re about to learn its name.
g07u02l02.c: A modern poem about a city morning uses ordinary things, such as concrete, noise and pavements, to make a picture. Learning the words for those things helps you read, and enjoy, the poem.
g07u02l02.t: **Die reus** (the giant), **die beton** (concrete), **die sypaadjie** (the pavement) and **die lawaai** (the noise). The lesson’s key line is **Die stad word wakker soos 'n moeë reus.** (The city wakes up like a tired giant), and the next one carries on: **Hy rek sy arms van beton en glas.** Notice how the poet treats the city as a person.
g07u02l02.a: Understand the vocabulary of a city poem and recognise a comparison when you see one.

g07u02l03.h: Grammar: figurative language. Similes, metaphors and personification, the three tools of every poet.
g07u02l03.c: Poems, song lyrics, advertisements and everyday speech are full of figurative language. Spotting it helps you understand what’s meant rather than what’s literally said.
g07u02l03.t: A **vergelyking** (simile) compares with **soos** or **so … soos**: **Die water is so koud soos ys.** A **metafoor** (metaphor) says one thing is another: **My hart is 'n trom wat vinnig slaan.** **Personifikasie** gives a thing human actions: **Die wind fluit.** A poem is built from **versreëls** and **strofes**, and some rhyme while many modern ones don’t.
g07u02l03.a: Spot a simile, a metaphor and personification, and write one of each.
g07u02l03.n: If you see **soos**, it’s a simile. If something simply *is* something else, it’s a metaphor. If a thing does something only a person could do, it’s personification.

g07u02l04.h: A poem called Maandagoggend: Monday morning. Read it aloud, because poems are meant to be heard.
g07u02l04.c: Reading a poem aloud is the best way to feel the rhythm of a language. A short modern poem about an ordinary scene is a gentle introduction, since you can recognise the things in it before you worry about what it means.
g07u02l04.t: The poem shows a city waking up: the giant of concrete and glass, impatient taxis, a woman at a bus stop with her coffee, newspapers fluttering like birds without a nest, and then a child laughing on the pavement. Read it aloud once, then look for the simile in the first line and the personification further on. After the questions, choose your favourite line and say why you like it.
g07u02l04.a: Read a modern poem aloud, spot the figurative language, and say which line you like best and why.

g07u02l05.h: Write your own poem: thirty to sixty words, one place, one simile and one example of personification. I’m hoping for a hadeda cameo.
g07u02l05.c: Writing a short poem is a low-pressure way to play with a language. There are no wrong answers, only good and better images, and a poem is a nice thing to give someone.
g07u02l05.t: Choose a place you know well: your kitchen, a beach or a taxi rank. Write a poem of 30 to 60 words with one comparison using **soos**, for example **helder soos 'n klokkie**, and one example of personification, where the place does something only a person could do, like **Die wind fluit.** Keep the lines short, and don’t worry about rhyme. Look back at Maandagoggend for ideas on how to build a picture from small details.
g07u02l05.a: Write a short poem with a simile and an example of personification.

g07u02l06.h: Poem check! Let’s see how well you read between the lines.
g07u02l06.c: A short look back at poetry words and figurative language before you read a short story.
g07u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die kind se lag is helder soos 'n klokkie.** and **My hart is 'n trom wat vinnig slaan.**, and sort similes from metaphors.
g07u02l06.a: See which poetry words and figures of speech are solid.

g07u03l01.h: What makes a story? Characters, a setting, a problem and a way out. Once you see those four, every story opens up.
g07u03l01.c: Whether you’re reading a short story for pleasure, discussing a film with friends or telling someone about your day, the same building blocks are at work. Knowing the words for them lets you talk about stories in Afrikaans, and in this unit you’ll read one and then write your own.
g07u03l01.t: **Die karakter** (the character), **die ruimte** (the setting, in time and place), **die konflik** (the conflict), **die intrige** (the plot) and **die misverstand** (the misunderstanding). The story in this unit is built on a misunderstanding, which is one of the oldest and most reliable ways to start a plot. Think about what a character wants and what’s getting in the way, and you’ll find the conflict.
g07u03l01.a: Talk about a story’s characters, setting, conflict and plot.

g07u03l02.h: The removal truck arrives and the neighbours are watching from the window. What could possibly go wrong?
g07u03l02.c: Moving house, new neighbours and the noise that comes with both: it’s a situation almost everyone has lived through. This lesson gives you the words for the story, so that when you read it, nothing slows you down.
g07u03l02.t: **Verhuis** (to move house), **die verhuiswa** (the removal truck), **die rolstoel** (the wheelchair) and **die oprit** (the ramp) set the scene. Then look at the time expressions that move a story along: **Presies om sewe-uur het die lawaai begin.** (At exactly seven o’clock the noise started) and **Op die vierde aand was haar geduld op.** (On the fourth night her patience ran out). Time phrases like these are how a writer keeps a plot moving.
g07u03l02.a: Use the vocabulary of moving house and the time phrases that move a story along.

g07u03l03.h: Grammar: reflexive verbs. Some Afrikaans verbs need a self word, and English barely notices.
g07u03l03.c: Describing how someone felt, owning up to a mistake or telling a friend not to worry: reflexive verbs show up whenever emotions or small personal actions are involved, so you’ll hear them daily.
g07u03l03.t: Some verbs need a self word: **ek vergis my, jy haas jou, hy skaam hom, sy verbeel haar.** English often has nothing there: **Ek vergis my** means I’m mistaken. Learn the whole sentences: **Ek het my heeltemal vergis.**, **Marike het haar diep geskaam.** and **Moenie jou bekommer nie.** Don’t add **-self** to these everyday verbs, and keep it for emphasis, as in **Hulle dink net aan hulleself.** In the past, verbs starting with **be-, ver-, ge-, er-, her-** or **ont-** don’t take **ge-**.
g07u03l03.a: Use common reflexive verbs correctly, in the present and in the past.
g07u03l03.n: Learn these as little chunks, not word for word. If you try to translate **ek vergis my** literally you’ll end up confused.

g07u03l04.h: A short story about new neighbours, a lot of noise and a spectacular misunderstanding. Don’t peek at the ending.
g07u03l04.c: A short story is ideal for close reading: long enough to follow a plot, short enough to read twice. Reading it twice, once for what happens and once for how it’s told, is the best way to learn from it.
g07u03l04.t: Marike watches the Naidoo family move in next door: a man, a woman, two teenagers and a grandmother in a wheelchair. The next evening, at exactly seven o’clock, a noise begins, and it goes on the evening after that too. By the fourth night, Marike has had enough. Look for the character, the setting, the conflict and how it all turns out, and notice how many reflexive verbs the writer uses. After the questions, tell the story in three sentences: beginning, conflict and end.
g07u03l04.a: Read a short story, name its character, setting, conflict and resolution, and retell it in three sentences.

g07u03l05.h: Write your own story about a misunderstanding. Eighty to a hundred words, and an ending that makes the reader smile.
g07u03l05.c: Writing a short story brings together everything you’ve learned about tenses, joining words and vocabulary, and it’s one of the most rewarding things you can write.
g07u03l05.t: Write 80 to 100 words about a misunderstanding with a neighbour, a colleague or a friend. Use the past tense and at least two reflexive verbs, such as **Ek het my vergis.** or **Sy het haar geskaam.** Give your story a clear beginning, a conflict and an end, and use time phrases like **presies om** and **die volgende aand** to move it along. A small surprise in the last sentence makes the story memorable.
g07u03l05.a: Write a short story with a clear plot, in the past tense, using reflexive verbs.

g07u03l06.h: Story check! Let’s see who’s been paying attention.
g07u03l06.c: A short look back at story vocabulary and reflexive verbs before you read an email from overseas.
g07u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek het my heeltemal vergis.** and **Marike het haar diep geskaam.** Watch the reflexive word and the past tense.
g07u03l06.a: See which story words and reflexive verbs are solid.

g07u04l01.h: Far from home. Plenty of families have someone living overseas, so this vocabulary is very real.
g07u04l01.c: Talking to friends and family who live abroad, or living abroad yourself, means talking about leaving, missing people and adjusting. These words give you the language of emigration, and they set up the e-mail you’ll read from a friend in Perth.
g07u04l01.t: **Emigreer** (to emigrate), **die heimwee** (homesickness), **aanpas** (to adjust, adapt), **die tydsverskil** (the time difference) and **die visum** (the visa). **Heimwee** is a lovely word: it’s built from the Afrikaans word for home and the word for pain. Note that **aanpas** is separable, so you’ll hear it as **Hulle pas goed aan** when someone is settling in well.
g07u04l01.a: Talk about living abroad, using words for emigrating, homesickness and the time difference.

g07u04l02.h: Ek verlang na julle: I miss you all. A warm sentence to learn, and an easy one to use.
g07u04l02.c: Writing to someone far away, or telling them you miss them, uses a simple and warm vocabulary that you’ll use for the rest of your life, from a message to a cousin to a card to an old friend.
g07u04l02.t: **Verlang** (to long for, miss), **gewoond** (used to), **vreemd** (strange) and **die video-oproep** (the video call). In sentences: **Ek verlang na my familie.** and **Ek is nog nie gewoond aan die koue nie.** Notice that **verlang** takes **na**, so in Afrikaans you long *for* someone with **na**. The time difference also gets a sentence, and it’s a topic anyone with family overseas will recognise.
g07u04l02.a: Say that you miss someone, describe what’s still strange, and talk about a video call.

g07u04l03.h: Grammar: al, sedert, gelede. How long have you been living there? The answer is surprisingly simple.
g07u04l03.c: Telling someone how long you’ve lived somewhere, how long you’ve worked at a job or how long ago something happened is one of the most common things you’ll say in a conversation.
g07u04l03.t: For something that started in the past and is still going on, Afrikaans uses the **present** tense with **al**: **Ons woon al drie jaar in Perth.** For a point in time, use **sedert**: **Sedert Januarie werk ek by 'n hospitaal.** For something finished, use **gelede** with the past tense: **Ons het drie jaar gelede geëmigreer.** Don’t say **vir drie jaar** for something still going on.
g07u04l03.a: Say how long something has been going on, since when and how long ago it happened.
g07u04l03.n: English speakers often say "for three years" and reach for **vir**. Afrikaans uses **al** and the present tense instead, and it sounds much more natural.

g07u04l04.h: An e-mail from Annelize in Perth: she’s sorry she hasn’t written, she has news and she misses home. Read it as if it were meant for you.
g07u04l04.c: E-mails between friends who live far apart are lovely to read: personal, a little apologetic, and full of everyday news. They’re also full of the time words you’ve just learned.
g07u04l04.t: Annelize writes to her friend Busi. She apologises for not writing sooner and says they’ve now lived in Perth for three years. Since January she’s worked at a hospital near the sea, and Pieter started his own business last month. Her children speak English with an Australian accent, but at home they speak only Afrikaans. She misses Saturday mornings at the market, and she says that nobody there knows what a **koeksister** is. Find **al drie jaar**, **Sedert Januarie** and **drie jaar gelede**. After the questions, you’ll talk about what you’ve been doing for a long time and what you did long ago.
g07u04l04.a: Read a friendly e-mail from abroad, find how long and since when, and talk about your own long-running habits.
g07u04l04.n: She ends with an invitation: **Kom kuier liewer vir ons!** Telling a friend to come and visit is a warm way to close an e-mail.

g07u04l05.h: Write a reply to Annelize. Tell her what you’ve been up to, and ask her something back, because friends write back.
g07u04l05.c: Replying to a friendly e-mail is something you’ll do for the rest of your life, and it’s the ideal place to use **al**, **sedert** and **gelede** together in a natural way.
g07u04l05.t: Write 60 to 80 words. Say what you’ve been doing for a while using **al**, mention something that happened not long ago with **gelede**, and say whether you’re planning to visit her. Use **sedert** with a clear point in time, and end with a question for her. Annelize mentions her work, the beach, the market and the flights, so you have plenty to respond to.
g07u04l05.a: Write a friendly reply that uses al, sedert and gelede correctly.

g07u04l06.h: Perth check! Let’s see whether you’ve got the timing right.
g07u04l06.c: A look back at living abroad, missing people and the time words before you read a magazine profile.
g07u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ons woon al drie jaar in Perth.** and **Ons het drie jaar gelede geëmigreer.** and choose between **al, sedert** and **gelede**.
g07u04l06.a: See which time words are solid.

g07u05l01.h: Some people make a difference without making any noise. Hettie salutes them, and takes notes.
g07u05l01.c: Magazine profiles, community newsletters and local news often celebrate people who give their time to others. Reading one is a gentle way to practise longer sentences, and the words in this lesson are the ones those profiles use again and again.
g07u05l01.t: **Die profiel** (the profile), **die vrywilliger** (the volunteer), **die sopkombuis** (the soup kitchen), **skenk** (to donate) and **die gemeenskap** (the community). **Sopkombuis** is a compound word: soup plus kitchen, a kitchen that serves soup. Afrikaans is very good at gluing words together like this, so when you meet a long word, try splitting it into its parts.
g07u05l01.a: Talk about community work and volunteers, with the words you need for a profile.

g07u05l02.h: Every contribution counts: small acts, big difference, and a lot of vegetables.
g07u05l02.c: Describing what someone does for others, and why it matters, is the heart of a profile. Here you’ll learn the verbs and adjectives that do that job, and see them in short sentences with real numbers.
g07u05l02.t: **Ondersteun** (to support), **inspireer** (to inspire), **toegewyd** (dedicated) and **die bydrae** (the contribution). In sentences: **Boere skenk elke week groente.** and **Hulle kook elke dag tweehonderd borde kos.** These are short, clear sentences with specific details, which is exactly how a good profile reads, because details are more convincing than general praise. Try saying each one aloud, then swap in your own numbers and your own community.
g07u05l02.a: Describe what a person or group contributes, with specific details.

g07u05l03.h: Grammar: relative clauses. The vrou wat, the man met wie: how to add information without starting a new sentence.
g07u05l03.c: Describing someone as "the woman who runs the soup kitchen" or "the man I work with" lets you say much more in one sentence, and it’s how longer, more natural writing is built.
g07u05l03.t: **Wat** adds information about a person or thing, with the verb at the end of that part: **Die vrou wat die sopkombuis bestuur, is my buurvrou.** After a preposition, use **wie** for people: **die man met wie ek werk** and **die kinders vir wie sy kook**. For things, join the preposition to **waar-**: **die pot waarin sy kook** and **die bakkie waarmee hulle ry**. **Wie se** means whose.
g07u05l03.a: Use wat, wie and waar- words to add information to a sentence.
g07u05l03.n: You may hear **wat se** in speech, but write **wie se** for whose. Teachers and editors will thank you.

g07u05l04.h: Ma Dora’s big pot: a profile of a woman who feeds a whole community, one plate at a time.
g07u05l04.c: Profiles in community magazines are written to inform and inspire, and they’re built from short facts, a few quotes and some well-chosen details. This one is a very good model to borrow from.
g07u05l04.t: Every weekday at twelve o’clock, a queue forms outside the old church hall in Rivierdal. The people are waiting for Dora Mthembu, who has run the community soup kitchen for eleven years. She started with one pot of soup, and now she and twelve volunteers cook about two hundred plates a day. Farmers donate vegetables, a bakery sends bread, and her dream is a vegetable garden behind the hall. Look for the relative clauses with **wat**, **wie se** and **waarin**, and for the quotes in Dora’s own words. After the questions, talk about someone you admire.
g07u05l04.a: Read a magazine profile, find the facts and quotes, and talk about someone you admire.

g07u05l05.h: Write a profile of someone in your community you admire: eighty to a hundred words, and at least three relative clauses.
g07u05l05.c: Writing a profile means choosing what matters most about a person and saying it clearly, which is a skill you’ll use in a bio, a speech or a newsletter.
g07u05l05.t: Write 80 to 100 words about someone you admire. Say who they are, what they do and why it matters. Use at least three relative clauses with **wat, met wie, waarmee** or **vir wie**, and include one specific detail, such as a number or a place, the way the writer did for Dora. If you can add a short quote, even better. Keep it factual and warm, and check each relative clause for the verb at the end.
g07u05l05.a: Write a short profile of a person you admire, using relative clauses.

g07u05l06.h: Profile check! Let’s see if your relative clauses hold up.
g07u05l06.c: A look back at community vocabulary and relative clauses before the sleep unit.
g07u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die vrou wat die sopkombuis bestuur, is my buurvrou.** and **Dit is die man met wie ek werk.**, and choose between **wat, wie** and **waar-** words.
g07u05l06.a: See which relative clauses are solid.

g07u06l01.h: Tired, sleepy and a bit grumpy: sleep is a topic everyone has an opinion on. (This is language practice, not health advice.)
g07u06l01.c: Information texts about everyday topics, like sleep, appear in magazines and on websites, and reading them is a good way to practise longer, factual sentences. Everything in this unit is for language learning only, not for medical or health advice.
g07u06l01.t: **Die slaaptyd** (bedtime), **slapeloos** (sleepless), **die kafeïen** (caffeine), **die moegheid** (tiredness) and **vaak** (sleepy). **Slapeloos** is built from the word for sleep plus **-loos**, meaning without. Words ending in **-loos** are common in Afrikaans, so once you know the ending, you’ll recognise many more of them. Say each new word aloud once, and then try it in a sentence about your own evenings.
g07u06l01.a: Talk about sleep and tiredness, using the vocabulary of an information text.

g07u06l02.h: Screens and sleep: the great modern trouble. Let me put my phone down while we learn the words. (Language practice, not health advice.)
g07u06l02.c: Magazine articles and websites about everyday topics are written in clear, direct sentences, and they often give advice. You’ll learn the vocabulary here, and you’ll use it in the information text in the same unit. It’s for language learning, not health advice.
g07u06l02.t: **Konsentreer** (to concentrate), **die skerm** (the screen), **ontspan** (to relax) and **die luukse** (the luxury). In sentences: **Jou kamer moet donker, stil en koel wees.** and **Die lig van fone hou jou brein wakker.** Notice **moet** with the verb at the end of the clause, a pattern you’ll see throughout the reading text.
g07u06l02.a: Understand the main points of an information text about screens and sleep, in simple sentences.

g07u06l03.h: Grammar: om … te. Afrikaans for to, and for in order to. A small phrase that does a lot.
g07u06l03.c: Explaining a purpose (I drink coffee to stay awake) or giving general advice (it’s important to sleep enough) uses **om … te** in nearly every language-learning text, and in real speech.
g07u06l03.t: **Om … te** plus a verb often means to: **Dit is belangrik om genoeg te slaap.** The verb comes last, straight after **te**. It also gives a purpose: **Ek drink koffie om wakker te bly.** If the **om** part starts the sentence, the main verb comes right after the comma: **Om goed te slaap, moet jy elke aand op dieselfde tyd gaan lê.** Separable verbs split around **te**: **om op te staan**. **Behoort** (should) and **hoef nie** take **te** without **om**.
g07u06l03.a: Use om … te to say to and in order to, and put the verb in the right place.
g07u06l03.n: Think of **om … te** as a sandwich: the verb always goes in the middle, between **om** and **te**, with any extra words before **te**.

g07u06l04.h: An information text about sleep, with facts, advice and a title that sounds like a lullaby. Read it, then pass on three tips. (Language practice, not health advice.)
g07u06l04.c: Information texts about everyday topics are a very common kind of reading, and they’re the basis for summaries at school and at work. This text is for language learning only, not for health advice.
g07u06l04.t: The text says that people spend about a third of their lives asleep, but many don’t get enough, and then it gives advice in a clear order: first a fixed routine, second the room, third screens, and then caffeine, exercise and what to do if you can’t fall asleep. Look for **om … te** in the advice, and for the signal words **Eerstens**, **Tweedens** and **Derdens** that organise the points. After the questions, you’ll give a friend three tips using **om … te**.
g07u06l04.a: Read an information text, find its main points, and give three tips with om … te.

g07u06l05.h: Summarise the text: six tips, one paragraph, fifty to sixty words, in your own words. Short and sharp, like a hadeda alarm call.
g07u06l05.c: Summarising is one of the most useful writing skills in school and at work: you read something long and give someone just the key points.
g07u06l05.t: Choose six tips from the sleep text, and leave out the introduction, the background and the extra detail. Then write one paragraph of 50 to 60 words in full sentences and in your own words, not copied lines. Use **om … te** where it fits, and the signal words **Eerstens**, **Tweedens** and **Derdens** to give the paragraph a clear order. This is language practice, not health advice.
g07u06l05.a: Pick the main points from an information text and summarise them in 50 to 60 words.

g07u06l06.h: The last check of Graad 7! Sleep, om … te and a whole year of learning.
g07u06l06.c: A final look at the sleep vocabulary and **om … te** before the next level.
g07u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek drink koffie om wakker te bly.** and **Dit is belangrik om genoeg te slaap.** and place the verb correctly.
g07u06l06.a: See which om … te patterns are solid.

g08u01l01.h: Adverts are everywhere, and they’re trying to make you buy something. Today you learn to see how they do it, and what they hope you won’t read.
g08u01l01.c: You meet adverts on billboards, on social media, in shop windows and in the post. Being able to read one critically, in Afrikaans too, protects your wallet and sharpens your reading. In this unit you’ll take apart an advert for an e-bike, fine print and all, and then write one of your own.
g08u01l01.t: Five key words: **die advertensie** (the advertisement), **die aanbod** (the offer), **die afslag** (the discount), **die voorraad** (the stock) and **die kleinletters** (the fine print). Literally, **kleinletters** means small letters, which is just what fine print is. Remember that an offer, a discount and limited stock are all ways of making you hurry, and the small letters often hold the real conditions.
g08u01l01.a: Name the parts of an advert, and talk about offers, discounts and the fine print.
g08u01l01.n: In any language, the part of an advert that’s hardest to read is often the part that matters most. **Kleinletters** is a very useful word to know.

g08u01l02.h: Read the fine print: it’s where adverts keep their secrets, and where you keep your money.
g08u01l02.c: Adverts persuade by speaking to a particular group of people and making them feel they need to act now. Spotting these techniques in Afrikaans lets you read an advert as a critical customer, not just a target.
g08u01l02.t: **Oorreed** (to persuade), **die teikenmark** (the target market), **die slagspreuk** (the slogan) and **beperk** (limited). Look at the techniques in real sentences: a question that names your problem, **Moeg vir verkeer?**; urgency, **Moenie wag nie: die voorraad is beperk!**; a deadline with a bonus, **Koop voor die einde van Maart en kry 'n gratis helm.**; and the warning at the bottom, **Terme en voorwaardes geld.**
g08u01l02.a: Name persuasion techniques in an advert, and understand what the fine print is telling you.

g08u01l03.h: Grammar: prefixes and suffixes. Once you know five little word-parts, a few words become hundreds.
g08u01l03.c: Adverts, news and everyday speech are full of words built from smaller pieces, such as **ongelooflik** or **moeiteloos**. If you know how they’re built, you can work out new words without a dictionary, and you can make strong, persuasive words of your own.
g08u01l03.t: **On-** means not: **ongelooflik** (unbelievable), **onbreekbaar** (unbreakable). **-Loos** means without: **moeiteloos** (effortless). **-Baar** means can be done: **draagbaar** (portable). **-Lik** often makes adjectives: **vriendelik**. **-Heid** makes nouns: **veiligheid** from **veilig**. Before a noun, adjectives take **-e**: **'n onvergeetlike rit** and **'n onbreekbare raam**.
g08u01l03.a: Build and understand new words with on-, -loos, -baar, -lik and -heid.
g08u01l03.n: Advert writers love these endings because they sound big and sure. Try spotting them on billboards this week.

g08u01l04.h: An advert for the Zoem e-bike. It promises freedom, but is it telling you everything? Read the small letters too.
g08u01l04.c: Reading an advert closely, including the fine print, is a useful life skill in any language. This one is built like a real advert, with a question, a list of benefits, a quote from a customer, a price and a deadline.
g08u01l04.t: The Zoem E-fiets advert asks if you’re tired of traffic and of expensive petrol. It promises a range of up to 60 km on one charge, a nearly unbreakable aluminium frame and a small, portable charger. It also gives a price of R14 999, or R699 a month, a free helmet if you buy before 31 March and a warning that stock is limited. The fine print adds a total cost and conditions. Look for words with **on-**, **-loos**, **-baar** and **-lik**. After the questions, try to persuade a friend to buy something, in three sentences.
g08u01l04.a: Read an advert critically, find its persuasion techniques and its fine print, and persuade a friend in three sentences.

g08u01l05.h: Now you’re the advertiser. Write the advert: a question, a slogan and a good dose of -loos, -baar and -lik.
g08u01l05.c: Writing a short advert tests everything you’ve learned in this unit: choosing strong words, speaking to a target market and keeping it short. It’s also a very practical skill if you ever sell something or run a small business.
g08u01l05.t: Write 40 to 60 words for something you sell or a service you offer. Include a rhetorical question, as in **Moeg vir verkeer?**, a short slogan, and at least two words that use **on-**, **-loos**, **-baar** or **-lik**. Decide who your target market is before you start, and keep your offer honest. A clear price and a deadline will make it feel like a real advert.
g08u01l05.a: Write a short advert with a rhetorical question, a slogan and words built with prefixes and suffixes.

g08u01l06.h: Advert check! Can you spot the technique and build the word?
g08u01l06.c: A look back at adverts, persuasion and word-building before you read the classifieds.
g08u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ry moeiteloos werk toe.** and **Dit was 'n onvergeetlike rit.**, and match words to their parts.
g08u01l06.a: See which advert words and word-building patterns are solid.

g08u02l01.h: Te huur, te koop: for rent, for sale. The classifieds are the most efficient bit of writing in any language.
g08u02l01.c: Classified ads appear in newspapers, on community notice boards and on websites, and they’re how people rent flats, sell bicycles and find lost cats. They’re written to be short, so every word and abbreviation counts, and you need to read them closely.
g08u02l01.t: **Die kleinadvertensie** (the classified ad), **te huur** (to let, for rent), **te koop** (for sale), **die beloning** (the reward) and **gevra** (wanted). These small headings tell you what kind of ad you’re reading before you read a single detail. **Te huur** and **te koop** are on signs everywhere, so you’ll see them on your next drive.
g08u02l01.a: Sort classified ads by type, and understand the common headings.

g08u02l02.h: The notice board outside the shop has a flat, a lost cat and a free first lesson. Let’s decode it.
g08u02l02.c: Notice boards and classifieds pack a lot into very little space, so you need to know which details matter: what, how much, from when, and how to get in touch.
g08u02l02.t: **Ingesluit** (included), **die ondervinding** (experience), **bykans** (almost, nearly) and **vermis** (missing, lost). In sentences: **Die woonstel is beskikbaar vanaf een Mei.**, **Negehonderd rand of naaste aanbod.**, **Geen troeteldiere nie.** and **Groot beloning!** Notice that money is said in full when read aloud: nine hundred rand, not the digits. Read each ad twice, once for the details and once for what’s missing.
g08u02l02.a: Pick out the key details in a classified ad: price, date, conditions and contact.

g08u02l03.h: Grammar: abbreviations. Bv., ens., p.m.: ads save space with them, and you need to read them back in full.
g08u02l03.c: Classifieds, notes and forms are full of abbreviations, and knowing them lets you read quickly and write short, tidy notices. Reading them aloud in full is also a good test of whether you’ve really understood.
g08u02l03.t: Common ones: **bv.** (byvoorbeeld), **ens.** (ensovoorts), **m.a.w.** (met ander woorde), **d.w.s.** (dit wil sê) and **asb.** (asseblief). Titles: **mnr.** (meneer), **me.** (mevrou or mejuffrou), **dr.** (dokter). Time, money and places: **vm.** (voormiddag), **nm.** (namiddag), **p.m.** (per maand), **insl.** (insluitend), **nr.** (nommer) and **bl.** (bladsy). Read them in full: **R7 500 p.m.** is seven thousand five hundred rand per month.
g08u02l03.a: Read and write the common Afrikaans abbreviations, and say them in full.
g08u02l03.n: Watch out for **p.m.**: in English it means afternoon, but in Afrikaans classifieds it means per month. The afternoon is **nm.**

g08u02l04.h: Rivierdal’s notice board: a flat, a bicycle, lessons, a missing cat and some volunteers. Real life in five little ads.
g08u02l04.c: Reading a whole page of classified ads trains you to find what you need quickly, ignoring everything else. It’s the same skill you use when scanning a timetable or a menu.
g08u02l04.t: The board has five ads. A two-bedroom flat is to let in Rivierdal-Noord for R7 500 a month, including water and electricity. A red child’s bicycle is for sale for R900 or nearest offer. Maths and Afrikaans lessons are on offer, with a free first lesson. A grey cat called Wollie has gone missing, with a big reward, and the soup kitchen wants volunteers. Look for abbreviations such as **p.m.**, **insl.**, **ens.**, **nm.** and **asb.** After the questions, read the first ad aloud, saying every abbreviation in full.
g08u02l04.a: Read a page of classified ads, find details quickly, and read abbreviations aloud in full.

g08u02l05.h: Write two classifieds of your own: one to sell or rent something, and one to find something. Short, clear and tidy.
g08u02l05.c: A good classified says exactly what a reader needs, and nothing more. Writing two of them in a small word limit is a lesson in choosing your words carefully.
g08u02l05.t: Write two ads, forty to sixty words in total: one for something you sell or rent out, using **te koop** or **te huur**, and one for something you’re looking for, using **gevra**. Include a price, when it’s available and how to get in touch, and use at least three abbreviations, such as **bv.**, **asb.** or **p.m.** Read your ads aloud with the abbreviations in full to check that they make sense.
g08u02l05.a: Write two classified ads that use abbreviations correctly.

g08u02l06.h: Classifieds check! Can you read between the abbreviations?
g08u02l06.c: A look back at classifieds and abbreviations before you read an interview.
g08u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die woonstel is beskikbaar vanaf een Mei.** and match abbreviations to their full forms, such as **bv.**, **ens.** and **asb.** Say each in full as you go.
g08u02l06.a: See which classified words and abbreviations are solid.

g08u03l01.h: An interview: someone asks, someone answers, and a good journalist gets to the story. Let’s learn the words for it.
g08u03l01.c: Magazines, podcasts and websites are full of interviews, and being asked good questions is how we find out about each other’s lives. This unit builds the language for reading an interview and then conducting one yourself.
g08u03l01.t: **Die onderhoud** (the interview), **die joernalis** (the journalist), **die uitdaging** (the challenge), **die raad** (the advice) and **beantwoord** (to answer). Note that **die onderhoud** also means maintenance, and context tells you which one is meant. A good interview uses open questions, which begin with words like **Hoekom**, **Wat** and **Hoe**, because they can’t be answered with a simple yes or no. Listen for them in the next lessons.
g08u03l01.a: Talk about interviews, using the words for journalist, challenge, advice and answering.

g08u03l02.h: On the farm: a drought, a field of lavender and a woman with a plan. This is the story we’re about to read.
g08u03l02.c: Interviews with people who’ve changed their lives are a classic of magazine writing, and they come with useful vocabulary about work, difficulty and advice. These are the words behind the interview you’ll read next.
g08u03l02.t: **Oorneem** (to take over), **die droogte** (the drought), **die laventel** (lavender) and **skepties** (sceptical). In sentences: **In my eerste jaar het dit amper nie gereën nie.**, **Laventel het min water nodig.**, **Begin klein en vra baie vrae.** and **Moenie bang wees om foute te maak nie.** Notice how **amper nie** and **min** signal that something was lacking.
g08u03l02.a: Use the vocabulary of farming and starting over, and understand an interviewee’s advice.

g08u03l03.h: Grammar: male and female forms. Eienaar and eienares, boer and boerin: some Afrikaans nouns have two forms.
g08u03l03.c: Magazines, adverts and job descriptions often name people by their roles, such as owner, singer or teacher. Knowing both forms helps you read, and shows you what’s changing in modern Afrikaans.
g08u03l03.t: Some nouns have a female form: **eienaar** becomes **eienares**, **sanger** becomes **sangeres**, **boer** becomes **boerin** and **held** becomes **heldin**. Some change completely: **gasheer** and **gasvrou**, **akteur** and **aktrise**. Modern Afrikaans often uses the base form for anyone, for example **Sy is 'n goeie onderwyser.** Both are correct, and the **-es** and **-in** forms are still common in writing, so you need to recognise them.
g08u03l03.a: Recognise and use male and female noun forms, and know when the base form is fine.
g08u03l03.n: If you’re not sure which to use, the base form is safe for anyone in everyday speech. Use the female forms when you want to be specific or traditional.

g08u03l04.h: An interview with Anri Steyn, who left an accounting job in Johannesburg to run a lavender farm. Spoiler: it was harder than she thought.
g08u03l04.c: Reading an interview shows you real people speaking, and the questions give you a model of how to ask. This one is a good example of a magazine Q and A, with a short introduction followed by questions and answers.
g08u03l04.t: Anri Steyn, 34, resigned as an accountant in Johannesburg three years ago and took over the family farm near Rivierdal, where she now grows lavender and makes soap and oil. She says her father became ill, and the biggest challenge was the drought. A neighbour, Oom Koos, helped her a lot, and she calls him her hero. Notice the open questions with **Hoekom**, **Wat** and **Hoe**, and the male and female forms such as **eienares** and **boerin**. After the questions, you’ll ask a friend three open questions about their work.
g08u03l04.a: Read a magazine interview, find the questions and key answers, and ask three open questions of your own.

g08u03l05.h: Now you’re the journalist. Interview someone you know about their work, and write it up: an introduction, four questions and the answers.
g08u03l05.c: Writing an interview is a great way to practise questions in Afrikaans, and it makes you listen carefully to what someone says, which is a skill that matters well beyond language learning.
g08u03l05.t: Write 80 to 100 words: a short introduction, four questions and the answers. Ask open questions beginning with **Hoekom**, **Wat** or **Hoe**, and keep the answers short and in the person’s own voice. Where it fits, use a male or female form, such as **eienaar** or **eienares**. Anri’s interview is a good model for the shape of yours.
g08u03l05.a: Write a short interview with an introduction, four open questions and the answers.

g08u03l06.h: Interview check! Let’s see what you remember.
g08u03l06.c: A look back at interviews and male and female forms before the next topic.
g08u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Sy is die eienares van Laventelhoek.** and **Die sangeres sing vanaand in die saal.**, and match male and female forms.
g08u03l06.a: See which interview words and noun forms are solid.

g08u04l01.h: Five stars or one? A review tells you before you buy a ticket. Let’s learn to read, and write, a good one.
g08u04l01.c: Reviews of films, books, restaurants and products are everywhere, and they help you decide what to watch, read or buy. Reading one in Afrikaans means separating facts from opinions, and that’s a skill that works in any language.
g08u04l01.t: **Die resensie** (the review), **die regisseur** (the director), **die toneel** (the scene), **voorspelbaar** (predictable) and **aanbeveel** (to recommend). A review usually has a short summary of the story, a judgement on the acting and the look of the film, a mention of weak points and a final recommendation. Notice that **voorspelbaar** describes a plot you can guess in advance, which is rarely praise.
g08u04l01.a: Talk about a film review, using words for director, scene, predictable and recommend.

g08u04l02.h: Quiet and loud, breathtaking and believable: the adjectives that make a review come alive.
g08u04l02.c: A good review is built from precise adjectives, and Afrikaans has plenty of them. These ones appear again and again when people describe films, characters and landscapes.
g08u04l02.t: **Luidrugtig** (loud, noisy), **asemrowend** (breathtaking), **geloofwaardig** (believable) and **onverantwoordelik** (irresponsible). In sentences: **Die film is beslis die moeite werd.**, **Onderweg kry hulle 'n pap wiel.**, **Ek het 'n traan afgevee.** and **Ek het lanklaas met hom gepraat.** Notice **pap wiel**, literally a floppy wheel, for a flat tyre. A review often uses small details like this one to make a scene feel real, so try picking one out in each sentence and saying why it works.
g08u04l02.a: Describe characters and scenes with strong adjectives, and use phrases from a review in your own sentences.

g08u04l03.h: Words: synonyms, antonyms and toning words. Say it a little stronger or a little softer, as you please.
g08u04l03.c: Choosing between rather slow and extremely slow, or between a synonym and an antonym, changes how your review sounds. These tools let you be fair, precise and a bit funny.
g08u04l03.t: A synonym means almost the same: **rolprent** and **fliek**. An antonym is the opposite: **stil** and **luidrugtig**, or **verantwoordelik** and **onverantwoordelik**. Toning words turn a judgement up or down: **glad nie** (not at all), **effens** (slightly), **taamlik** and **nogal** (fairly, rather), **baie** and **uiters** (extremely). In sentences: **Die middel is nogal stadig.** and **Een grap is glad nie snaaks nie.** Remember that **glad nie** still needs the second **nie** at the end.
g08u04l03.a: Use synonyms, antonyms and toning words to make a judgement stronger or softer.
g08u04l03.n: A review that says everything is fantastic isn’t believable. Toning words like **taamlik** and **effens** let you criticise politely and keep your praise meaningful.

g08u04l04.h: A review of Stof op die pad: four stars out of five, two brothers and a very dusty road trip.
g08u04l04.c: Reading a full review shows you how the different parts fit together: story, acting, setting, weak points and a recommendation. It’s also a good model for your own.
g08u04l04.t: The review gives the film four stars. The film follows two brothers who haven’t seen each other in ten years and drive together from Cape Town to Namibia to scatter their grandfather’s ashes. Danie is stern and quiet, while his younger brother Ruan is loud, funny and slightly irresponsible. The reviewer praises the acting and the desert scenery, but says the middle is rather slow and the ending fairly predictable. Look for toning words such as **nogal**, **effens**, **taamlik** and **glad nie**. After the questions, you’ll tell a friend about a film, saying what was good and what was weak.
g08u04l04.a: Read a film review, tell fact from opinion, and recommend a film with good and weak points.

g08u04l05.h: Now you’re the critic. Review a film, series or book from the past few weeks, in eighty to a hundred words.
g08u04l05.c: Writing a review is practice in giving an opinion and backing it up with evidence, and people will read it to decide what to do with their evening.
g08u04l05.t: Write 80 to 100 words about a film, series or book you saw or read recently. Give a brief summary without spoiling the end, say what you liked, name one weak point, and finish with a recommendation. Use at least two toning words, such as **taamlik**, **effens** or **glad nie**, and one synonym or antonym. Ending with a rating, such as four stars, is a nice touch.
g08u04l05.a: Write a short review with a summary, an opinion, a weak point and a recommendation.

g08u04l06.h: Review check! Four stars or three? Let’s see.
g08u04l06.c: A look back at reviews, adjectives and toning words before you read an advice column.
g08u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die middel is nogal stadig.** and **Die einde is taamlik voorspelbaar.**, and sort synonyms from antonyms.
g08u04l06.a: See which review words and toning words are solid.

g08u05l01.h: Ask Vera: a magazine column where readers write in with a problem, and Vera answers. Let’s learn how it works.
g08u05l01.c: Advice columns are a long-standing magazine tradition, and they’re a good place to see how people describe a problem and how a writer gives advice kindly but clearly. This unit teaches you to read one and reply to a reader. (The columns here are for language practice, not professional advice.)
g08u05l01.t: **Die rubriek** (the column in a magazine), **die situasie** (the situation), **die oplossing** (the solution), **respekteer** (to respect) and **bekommerd** (worried). Letters to a column are usually signed with a nickname, such as **Bekommerd**. The reply follows a pattern: sympathy, advice, a reason for it and an encouraging goodbye.
g08u05l01.a: Talk about an advice column, using the words for situation, solution, worry and respect.

g08u05l02.h: The wedding: a bridesmaid’s dilemma. It’s a great story for learning the language of worry and choice.
g08u05l02.c: Dilemmas about money, friendship and family are what advice columns are made of, and you’ll recognise the words from real conversations. You’ll need them for the letter in the next lessons.
g08u05l02.t: **Die strooimeisie** (the bridesmaid), **teleurstel** (to disappoint), **bekostig** (to afford) and **die skuld** (debt). In sentences: **Ek wil haar nie teleurstel nie.**, **Ek kan nie die reis bekostig nie.**, **Moenie skuld maak vir 'n troue nie.** and **Jou vriendskap is meer werd as een dag.** Notice **nie** at the end of a negative sentence, and **moenie** for a gentle instruction. Try saying two of these sentences about a friend’s problem, to get ready for the advice you’ll give in the grammar lesson.
g08u05l02.a: Describe a difficult choice, and give a short piece of advice about money and friendship.

g08u05l03.h: Grammar: sou. If I were you, I would. It’s how we give advice politely, and imagine what isn’t real.
g08u05l03.c: Giving advice, making a polite request or imagining something unreal all use **sou**. It’s one of the most useful little words in Afrikaans, and it makes you sound kind rather than bossy.
g08u05l03.t: **Sou** plus an infinitive means would: **Ek sou met haar praat.** The infinitive goes to the end. For something that isn’t real, use **as ek … was**, then **sou**: **As ek jy was, sou ek met haar praat.** After the **as**-clause the verb comes first, so it’s **sou ek**, not **ek sou**. **Sou** also makes a request polite: **Sou jy my kon help?** For something that can really happen, use **sal**: **As dit môre reën, sal ons binne bly.**
g08u05l03.a: Give advice with as ek jy was … sou, make polite requests, and tell real from unreal conditions.
g08u05l03.n: If the situation is imaginary, use **was** and **sou**. If it could really happen, use **sal**. Asking yourself "is this real?" fixes most mistakes.

g08u05l04.h: Vera answers a worried bridesmaid. Read the letter, then see whether you’d give the same advice. (Language practice, not financial advice.)
g08u05l04.c: An advice column is a short, friendly text with a clear structure, and the reply is full of **sou**, so it’s an ideal text for practising everything in this unit. It’s for language learning only.
g08u05l04.t: A reader signing herself **Bekommerd in Bellville** writes that her best friend has asked her to be a bridesmaid at a wedding in Mauritius, but the flight and hotel would cost about R25 000, which she doesn’t have. Vera replies with warmth: talk to your friend honestly, say how proud you are, and offer to help with preparations at home. She also says not to go into debt for a wedding. Look for **As ek jy was, sou ek …**, **sou** and **sal**. After the questions, you’ll give a friend advice about a broken-down car.
g08u05l04.a: Read an advice column, find the advice and its reasons, and give your own advice with As ek jy was … sou.

g08u05l05.h: You’re Vera now. A reader has a neighbour whose dog barks every night. What would you say? (Language practice only.)
g08u05l05.c: Replying to a reader’s letter puts everything together: sympathy, advice with **sou**, a reason, and an encouraging ending. It’s a short piece of writing that has to sound kind and sensible.
g08u05l05.t: Read the letter from **Moeg in Mosselbaai**, whose neighbour’s dog barks until midnight, and write Vera’s reply in 80 to 100 words, not counting the greeting and sign-off. Start with a line of sympathy, give two pieces of advice using **As ek jy was, sou ek …**, say why they might help, and end warmly. Use **sal** only for things that can really happen. This is practice for writing in Afrikaans, not real advice.
g08u05l05.a: Write a kind and clear reply to a reader’s letter, using sou correctly.

g08u05l06.h: Advice check! What would you do?
g08u05l06.c: A look back at advice columns and **sou** before the next topic.
g08u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **As ek jy was, sou ek met haar praat.** and **Wat sou jy doen?**, and choose between **sou** and **sal**.
g08u05l06.a: See which sou patterns are solid.

g08u06l01.h: A library under threat, a petition and a town that cares. Let’s learn the words to argue for it.
g08u06l01.c: Public libraries, clinics and parks sometimes face cuts, and communities respond with petitions, letters and meetings. This unit teaches you to read and write a persuasive article, the kind that goes into a local paper.
g08u06l01.t: **Die biblioteek** (the library), **die petisie** (the petition), **die raadslid** (the councillor), **betroubaar** (reliable) and **oortuig** (to persuade). A persuasive article states a position, gives reasons in order and ends with a call to act. **Betroubaar** is useful far beyond libraries: you’ll want it whenever you talk about information, people or machines. Try using it about a news source, a friend and a bus.
g08u06l01.a: Talk about a library campaign, using words for petition, councillor, reliable and persuade.

g08u06l02.h: Who uses the library? Job seekers, pensioners, kids doing homework and more. Let’s see who’s walking through the door.
g08u06l02.c: A strong argument is built from people and details, not just opinions. This lesson gives you the vocabulary to say who benefits and how.
g08u06l02.t: **Die werksoeker** (the job seeker), **die pensioenaris** (the pensioner), **die bibliotekaris** (the librarian) and **die middestad** (the town centre). In sentences: **Nie almal kan data bekostig nie.**, **Kinders doen ná skool hier huiswerk.**, **Werksoekers druk hul CV’s by die biblioteek.** and **Teken asseblief die petisie.** The last one is an instruction, and it’s how a campaign ends. Imagine saying it to a neighbour at your gate, and you’ll remember it.
g08u06l02.a: Say who uses a public service and why it matters, and invite people to sign a petition.

g08u06l03.h: Grammar: hoewel, nogtans, gevolglik. Linking words make an argument flow, but they move the verb around.
g08u06l03.c: In a persuasive text or a debate, linking words show how your ideas relate: although, so that, as a result, moreover. Getting the word order right makes your argument sound clear and confident.
g08u06l03.t: Some linking words send the verb to the end of their clause: **hoewel** (although), **sodat** (so that), **omdat** and **terwyl**. For example, **Hoewel geld skaars is, is die plan 'n fout.** Others start a main clause, and the verb comes right after them: **tog**, **nogtans** (yet, nevertheless), **gevolglik** (as a result), **boonop** (moreover) and **daarom**. For example, **Gevolglik verdien die winkels meer.** After a **hoewel**-clause at the start, the main verb comes first. Use **eerstens**, **tweedens**, **derdens** and **laastens** to order your reasons.
g08u06l03.a: Join ideas with linking words, put the verb in the right place, and order your reasons.
g08u06l03.n: Ask yourself whether the linking word begins a small clause or a main one. Small clause: verb to the end. Main clause: verb straight after the linking word.

g08u06l04.h: Hou ons biblioteek oop! A persuasive article by Thandi Mokoena. Count the reasons, then decide if you’re convinced.
g08u06l04.c: A persuasive article is a text with a clear structure: a position, reasons in order, a call to act. Reading one closely is the best preparation for writing your own, and for summarising it.
g08u06l04.t: The municipality of Rivierdal wants to close the public library at the end of the year, saying the building costs too much. The writer disagrees, with reasons in order: the library is free, job seekers use its computers, older people have a safe and quiet place to meet, librarians help with forms and reliable information, and the library brings visitors to the town centre. Look for **Eerstens**, **Tweedens**, **Derdens**, **Boonop**, **Gevolglik** and **Laastens**, and for the verb at the end after **Hoewel**. After the questions, you’ll persuade a neighbour to sign the petition with two reasons.
g08u06l04.a: Read a persuasive article, pick out its reasons in order, and give two reasons to persuade a neighbour.

g08u06l05.h: Summarise the article: six reasons, one paragraph, sixty to seventy words, in your own words. Short, sharp and fair.
g08u06l05.c: Summarising a persuasive text means finding the real reasons and leaving out the decoration. It’s a skill you’ll use in school, at work and any time you need to explain what an article says.
g08u06l05.t: Find the six reasons in the article, and skip the introduction and the examples. Write one paragraph of 60 to 70 words in full sentences and in your own words, and use linking words such as **eerstens**, **boonop** and **gevolglik** so the paragraph has a clear order. Check that each reason is a separate idea, and that the verb is in the right place after each linking word.
g08u06l05.a: Pick out the reasons from a persuasive article and summarise them in 60 to 70 words.

g08u06l06.h: The last check of Graad 8! Linking words, libraries and a whole year of learning.
g08u06l06.c: A final look at persuasive language and linking words before the next level.
g08u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Hoewel geld skaars is, is die plan 'n fout.** and **Gevolglik verdien die winkels meer.**, and place the verb correctly after each linking word.
g08u06l06.a: See which linking words and word-order patterns are solid.

g09u01l01.h: A job advert, a blank page and a deadline. Let’s learn the words that get your application read, in Afrikaans.
g09u01l01.c: Applying for a job, a bursary or a course often means writing a formal letter, and in many workplaces that letter will be in Afrikaans or in both languages. This unit takes you from reading a vacancy to writing a full application letter, and then introducing yourself at an interview.
g09u01l01.t: Five core words: **die vakature** (the vacancy), **die kandidaat** (the candidate), **die kwalifikasie** (the qualification), **die ervaring** (experience) and **aanheg** (to attach). An employer reads dozens of letters, so clear, correct vocabulary tells them at a glance that you’re serious. **Aanheg** is separable, so you’ll write **Ek heg my CV en sertifikate aan.** in a sentence, with the small part at the end.
g09u01l01.a: Talk about a vacancy, a candidate’s qualifications and experience, and attaching documents.
g09u01l01.n: Always match the job advert’s wording. If it says **ervaring** and **kwalifikasie**, use those words back.

g09u01l02.h: What can you do? An application is your chance to say, clearly and without bragging, what makes you suitable.
g09u01l02.c: Whether you’re writing a letter or answering a question at an interview, you need to describe your duties, strengths and availability in short, confident sentences.
g09u01l02.t: **Die pligte** (the duties), **stiptelik** (punctual), **geskik** (suitable) and **die afskrif** (the copy of a document). Learn these sentences whole: **Ek is gewoond daaraan om onder druk te werk.**, **Ek praat drie tale vlot.**, **Ek is beskikbaar vir 'n onderhoud.** and **Ek kan op 'n maand se kennisgewing begin.** Notice that they say what you do, with a concrete detail, rather than just calling yourself hardworking. Try changing each one so that it’s true for you, and say it aloud.
g09u01l02.a: Describe your strengths, duties and availability in clear, formal sentences.

g09u01l03.h: Grammar: the formal register. Geagte, u and Die uwe: a different Afrikaans for a different occasion.
g09u01l03.c: A job application, a letter to a bank or a note to a school principal needs a more formal tone than a message to a friend. Getting the register right is part of getting the job, and it shows respect.
g09u01l03.t: This is a recap from Graad 6, now for job applications. Use **u** for a stranger or in a formal letter, and the possessive is also **u**: **u hotel**, not “u se hotel”. Start with **Geagte** plus a title and surname, such as **Geagte mev. Pretorius**, and end with **Die uwe** and your full name. Write in full, so **dit is**, not “dis”, and leave out slang, emoji and exclamation marks. Fixed phrases to learn: **Ek doen hiermee aansoek om die pos.**, **Ek heg my CV en sertifikate aan.** and **Ek sien daarna uit om van u te hoor.** The subject line goes under the salutation, in capitals.
g09u01l03.a: Write a formal letter with the right salutation, sign-off, u forms and fixed phrases.
g09u01l03.n: Only use **u** with people you’d address formally. If the advert gives a name, use it: **Geagte mev. Pretorius** beats a general greeting every time.

g09u01l04.h: A real-looking application letter for a receptionist post at a hotel. Read it like an employer, and spot why it works.
g09u01l04.c: Reading a good model letter shows you the layout, the tone and the order of information that employers expect. You’ll use it as the pattern for your own.
g09u01l04.t: The letter is addressed to the manager of Hotel Bergsig, and it applies for the post of receptionist as advertised in the local paper. The writer is 32, lives in Rivierdal, completed matric and then a tourism certificate, and has worked in the town’s tourism office for six years. She lists her duties, says she speaks Afrikaans, English and isiXhosa fluently, and explains why she wants to work at the hotel. Notice the layout, with the addresses and date at the top, the subject line in capitals, and the paragraph order: who you are, what you’ve done, why you suit the post and why you want it. After the questions, you’ll introduce yourself formally, as you would at an interview.
g09u01l04.a: Read a formal application letter, find its structure, and introduce yourself formally at an interview.

g09u01l05.h: Write your own application letter for a post that interests you. A hundred to a hundred and twenty words for the body, formal and clear.
g09u01l05.c: This is the real thing: a letter you could adapt and send. Employers notice a letter that’s clear, correct and polite, and you’ll use this skill for years.
g09u01l05.t: Write a formal letter for a post you’d like. The body (not counting the addresses, date, salutation and sign-off) should be 100 to 120 words. Start with **Ek doen hiermee aansoek om …**, give your qualifications and experience, mention one or two strengths with a concrete example, say why you want the post, and close with **Ek sien daarna uit om van u te hoor.** Use **u**, write words in full and leave out slang and exclamation marks.
g09u01l05.a: Write a formal application letter in the correct layout and register.

g09u01l06.h: Application check! Are you the right candidate?
g09u01l06.c: A look back at formal letters and job vocabulary before you read the news.
g09u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek doen hiermee aansoek om die pos.** and **Ek sien daarna uit om van u te hoor.** and pick the right formal form each time.
g09u01l06.a: See which formal phrases and job words are solid.

g09u02l01.h: Stop the press! News reports have their own vocabulary, and you’re about to learn it.
g09u02l01.c: Whether you read a local paper, a news site or a community Facebook page, you’ll meet the same words and the same structure: who, what, where, when and why. This unit teaches you to read a news report and write your own.
g09u02l01.t: **Die verslaggewer** (the reporter), **die burgemeester** (the mayor), **die nuusberig** (the news report), **oopstel** (to open to traffic or the public) and **die ingenieur** (the engineer). **Oopstel** is separable, so the small part goes to the end: **Hulle stel die brug oop.** A news report opens with the most important facts, then adds detail and quotes.
g09u02l01.a: Talk about a news report, using words for reporter, mayor, engineer and opening.

g09u02l02.h: The flood: damage, a washed-out bridge and a lot of people cut off. The words here come straight from the story.
g09u02l02.c: News about floods, storms and repairs is common, and these verbs and nouns describe what happened and who was affected. You’ll meet them again in the report on the bridge.
g09u02l02.t: **Die vloed** (the flood), **beskadig** (to damage), **wegspoel** (to wash away) and **afsny** (to cut off). In sentences: **Kos en medisyne is per helikopter afgelewer.**, **Haar besigheid het swaar gely.**, **Die werk is vinniger as verwag voltooi.** and **Die inwoners het hande geklap.** Notice that several of them are in the passive, which is how news often reports events.
g09u02l02.a: Describe a flood and its effects, and what was done afterwards, with the vocabulary of a news report.

g09u02l03.h: Grammar: the passive. The bridge is being repaired. By whom? That’s what deur is for.
g09u02l03.c: News reports, notices and official documents often use the passive, because what happened matters more than who did it, or the doer isn’t known. You need it to read the news, and to write it.
