g09u02l03.t: In an active sentence the doer is the subject: **Ingenieurs inspekteer die brug.** In the passive, what undergoes the action is the subject: **Die brug word deur ingenieurs geïnspekteer.** Present: **word** plus a past participle, as in **Die brug word nou herstel.** Past: **is** plus a past participle, as in **Die brug is vyftig jaar gelede gebou.** Future: **sal** plus a past participle plus **word**, as in **'n Nuwe stelsel sal volgende jaar geïnstalleer word.** Name the doer with **deur**.
g09u02l03.a: Use the passive in the present, past and future, and name the doer with deur.
g09u02l03.n: Don’t overuse the passive in your own writing. It’s best when the doer is unknown, obvious or less important than the action.

g09u02l04.h: A news report: the Buffelsbrug reopens after four months. Who’s pleased, who isn’t, and who’ll pay?
g09u02l04.c: Reading a full news report teaches you how journalists organise facts, quotes and different views. It’s also the model for the one you’ll write.
g09u02l04.t: The Buffelsbrug, damaged by a flood in July, has reopened after four months. Built in 1968, it’s the only road between Rivierdal and the towns north of the river. About 3 000 residents were cut off, schoolchildren were taken across by boat and food and medicine came by helicopter. A local firm did the repairs, which the mayor says cost R18 million, and he thanked the workers. But a shop owner says her business suffered badly and that nobody warned them the bridge was so weak. Look for the passive and for the two different views. After the questions, you’ll retell the news in three sentences using the passive.
g09u02l04.a: Read a news report, pick out the facts and the different views, and retell the news in the passive.

g09u02l05.h: Write a news report about something that happened in your area. A hundred to a hundred and twenty words, with three passives.
g09u02l05.c: Writing a news report means choosing the key facts and giving them in the right order, plain and clear. It’s a skill for school, for community groups and for any work where you have to report what happened.
g09u02l05.t: Write 100 to 120 words, not counting the headline, about something recent in your town or area. Open with the most important facts: what happened, where and when. Then add details and, if you can, a quote. Use at least three passive sentences, and name the doer with **deur** at least once. Keep to facts, and don’t invent details of real people.
g09u02l05.a: Write a short news report with the key facts first and at least three passive sentences.

g09u02l06.h: News check! Passive voice, reporters and a very long bridge.
g09u02l06.c: A look back at news language and the passive before you describe a market.
g09u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die brug word nou herstel.** and **Die brug is vyftig jaar gelede gebou.**, and switch active sentences into the passive.
g09u02l06.a: See which passive forms and news words are solid.

g09u03l01.h: Smell, taste, touch, sound, sight: your senses are the best writing tool you have. Let’s find the Afrikaans for them.
g09u03l01.c: A description that uses the senses puts the reader in the place. That’s what makes a travel article, a memoir or a good school essay stand out. This unit builds up to a descriptive essay about a Saturday morning market.
g09u03l01.t: **Die sintuie** (the senses), **die reuk** (the smell), **die geur** (the aroma, scent), **die geluid** (the sound) and **beskryf** (to describe). **Reuk** and **geur** are close: **reuk** is the general word for smell, including unpleasant ones, while **geur** is more often a pleasant scent or flavour. A good description picks the sense that fits each detail, rather than telling the reader how to feel.
g09u03l01.a: Name the senses and describe a place with smell, sound and more.

g09u03l02.h: At the market: baskets, flour, calling sellers and tents coming down. You can almost smell it.
g09u03l02.c: The market in this unit is a typical Saturday-morning scene, and the vocabulary covers a lot of everyday places: stalls, shops and street corners. These are the words you’ll want to describe them.
g09u03l02.t: **Die mandjie** (the basket), **die meel** (flour), **skor** (hoarse, rough) and **verslyt** (to wear out). In sentences: **Verkopers roep hul pryse uit.**, **Dit lyk soos 'n reënboog.**, **Dit is nog donker wanneer die bakkies stilhou.** and **Die tente word een vir een afgehaal.** Notice the comparison with **soos**, the time clause with **wanneer**, and the passive in the last sentence. Say the whole set aloud once, as if you were walking past the stalls.
g09u03l02.a: Use market vocabulary to describe sights, sounds and the passing of a morning.

g09u03l03.h: Grammar: participles. Gebakte brood, glimmende soetrissies: an adjective made out of a verb.
g09u03l03.c: Descriptive writing is full of participles, because they say what’s happening or what has happened to something in just one word. They’re how a paragraph goes from flat to vivid.
g09u03l03.t: A present participle is a verb plus **-ende**, for something happening now: **'n blaffende hond**, **glimmende soetrissies**. A past participle is the **ge-** form, for something already done: **gebakte brood**, **gemaalde koffie**. Before a noun, a **ge-** form usually adds **-de** or **-te**, and some older forms differ, such as **verslete**. After the noun there’s no ending: **Die brood is gebak.** and **Haar hande is gekreukel.**
g09u03l03.a: Use present and past participles as adjectives to describe things vividly.
g09u03l03.n: Before a noun, add the ending. After the noun, leave it off. That one rule sorts most participle mistakes.

g09u03l04.h: Saturday morning at the market: a descriptive essay that you can see, smell and hear. Read it with your senses switched on.
g09u03l04.c: A descriptive essay is built from carefully chosen details, organised by sense or in the order you’d walk through the place. This one is a very good model for your own.
g09u03l04.t: The essay begins in the dark, when the first bakkies pull up on the old rugby field behind the town hall, and by seven o’clock the field is full of white tents. It moves through smell, with freshly ground coffee, baked bread, koeksisters in the oil and boerewors on a fire, then colour, then sound, with a man playing a worn guitar, and then a favourite stall belonging to Tant Rosie. Count the senses the writer uses, and look for participles like **gebakte**, **gemaalde**, **glimmende** and **verslete**. After the questions, describe your favourite place in three sentences, using three different senses.
g09u03l04.a: Read a descriptive essay, find the senses and participles it uses, and describe your favourite place.

g09u03l05.h: Write a descriptive essay about a place you know well. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty words, three senses, two participles.
g09u03l05.c: Describing a place you know is a satisfying kind of writing, because the details are already in your head. You’ll use the same skill in letters, blogs and school essays.
g09u03l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words, not counting the title. Choose a place you know well, such as your kitchen, a taxi rank or a beach. Use at least three senses and two participles, such as **gebakte**, **glimmende** or **blaffende**. Plan your order first: walk through the place in your head, from the entrance to the middle. Use a simile with **soos** once, and end with a small picture rather than a summary.
g09u03l05.a: Write a descriptive essay with three senses and participles, in a clear order.

g09u03l06.h: Market check! Participles, senses and a lot of fresh bread.
g09u03l06.c: A look back at description and participles before the next unit.
g09u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek ruik vars gemaalde koffie.** and **Die gebakte brood is nog warm.**, and choose the right participle ending.
g09u03l06.a: See which participles and sense words are solid.

g09u04l01.h: Someone forwards a scary message to the whole family group. Before you share it, let’s learn how to ask where it came from.
g09u04l01.c: Rumours, fake messages and half-truths spread on WhatsApp, Facebook and in the pub, and everyone gets caught out sometimes. This unit gives you the Afrikaans to question what you read, name your doubts and write to a newspaper about it. The town and message in the reading text are made up for the lesson.
g09u04l01.t: **Die gerug** (the rumour), **die bron** (the source), **vals** (false, fake), **versprei** (to spread) and **aanstuur** (to forward a message). **Aanstuur** is separable, so you’ll see **Hy stuur dit aan.** in the present and **Hy het dit aangestuur.** in the past. The word **bron** works for a spring of water as well as for a source of information, which is a handy picture: ask where the water first comes from.
g09u04l01.a: Talk about rumours, sources, fake messages and forwarding, with the right Afrikaans words.

g09u04l02.h: Panic in town: one message, two days and no bottled water left on the shelves. Here are the words for what happened.
g09u04l02.c: Stories about messages that cause real panic are all too familiar. These words let you describe how a message spreads, what people do and what a careful reader does.
g09u04l02.t: **Uitverkoop** (sold out), **die woordvoerder** (the spokesperson), **die uitslag** (the result) and **twyfel** (to doubt). In sentences: **Die boodskap het soos 'n veldbrand versprei.**, **Die bottelwater was binne twee dae uitverkoop.**, **Die water word elke dag getoets.** and **Moenie iets deel as jy nie seker is nie.** The last sentence is a very good rule to keep: if you’re not sure, don’t share.
g09u04l02.a: Describe how a rumour spreads and what a careful person does before sharing it.

g09u04l03.h: Grammar: how sure are you? Beslis, waarskynlik, moontlik: three little words that say exactly how certain you are.
g09u04l03.c: In news, advice and everyday talk, the strength of a claim matters. Saying something is definitely true when it’s only probably true is how rumours start, so choosing the right word is a real skill.
g09u04l03.t: From certain to doubtful: **beslis** and **sekerlik** (definitely), then **waarskynlik** (probably), then **moontlik**, **miskien** and **dalk** (possibly). **Blykbaar** means apparently, because it seems so from what we can see, while **glo** means supposedly: people say so, but nobody has checked. The word goes after the finite verb: **Dit is waarskynlik nie waar nie.** At the start of a sentence the verb comes next: **Waarskynlik het iemand die naam verander.** Note **Die water is glo vergiftig.**, where **glo** shows the writer isn’t vouching for it.
g09u04l03.a: Show how sure you are with beslis, waarskynlik, moontlik, blykbaar and glo, with the verb in the right place.
g09u04l03.n: When you report something you haven’t checked, **glo** is the honest word. It tells the listener that you’re passing something on, and you’re not vouching for it.

g09u04l04.h: Moenie alles glo wat jy lees nie: an article about a fake message, and a few good tests for what’s real.
g09u04l04.c: An information article that explains how to question a message is useful to read in any language, and it models clear, practical writing. It’s also a good text for spotting words like **blykbaar** and **waarskynlik** doing their job.
g09u04l04.t: The article begins with a message that spread through Rivierdal’s WhatsApp groups, saying that the tap water was poisoned. Within two days the shops had sold out of bottled water, and the clinic had received dozens of calls. But the message was false: the municipality never said it, and the water is tested every day. The writer says the message apparently began in a group in another province, and that someone probably forwarded it without checking. The article then gives tips on spotting fake news, starting with looking at the source. After the questions, you’ll tell a friend why you doubt a strange message.
g09u04l04.a: Read an article about fake news, find the signs it gives, and explain why you doubt a message.

g09u04l05.h: Write to the editor about the fake message. A hundred to a hundred and twenty words, formal and firm, and no shouting.
g09u04l05.c: A letter to the editor is a public way to give your view on something that matters, and it’s short, formal and focused. It’s a good use of the formal register and of words showing how sure you are.
g09u04l05.t: Write a letter to the editor of **Die Rivierdal Nuus** about the fake message. The body, without the salutation and sign-off, should be 100 to 120 words. Say what happened, give your opinion about it, and suggest what readers could do next, such as checking the source before sharing. Use words like **waarskynlik**, **blykbaar** and **beslis** to show how sure you are, and **u** if you address the editor directly. Keep the tone calm.
g09u04l05.a: Write a formal letter to the editor that gives an opinion and shows how sure you are.

g09u04l06.c: A look back at questioning messages and words of certainty before you read a speech.
g09u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Iemand het dit waarskynlik net aangestuur.** and **Ons water is beslis veilig.**, and rank the words from certain to doubtful.
g09u04l06.a: See which certainty words and word-order patterns are solid.

g09u05l01.h: Please raise your glasses: it’s time for a speech. Let’s learn the words for making one, and for listening to one.
g09u05l01.c: Speeches happen at weddings, farewells, birthdays and award evenings, and sooner or later somebody will hand you a glass and say a few words. This unit takes you through a farewell speech for a retiring librarian, and ends with writing one of your own.
g09u05l01.t: **Die toespraak** (the speech), **die gehoor** (the audience), **die voorreg** (the privilege), **namens** (on behalf of) and **die afskeid** (the farewell). Speeches have a standard opening, such as greeting the audience and saying who you are, and **namens** is the usual way to speak for a group, as in **namens almal**. **Voorreg** appears in a lot of speeches, as in the privilege of working with someone.
g09u05l01.a: Talk about speeches, using words for audience, privilege, on behalf of and farewell.

g09u05l02.h: After thirty-three years: a retirement, a toast and a lot of thank-yous.
g09u05l02.c: Retirement and farewell speeches have a gentle, grateful tone, and a particular set of phrases. You’ll learn them here, and then see them in the speech for Marie.
g09u05l02.t: **Aftree** (to retire), **grootliks** (largely), **danksy** (thanks to) and **belowe** (to promise). In sentences: **Ek onthou my eerste dag goed.**, **Mag ek almal vra om hul glase te lig?**, **Dit is grootliks danksy haar.** and **Ons sal jou mis.** Those four lines are the heart of many speeches: a memory, a toast, a thank-you and a goodbye. Try writing your own version of each for someone you know, and notice how the toast is a question, not an order.
g09u05l02.a: Use warm, grateful phrases for a farewell speech, including a toast.

g09u05l03.h: Grammar: reported speech. She said that I shouldn’t worry: how to tell someone what somebody else said.
g09u05l03.c: In a speech or a chat, you often pass on what someone else said, asked or promised. Reported speech lets you do that without quotation marks, and gets the verb right.
g09u05l03.t: Recap: **Sy sê: "Ek is moeg."** becomes **Sy sê dat sy moeg is.** Change the pronoun, and send the verb to the end after **dat**. Yes or no questions use **of**: **Ek het haar gevra of sy bly is.** Question words stay: **Hy wil weet waar die boeke is.** Commands use **moet**: **Sy het gesê dat ek nie bekommerd moet wees nie.** When the reporting verb is in the past, **sal** becomes **sou** and **kan** becomes **kon**: **Sy het belowe dat sy die volgende dag sou kom.** Time words shift too: **nou** becomes **toe**, **hier** becomes **daar** and **môre** becomes **die volgende dag**.
g09u05l03.a: Report what people said, asked and promised, with the right pronouns, word order and time words.
g09u05l03.n: Check three things in this order: the pronoun, the verb at the end and the time word. Most mistakes hide in one of those three.

g09u05l04.h: A farewell speech for Marie Fourie, who led the library for thirty-three years. It’s affectionate, funny and a little emotional.
g09u05l04.c: A good speech has an opening, a few personal stories, a main point and a warm ending. Reading one in full gives you a model for every occasion.
g09u05l04.t: Thabo Molefe, who worked with Marie in the Rivierdal library for twelve years, greets the audience and says it’s a privilege to say goodbye to someone who led the library for thirty-three years. He remembers his first day, when Marie made him a cup of tea and said he shouldn’t worry, because a good librarian doesn’t know everything but knows where to look. He talks about the reading club, the homework hour and the job seekers she helped, and about how Marie helped to spread the petition that kept the library open. Look for reported speech such as **gesê dat ek nie bekommerd moet wees nie**. After the questions, you’ll pass on a message in reported speech.
g09u05l04.a: Read a farewell speech, pick out its stories and thanks, and pass on a message in reported speech.

g09u05l05.h: Write a short speech for a special occasion: a farewell, a birthday or a wedding. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty words, with a story and a toast.
g09u05l05.c: Having a few words ready for a special occasion is a real social skill, and a short, warm speech is always better than a long, wandering one.
g09u05l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words, not counting the title. Greet the audience, say who you are and how you know the person, share a short memory, say what you admire about them, and close with a toast, such as **Mag ek almal vra om hul glase te lig?** Use at least two sentences of reported speech, such as what the person once said or promised. Read it aloud to check that it sounds like you.
g09u05l05.a: Write a short, warm speech that includes a memory, reported speech and a toast.

g09u05l06.h: Speech check! Who said what, and who’s passing it on?
g09u05l06.c: A look back at speech vocabulary and reported speech before the last unit of the year.
g09u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Sy het gesê dat ek nie bekommerd moet wees nie.** and **Ek het haar gevra of sy bly is.**, and turn direct speech into reported speech.
g09u05l06.a: See which reported-speech patterns are solid.

g09u06l01.h: The interview: the part where the letter finally meets a face. Let’s get you ready, in Afrikaans.
g09u06l01.c: Job interviews are stressful in any language, and for many people they happen in Afrikaans or in a mix of languages. This unit gives you the vocabulary, the advice and the grammar to talk about interviews, and to read tips about them. The text is for language practice, not professional career advice.
g09u06l01.t: **Die indruk** (the impression), **die paneel** (the panel), **die vaardigheid** (the skill), **die maatskappy** (the company) and **die lyftaal** (body language). A **paneel** is a group of interviewers, so you may be speaking to several people at once. In the text you’ll also meet the idea that dressing a little more formally than the staff do shows you took it seriously. **Lyftaal** is literally body language, which is useful to know because the text will talk about how you sit and look.
g09u06l01.a: Talk about job interviews with words for impression, panel, skills, company and body language.

g09u06l02.h: Sit up straight, smile and look them in the eye. The words for interview behaviour are short and very practical.
g09u06l02.c: Interview tips use a lot of short instructions, and you’ll need to read them quickly and carry them out. They also give you the commands you’d use when you coach a friend.
g09u06l02.t: **Die oogkontak** (eye contact), **noukeurig** (carefully), **die swakheid** (the weakness) and **uitstaan** (to stand out). Learn these instructions whole: **Kom tien minute vroeg.**, **Sit regop en glimlag.**, **Oefen jou antwoorde hardop.** and **Stuur dieselfde dag 'n kort e-pos.** **Uitstaan** is separable, so you’ll hear **Jy wil uitstaan** with the small part at the end. Say all four instructions aloud as if you were coaching a friend in the car park.
g09u06l02.a: Give and follow short, practical instructions about preparing for and behaving at an interview.

g09u06l03.h: Grammar: fixed prepositions. Trots op, bang vir: certain words always bring their own small partner.
g09u06l03.c: Prepositions rarely match from one language to the next, and getting them right makes you sound natural. You’ll use them in every kind of conversation, including interviews, where you’ll talk about what you’re proud of, interested in and prepared for.
g09u06l03.t: Many verbs and adjectives take a fixed preposition, so learn them as pairs. Verbs: **belangstel in**, **afhang van**, **dink aan**, **voorberei op**, **sorg vir** and **glo in**. Adjectives: **trots op**, **bang vir**, **lief vir**, **gewoond aan** and **tevrede met**. English can mislead you: **afhang van** and not *op*, **bang vir** and not *van*. In questions and clauses, use **waar-** plus the preposition: **Waarin stel jy belang?** and **Ek weet waarvan dit afhang.**
g09u06l03.a: Use the common fixed prepositions after verbs and adjectives, including with waar- words.
g09u06l03.n: Learn them in small chunks, such as **trots op my werk**, and not as single words. The preposition then comes along with the phrase.

g09u06l04.h: An information text for anyone with an interview coming up: practical tips from people who do the interviewing.
g09u06l04.c: Information texts like this one appear on career pages, in newspapers and in school books. They give advice in a clear order, which makes them ideal for practising summaries. This text is for language practice, not career advice.
g09u06l04.t: The text starts by saying that many people get nervous before an interview, that this is normal, and that an interview is something you can practise. It then gives tips: do your homework on the company, read the advert again carefully and think of examples from your own life instead of just listing words like hardworking, practise your answers aloud with a friend and don’t memorise them. It also says to dress slightly more formally than the staff, to make eye contact, sit up straight and smile, to be honest if you don’t know something, to ask the panel a question at the end, and to send a thank-you e-mail the same day. Look for fixed prepositions such as **belangstel in** and **afhang van**. After the questions, you’ll give a friend three tips.
g09u06l04.a: Read an information text, find its tips, and give a friend three tips for an interview.

g09u06l05.h: Summarise the tips: seven tips, one paragraph, sixty to seventy words, in your own words. This one is great practice for the interview itself.
g09u06l05.c: A summary of an information text shows that you’ve understood it, and it’s the skill that lets you tell someone else what matters. You’ll use it at school, at work and in any course.
g09u06l05.t: Find the seven tips in the text, and leave out the introduction and the examples. Write one paragraph of 60 to 70 words in full sentences and in your own words, not copied. Use fixed prepositions where they fit, such as **voorberei op** and **dink aan**, and signal words such as **eerstens**, **verder** and **laastens** to keep the order clear. This is language practice, not career advice.
g09u06l05.a: Pick out the main tips from an information text and summarise them in 60 to 70 words.

g09u06l06.h: The last check of Graad 9! Fixed prepositions, interviews and a whole year behind you.
g09u06l06.c: A final look at interview language and fixed prepositions before the next level.
g09u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek is trots op my werk.** and **Moenie bang wees vir moeilike vrae nie.**, and choose the right preposition for each word.
g09u06l06.a: See which fixed prepositions are solid.

g10u01l01.h: Welcome to Graad 10! First question: is what you just read a fact, or someone’s opinion? Let’s find the words to tell the difference.
g10u01l01.c: In Graad 10 you read longer, more demanding texts, and the first skill you need is telling what’s proven from what’s merely claimed. That’s useful in a magazine, a news feed and a family argument. This unit centres on a 400-to-500-word magazine article about phones at the dinner table.
g10u01l01.t: Five words for talking about claims: **beweer** (to claim), **meen** (to think, to be of the opinion), **volgens** (according to), **regverdig** (fair) and **eensydig** (one-sided). A writer who says **Hy beweer dat …** is reporting what someone says, and isn’t vouching for it. **Eensydig** is literally one-sided, which is a very useful word when you review an argument.
g10u01l01.a: Use the words for claiming, thinking and judging whether an argument is fair.

g10u01l02.h: Grammar: the simple sentence. Subject, verb, object: the skeleton under every sentence you’ll ever write.
g10u01l02.c: To read a long sentence and to write a clear one, you need to be able to find who does what to whom. Teachers, editors and exam questions all use these terms, so they’re worth knowing properly in Afrikaans.
g10u01l02.t: The **onderwerp** (subject) is who or what does the action: **Die kinders herinner hulle ouers.** The **gesegde** (predicate) is the verb plus any helping verb: **herinner**, **het … herinner** or **sal … herinner**. The **voorwerp** (object) is who or what the action is done to. In a statement the conjugated verb is always the second idea: **Elke aand kyk Ruan na die krieket.** If something else comes first, the subject moves behind the verb. The present tense uses one verb form for everyone: **ek eet, sy eet, hulle eet.**
g10u01l02.a: Find the subject, predicate and object of a sentence, and keep the verb in second place.
g10u01l02.n: If you’re lost in a long sentence, find the verb first, and then ask who is doing it. The rest usually falls into place.

g10u01l03.h: Foon af, gesels aan? Phones off, talking on? A magazine article about the one thing that happens at nearly every family table.
g10u01l03.c: Magazine articles are written to be read in one sitting: they hook you with a familiar scene, give both sides and finish with a suggestion. This one is a good first long text for Graad 10.
g10u01l03.t: The article opens on a Sunday lunch where, within five minutes, three people are looking at their phones. It then gives both sides: phones help families stay in touch, such as a grandmother in Bloemfontein video-calling her grandchildren in Perth, but others feel something is lost when the screens come out. It describes a family in Durban who put all phones in a basket at the door, and a teenager who points out that adults do it too. The writer’s conclusion is simple: talk about it. Look for claims, opinions and figurative phrases, and notice how the writer uses **volgens** and **sommige** to report other people’s views.
g10u01l03.a: Read a long magazine article, pick out the main idea and the different views, and tell what the writer concludes.

g10u01l04.h: Feit of mening? The most important question in reading, and a very good one to ask the next time somebody says "everyone knows".
g10u01l04.c: Telling facts from opinions is the basis of critical reading: in newspapers, on social media and in exam passages. A fact can be checked, an opinion can only be agreed or disagreed with.
g10u01l04.t: A **feit** can be checked and is true or false for everyone: **Die mark het om agtuur oopgemaak.** A **mening** is what someone thinks or feels, and others may disagree: **Fone maak gesprekke vervelig.** Watch for opinion signals such as **ek dink**, **ek meen**, **na my mening**, **volgens my**, **sekerlik** and **waarskynlik**, and for judging words like **die beste**, **die ergste**, **vervelig**, **regverdig** and **belangrik**. **Volgens hulle …** or **Hy beweer dat …** shows that the writer is reporting someone else’s opinion.
g10u01l04.a: Tell fact from opinion in a text, by checking whether a statement can be proven.
g10u01l04.n: Ask yourself: could I check this? If yes, it’s a fact. If I can only agree or disagree, it’s an opinion.

g10u01l05.h: Summarise a text about saving water: seven tips, sixty to seventy words, in your own words. Short, clear and useful.
g10u01l05.c: Summaries are a standard Graad 10 task, and they’re also a real-life skill: you read something long, and give someone the main points. This text is about saving water at home.
g10u01l05.t: The text gives practical advice on saving water at home, from the kitchen to the garden. It tells you to choose plants that need little water, catch rainwater in a tank or bucket and sweep the driveway with a broom instead of hosing it down. It ends by saying that saving water works best when everybody you live with takes part. Choose seven tips, leave out the introduction and the examples, and write one paragraph of 60 to 70 words in full sentences and in your own words, not copied.
g10u01l05.a: Pick out the main tips in an information text and summarise them in 60 to 70 words.

g10u01l06.h: Grammar: intensives and similes. Dead tired, dead still and as strong as an ox: Afrikaans is wonderfully colourful.
g10u01l06.c: Everyday Afrikaans is full of strong adjectives and fixed comparisons, and a reader who doesn’t know them will miss the humour and feeling. You’ll meet them in magazines, speeches and conversations at every braai.
g10u01l06.t: Intensive forms make an adjective stronger and are written as one word: **doodmoeg**, **stokstil**, **stampvol**, **yskoud** and **spierwit**. A **vergelyking** (simile) compares with **so … soos**: **so sterk soos 'n os**, **so doof soos 'n kwartel**. These are fixed, so you can’t swap the animal. A **metafoor** says one thing is another: **Sy het 'n hart van goud.** **Letterlik** means the words mean what they say, and **figuurlik** means they paint a picture. **Die foon steel die aandag** is figurative, because a phone can’t really steal.
g10u01l06.a: Use intensive adjectives and fixed similes, and tell literal from figurative meaning.
g10u01l06.n: Learn the fixed similes whole. If you change the animal, an Afrikaans speaker will notice straight away.

g10u01l07.h: Your family has made a new rule: no phones at the table. Write to a friend about it, in a friendly, natural voice.
g10u01l07.c: A friendly letter is a common Graad 10 writing task, and a good chance to sound like yourself while showing control of the language. It’s informal, personal and warm.
g10u01l07.t: Write 120 to 150 words, body only, to a friend or a friend’s family in South Africa. Say what the rule is, how it started and what you think about it. Use a warm, informal tone, a simile with **so … soos** or an intensive such as **stokstil** or **stampvol**, and give your opinion with a reason. The magazine article gives you a few real-life ideas, such as a phone basket by the door.
g10u01l07.a: Write a friendly letter that explains a family rule and gives your opinion.

g10u01l08.h: Fact-or-opinion check! Can you tell what’s proven from what’s merely claimed?
g10u01l08.c: A look back at opinions, sentence parts and colourful language before you read a short story.
g10u01l08.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die kinders herinner hulle ouers.** and **Hy is so sterk soos 'n os.**, and sort statements into facts and opinions.
g10u01l08.a: See which facts-and-opinions skills, sentence parts and similes are solid.

g10u02l01.h: What is a story really about? Let’s learn the words for talking about narrators, themes and twists before we board the last train.
g10u02l01.c: In Graad 10 you’re expected to discuss a story’s character, setting, conflict and theme, in your own words and with evidence from the text. These are the tools for that discussion, and you’ll use them again in each following year.
g10u02l01.t: **Die tema** (the theme), **die verteller** (the narrator), **die hoofkarakter** (the main character), **die klimaks** (the climax) and **die eindwending** (the twist at the end). The theme is the big idea under the plot, such as loneliness or kindness, and it’s different from what happens. The narrator is the voice that tells the story, which isn’t always the author.
g10u02l01.a: Talk about a story’s theme, narrator, main character, climax and twist.

g10u02l02.h: On the platform: a late-night station, a flat phone battery and a stranger on the bench. Let’s learn the words before you meet him.
g10u02l02.c: Stories pack a lot into small details, such as a bench, a battery or a quiet house. These words and sentences come straight from the short story you’re about to read, so you meet each one in context.
g10u02l02.t: **Die perron** (the platform), **die skoot** (the lap), **verleë** (embarrassed) and **weier** (to refuse). In sentences: **Jy het hom net-net gemis.**, **My foon se battery is pap.**, **Ek pak nou self in, uit gewoonte.** and **Die huis is te stil.** Notice how **pap** describes a flat battery, and how **net-net** means only just.
g10u02l02.a: Use the vocabulary of the story’s setting, and understand the small details that build a mood.

g10u02l03.h: Grammar: time, manner, place. In an Afrikaans sentence, they queue in that order, and it’s the order that makes a sentence sound natural.
g10u02l03.c: Longer sentences contain several pieces of information: when, how, where. Getting the order right is what separates a stiff sentence from a smooth one, and it’s tested in essays and speaking alike.
g10u02l03.t: In a main clause the finite verb is second: **Ons ry môre …** After it come time (**wanneer?**), then manner (**hoe?**), then place (**waar?** or **waarheen?**): **Ons ry môre met die trein stad toe.** A second verb and a separable particle go to the very end: **Sy het die hele dag hard in die hospitaal gewerk.** If you begin with the time, the verb still comes second: **Môre ry ons met die trein stad toe.** A pronoun object comes straight after the verb.
g10u02l03.a: Put time, manner and place in the right order, with the verb in second place.
g10u02l03.n: Remember the three questions in order: when, how, where. If your sentence answers them in that order, it usually sounds right.

g10u02l04.h: Die laaste trein: a short story about a woman, a platform and a very unexpected conversation. Don’t skip ahead.
g10u02l04.c: A short story at this level is a first full piece of literature, with a narrator, a setting, a conflict and a theme. Reading it carefully, then retelling it in order, is the main skill for the exam and for enjoying a story.
g10u02l04.t: It’s almost eleven at night when Nomsa reaches the station. She’s worked all day in a hospital’s children’s ward, her feet hurt, and the sign says the last train left at 22:50. It’s now 22:58. Her phone battery is flat, the taxis have stopped, and home is nine kilometres away. Then a voice beside her says she only just missed it. Look for the character, the setting, the conflict and the theme, and for how the writer builds a mood in small details. After the questions, retell the story in three sentences with time, manner and place in the right order.
g10u02l04.a: Read a short story, discuss character, setting, conflict and theme, and retell it in order.

g10u02l05.h: Write a narrative essay called "'n Onverwagse ontmoeting": An unexpected meeting. A hundred and fifty to two hundred words, and a good opening line.
g10u02l05.c: A narrative essay is the most common creative writing task in Graad 10, and it’s marked on structure, language and imagination. A believable setting and one clear moment of change do more than a complicated plot.
g10u02l05.t: Write 150 to 200 words, not counting the title. Use the past tense. Plan a beginning that sets the scene, a middle with a meeting or surprise, and an ending that shows what has changed. Check each longer sentence for time, manner and place, such as **Sy het die hele dag hard in die hospitaal gewerk.**, and keep the verb in second place. Borrow the way the short story builds a mood from small details.
g10u02l05.a: Write a narrative essay with a clear structure, in the past tense, with time, manner and place in the right order.

g10u02l06.h: Story check! Let’s see whether you’ve understood the last train.
g10u02l06.c: A look back at story vocabulary and word order before the next unit.
g10u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ons ry môre met die trein stad toe.** and **Hulle het lank stil op die bankie gesit.**, and put time, manner and place in order.
g10u02l06.a: See which story words and word-order patterns are solid.

g10u03l01.h: A poem about rain on a tin roof. Before we hear it, let’s learn who’s speaking in a poem, and how it feels.
g10u03l01.c: Poetry is part of the Graad 10 syllabus, and you’re expected to talk about a poem’s mood, voice and sound with some confidence. These terms are the vocabulary for doing that, and they’re the same ones your teacher will use.
g10u03l01.t: **Die digter** (the poet), **die spreker** (the speaker in a poem), **die stemming** (the mood), **die klanknabootsing** (onomatopoeia) and **die enjambement** (a line running on into the next). The poet and the speaker aren’t always the same: the speaker is the voice inside the poem, which may or may not be the poet’s own. Mood is the feeling the poem leaves with the reader, which comes from the images and the sounds together.
g10u03l01.a: Talk about a poem’s poet, speaker, mood, onomatopoeia and enjambement.

g10u03l02.h: Rain on the farm after months of drought: the words here are about a feeling as much as the weather.
g10u03l02.c: Farm life and weather are a deep source of South African poetry, and a long dry spell breaking is a powerful moment. These words are the ones used in the poem you’ll read next.
g10u03l02.t: **Die sinkdak** (the tin roof), **die geut** (the gutter), **snuif** (to sniff, breathe in) and **trommel** (to drum). In sentences: **Die hele plaas hou sy asem op.**, **Sy snuif die nat aarde in.**, **Ná maande se droogte reën dit eindelik.** and **Sy staan met haar oë toe, asof sy bid.** Notice how the poem uses simple actions, such as holding your breath and closing your eyes, to show feeling without naming it.
g10u03l02.a: Use the vocabulary of rain, drought and a farm, and understand how simple actions show feeling.

g10u03l03.h: Poetry: sound devices. Tik, trommel, gorrel: a poet picks words for how they sound as well as what they mean.
g10u03l03.c: A poem is meant to be heard, and its sounds help create the mood. Naming the devices lets you explain why a line works, which is exactly what a poetry question asks.
g10u03l03.t: **Alliterasie** repeats the same consonant at the start of nearby words: **die geut gorrel en die gras groei**. **Assonansie** repeats a vowel sound: **so vaal en kaal**. **Klanknabootsing** is a word that sounds like its meaning: **tik**, **trommel**, **gorrel**. **Rym** is line endings that sound alike, such as **lank** and **bank**, and **herhaling** repeats a word or line for emphasis. Always ask what the sound does: quick t-sounds can feel like drumming rain, and long a-sounds feel slow or sad.
g10u03l03.a: Name sound devices in a poem and explain what they do to its mood.
g10u03l03.n: In an exam, don’t just name the device. Say what effect it has: naming the device is only half of a good answer, and the effect is the other half.

g10u03l04.h: Reën op 'n sinkdak: a short poem that you can hear before you finish reading it. Read it aloud, twice.
g10u03l04.c: A short, imagery-rich poem is ideal for close reading: you can look at every line, and still read it in under a minute. Reading it aloud lets you hear the rain.
g10u03l04.t: The poem begins with a single tap on the tin roof, then two, then ten, until the rain is drumming. The gutter gurgles, the grass drinks and the dust lies down like a tired dog. A mother opens the window and breathes in the wet earth, her eyes closed as if she were praying, and the whole farm holds its breath. Then, after months of drought, the dam sings. Look for alliteration, onomatopoeia, the simile and the way the mood shifts. After the questions, you’ll describe the sounds of rain in three sentences, with at least one onomatopoeic word.
g10u03l04.a: Read a poem closely, find its sound devices and images, and describe the mood.

g10u03l05.h: Write a paragraph about the poem: its mood, and how sound and images create it. Two examples, and say what each one does.
g10u03l05.c: A paragraph on a poem is a standard literature task: you make a point about the mood, support it with evidence and explain the effect. It’s a small essay in one paragraph.
g10u03l05.t: Write one paragraph of 100 to 120 words. Begin by naming the mood of the poem. Then give at least two examples from the text, such as **trommel** or **die dam sing**, and say what each one does. Use the terms you’ve learned, such as **klanknabootsing**, **alliterasie** and **stemming**. Keep the order simple: point, evidence, effect, and close with one sentence that ties the examples together.
g10u03l05.a: Write a paragraph that names a poem’s mood and explains how its sound and imagery create it.

g10u03l06.h: Poem check! Can you hear what the poet did?
g10u03l06.c: A look back at poetry terms and sound devices before the next unit.
g10u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die geut gorrel en die gras groei.** and **Die reën tik-tik op die dak.**, and name the sound device in each.
g10u03l06.a: See which poetry terms and sound devices are solid.

g10u04l01.h: A blog: personal, chatty and read by people you’ve never met. Let’s learn the words for that world.
g10u04l01.c: Blogs and social posts use an informal register that sounds like talking, and they’re a growing part of how people read in Afrikaans. In this unit you’ll read a food-truck owner’s blog and write one of your own.
g10u04l01.t: **Die blog** (the blog), **die inskrywing** (the entry, post), **die kommentaar** (the comments), **die volgeling** (the follower) and **die onderneming** (the business, venture). A blog entry usually has a title, a date and a personal voice, and it often ends with a question for readers to answer in the comments. Reading a blog post is a bit like listening to someone talk, so notice the short sentences and the humour.
g10u04l01.a: Talk about blogs, with words for entry, comments, followers and a business.

g10u04l02.h: The food truck: a risky leap, all the savings gone and a very worried mother.
g10u04l02.c: Starting a small business is a common dream, and the vocabulary of risk, effort and customers fits many situations. These are the words behind the blog post you’ll read.
g10u04l02.t: **Die kosvragmotor** (the food truck), **die spaargeld** (savings), **die ramp** (the disaster) and **bedien** (to serve customers). In sentences: **My ma het amper flou geword.**, **Ek het al my spaargeld daarin gesteek.**, **Ek werk dikwels veertien uur op 'n dag.** and **Ek het die regte besluit geneem.** Notice how plain the sentences are: a blog sounds like the writer speaking. Try saying each one aloud in your own voice, as if you were telling a friend about starting something new.
g10u04l02.a: Describe starting a small business, using words for savings, disaster and serving customers.

g10u04l03.h: Language: idioms and proverbs. Two flies with one blow, not two birds with one stone: Afrikaans has its own wisdom.
g10u04l03.c: Idioms and proverbs make writing and speech sound like a real Afrikaans speaker, and they’re tested in Graad 10. You’ll hear them in the family, in the news and in blog posts.
g10u04l03.t: An **idioom** is a fixed expression whose meaning isn’t the sum of its words: **die kat uit die boom kyk** means to wait and see. A **spreekwoord** is a whole saying with a lesson: **Oefening baar kuns.** and **Haastige spoed is selde goed.** Keep the exact words, so Afrikaans says **twee vlieë met een klap slaan**, not two birds with one stone. Idioms fit into the sentence and change tense: **Hy het aan die kortste end getrek.** Use them sparingly, since one or two well-chosen ones add colour, and ten sound forced.
g10u04l03.a: Use idioms and proverbs correctly, with their exact words and in the right tense.
g10u04l03.n: Learn the idiom as a whole phrase, with its exact words. If you swap in a different animal, it stops being the idiom.

g10u04l04.h: Kos op wiele: a food-truck owner’s first year, told with humour, idioms and a very honest list of what went wrong.
g10u04l04.c: A blog is the perfect text for noticing informal language: short sentences, idioms, humour and a direct address to the reader. This one follows a first year, with all its ups and downs.
g10u04l04.t: Ruben Adams quit a safe office job a year ago and put all his savings into an old, rust-brown food truck, and his mother nearly fainted. The first months were a disaster: the fridge broke in the first week, he sold his boerewors rolls too cheaply and his first big festival was rained out. He learned to wait and see, to talk to other food sellers and to make his menu small, now selling just three things. He works long days, but he’s glad he decided as he did. Look for idioms such as **die kat uit die boom kyk**, **twee vlieë met een klap** and **Oefening baar kuns**. After the questions, talk about something that started badly and ended well.
g10u04l04.a: Read a blog post, find the informal language and idioms, and tell a story of something that went from bad to good.

g10u04l05.h: Write your own blog post about something new you’ve taken on. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty words, two idioms, and a question for your readers at the end.
g10u04l05.c: Writing a blog post is a different voice from a school essay: it’s personal, lively and it speaks straight to the reader. It’s a good chance to use idioms and proverbs naturally.
g10u04l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words, not counting the title. Choose something new you’ve started, such as a hobby, job or move. Use a friendly, informal voice, include at least two idioms or proverbs, such as **Oefening baar kuns.** or **die kat uit die boom kyk**, and finish with a question for your readers, as Ruben does. Keep the exact words of each idiom, and check the tense.
g10u04l05.a: Write an informal blog post that uses two idioms or proverbs correctly.

g10u04l06.h: Food-truck check! Do you know your idioms?
g10u04l06.c: A look back at blog language and idioms before the next unit.
g10u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek het twee vlieë met een klap geslaan.** and **Haastige spoed is selde goed.**, and match each idiom to its meaning.
g10u04l06.a: See which idioms and proverbs are solid.

g10u05l01.h: A four-day work week: dream or disaster? Before we read the argument, let’s learn how to talk about being for something and against it.
g10u05l01.c: Debating a proposal is part of public life, from a school council to a national newspaper. In this unit you’ll read an argumentative article about the four-day work week, weigh both sides and write an argumentative essay of your own. The topic is for language practice, and the unit doesn’t tell you what to think.
g10u05l01.t: **Die voorstander** (the supporter of an idea), **die teenstander** (the opponent), **oortuigend** (convincing), **die gevolgtrekking** (the conclusion) and **afdwing** (to force, impose). A good argumentative text presents the case for, the case against, and then a conclusion that follows from both. **Afdwing** is separable, so the particle jumps to the end of a sentence.
g10u05l01.a: Talk about supporters and opponents, convincing arguments and the conclusion of a debate.

g10u05l02.h: At work: employers, rested people and a gap in the argument. Here are the words that the debate uses.
g10u05l02.c: Arguments about working life use a particular vocabulary of balance, fairness and effort, and you’ll hear it in the news and in conversations at work.
g10u05l02.t: **Die werkgewer** (the employer), **uitgerus** (rested), **die gaping** (the gap) and **balanseer** (to balance). In sentences: **Jou salaris krimp nie.**, **Uitgeruste mense lewer beter werk.**, **Hulle moet meer mense aanstel.** and **Werknemers moet ook 'n stem hê.** Notice how each sentence is a claim that someone could argue for or against, which is what makes it useful for the next lessons. Try turning each into a question and see who would answer yes, and who would answer no.
g10u05l02.a: Use the vocabulary of work, rest and balance to state a claim in a debate.

g10u05l03.h: Grammar: negation. Niemand, nooit, geen, nêrens: Afrikaans says no twice, and does it on purpose.
g10u05l03.c: In an argument, a negative sentence can make or break your point. The closing **nie** is one of the most common slips in written Afrikaans, so getting it right makes your writing clearer and more convincing.
g10u05l03.t: Afrikaans negates twice: **nie**, **niemand**, **niks**, **nooit**, **geen** or **nêrens** goes in its place, and a closing **nie** ends the clause: **Niemand hoef in die verkeer te sit nie.** The closing **nie** comes after the last verb or particle of its clause: **Ek het dit nie geweet nie.** If the clause already ends in **nie**, don’t add another: **Ek weet nie.** With **om … te**, **nie** comes straight after **om**, and the closing **nie** after **te** plus the verb: **Probeer om nie laat te wees nie.** And **nie net … nie, maar ook** means not only … but also.
g10u05l03.a: Negate longer sentences correctly, with the closing nie in the right place.
g10u05l03.n: Look at the end of your clause. If it doesn’t finish with a **nie**, and it’s a negative clause, you’ve probably forgotten one.

g10u05l04.h: Die vierdagwerkweek: droom of werklikheid? An argumentative article that gives both sides, and then dares to say what it thinks.
g10u05l04.c: An argumentative article presents arguments in order, answers the other side and ends with a conclusion. This one follows that pattern clearly, so it’s a good model for your own essay. The article is a language-learning text, and it doesn’t ask you to agree with it.
g10u05l04.t: The writer asks you to imagine a long weekend every week without a smaller salary, since more and more companies around the world are experimenting with a four-day week. Supporters say that rested workers are happier and do better work, that an extra free day helps balance family and work, and that nobody has to sit in traffic on the fifth day. Opponents point out that a shop can’t turn customers away and that employers would need to hire more people, and they ask who gets the benefit, such as cleaners and cashiers. The writer’s own view is that it’s no magic wand, but no impossible dream either. Look for **Eerstens**, **Tweedens** and **Derdens**, and for the negatives. After the questions, give one argument for and one against.
g10u05l04.a: Read an argumentative article, weigh the arguments for and against, and spot the conclusion.

g10u05l05.h: Write an argumentative essay: arguments for and against, and your own conclusion. Choose your topic, or tackle phones in meetings.
g10u05l05.c: An argumentative essay is a standard Graad 10 task, and it practises the skill of weighing both sides fairly before choosing one. It also trains you to negate correctly in longer sentences.
g10u05l05.t: Write 150 to 200 words, not counting the title. Pick your own topic, or write on whether phones should be banned in meetings. Give arguments for and against, using **eerstens**, **tweedens** and **derdens**, then finish with your own conclusion in **Na my mening …**. Check each negative sentence for the closing **nie**, and try **nie net … nie, maar ook** at least once. A fair essay deals honestly with the other side.
g10u05l05.a: Write an argumentative essay that weighs both sides and gives a clear conclusion.

g10u05l06.h: Argument check! Niemand, nooit, nie: let’s see where your negatives land.
g10u05l06.c: A look back at argument vocabulary and negation before the last unit.
g10u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Niemand hoef in die verkeer te sit nie.** and **Probeer om nie laat te wees nie.**, and place the closing **nie** correctly.
g10u05l06.a: See which negation patterns are solid.

g10u06l01.h: Buying a second-hand car: one of the biggest purchases you’ll ever make, and a very good topic for practical reading. (Language practice, not financial advice.)
g10u06l01.c: Information texts that give practical advice are a staple of magazines and websites, and at Graad 10 you’re asked to read them closely and summarise them. This unit’s text is about buying a used car, and it’s for language practice, not financial advice.
g10u06l01.t: **Die diensboek** (the service book), **die proefrit** (the test drive), **die meganikus** (the mechanic), **die eienaar** (the owner) and **die begroting** (the budget). A service book records a car’s maintenance, so a missing one is a warning sign. These words also appear in the text’s seven tips, which you’ll summarise at the end.
g10u06l01.a: Talk about buying a second-hand car with words for service book, test drive, mechanic, owner and budget.

g10u06l02.h: Look carefully: insurance, rust, a sales agreement and one very good rule: buy with your head, not with your eyes.
g10u06l02.c: Practical advice is full of short instructions, and the best way to learn them is to see them in short sentences. These are the instructions the text uses, and you can borrow them in your own advice.
g10u06l02.t: **Die versekering** (the insurance), **onderhandel** (to negotiate), **die roes** (rust) and **die koopkontrak** (the sales agreement). Learn these instructions whole: **Kyk na die motor in daglig.**, **Toets die remme.**, **Kry alles op skrif.** and **Koop met jou kop, nie met jou oë nie.** The last one is the main message of the whole text, in one line.
g10u06l02.a: Give short, practical advice about checking a car, using clear instructions.

g10u06l03.h: Spelling: ¨ ^ -. Three little marks that change how a word looks, and sometimes what it means.
g10u06l03.c: Spelling marks are easy to miss when you type quickly, but they affect both marks in tests and how professional your writing looks. They’re also a real source of mistakes in e-mails and messages.
g10u06l03.t: The **deelteken** (¨) shows that a new syllable starts, so two vowels aren’t read as one sound: **geïnteresseerd**, **beïnvloed**, **reën**, **oë**. Plurals of words ending in **-ie** or **-ee** often need it: **knie** becomes **knieë** and **idee** becomes **ideë**. The **kappie** (^) marks a long, open vowel in certain words, so learn them as whole words: **wêreld**, **sê**, **lê**, **môre**. Leaving it out can change the word, since **se** is possessive and **sê** means say. The **koppelteken** (-) links parts that would be misread, or that include a name, letter or number: **Suid-Afrikaanse**, **e-pos**, **12-jarige**.
g10u06l03.a: Spell words with a diaeresis, a circumflex and a hyphen correctly.
g10u06l03.n: Learn the kappie words as whole words, because there’s no simple rule for them. **Wêreld**, **sê**, **lê** and **môre** will cover a lot of everyday writing.

g10u06l04.h: Koop 'n tweedehandse motor sonder spyt: an information text with seven tips, and a very honest story about a shiny red car. (Language practice, not financial advice.)
g10u06l04.c: This is a typical practical information text: it opens with a reason to read, gives its advice in a clear order and ends with a short story that drives the point home. It’s the text you’ll summarise in the next lesson, and it’s for language practice only.
g10u06l04.t: The text says a car is one of the most expensive things most people buy, and a second-hand one can be a smart choice if you’re careful. It tells you to start with a budget that includes insurance, licence, fuel and maintenance, to research models and prices, to look at the car yourself in daylight, to ask for the service book, to take a test drive, to have an independent mechanic check it and to make sure the seller is the owner, and finally to get everything in writing. It ends with a neighbour who bought a shiny red car because it looked good, and the engine stopped a week later. After the questions, give your cousin three tips.
g10u06l04.a: Read an information text, find its tips in order, and give someone three tips for buying a car.

g10u06l05.h: Summarise the text: seven tips, one paragraph, sixty to seventy words, in your own words. Brisk and precise, like a good mechanic.
g10u06l05.c: Summaries are the most common Graad 10 reading-and-writing task, and the skill that’s most useful afterwards. It’s about picking out what matters and saying it in your own words.
g10u06l05.t: Choose seven tips from the car text, and leave out the introduction, the examples and the story at the end. Write one paragraph of 60 to 70 words in full sentences, in your own words and not copied. Use signal words such as **eerstens**, **verder** and **laastens**, and check any words with a deelteken or kappie. This is language practice, not financial advice.
g10u06l05.a: Pick out the main tips from an information text and summarise them in 60 to 70 words.

g10u06l06.h: The last check of Graad 10! Spelling marks, car-buying tips and a year of reading.
g10u06l06.c: A final look at spelling marks and practical-text language before Graad 11.
g10u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Is jy geïnteresseerd in die motor?** and **Dit is 'n Suid-Afrikaanse webwerf.**, and decide which spelling mark each word needs.
g10u06l06.a: See which spelling marks are solid.

g11u01l01.h: The driving test: clipboard, clutch and a very nervous candidate. Welcome to Graad 11, where we begin with a story about third time lucky.
g11u01l01.c: Almost everyone has a story about a test, an exam or an interview that went wrong the first time. This unit’s short story follows a young man on his third driving test, and teaches you to see how a character changes. It also gives you the words for the situation, which are useful in real life too.
g11u01l01.t: **Die eksaminator** (the examiner), **die poging** (the attempt), **die knipbord** (the clipboard), **die randsteen** (the kerb) and **die koppelaar** (the clutch). **Knipbord** is a lovely compound: **knip** means to clip, and **bord** is a board. These words make up the scene, and they’ll help when you describe your own test or when you read the story.
g11u01l01.a: Talk about a driving test with words for examiner, attempt, clipboard, kerb and clutch.

g11u01l02.h: Behind the wheel: handbrake, indicator and a heart that sinks into your boots. These are the words and the phrases the story uses.
g11u01l02.c: A story uses small, concrete details to show how a character feels, and a few well-known sayings to give the writing colour. Here you’ll learn the ones used in the story.
g11u01l02.t: **Die handrem** (the handbrake), **die flikkerlig** (the indicator), **mompel** (to mumble) and **skuldig** (guilty). In sentences: **Sy hart het in sy skoene gesak.**, **Drie maal is skeepsreg.**, **Ek het niks verniet gegee nie.** and **Jy het dit self gedoen.** **Drie maal is skeepsreg** is a proverb meaning third time lucky, and **sy hart het in sy skoene gesak** is an idiom for a sudden feeling of dread.
g11u01l02.a: Use the vocabulary of driving and the idioms the story uses to show a character’s feelings.

g11u01l03.h: Words: homonyms and paronyms. Bank and bang, kollega and kollege: words that look or sound alike and love to trip you up.
g11u01l03.c: Mixing up similar words is one of the most common ways to lose marks, and also to say something you didn’t mean. In a formal letter, a job interview or a story, the right word matters.
g11u01l03.t: **Homonieme** are one word with two or more meanings, such as **bank** (seat or bank) and **arm** (limb or poor). **Homofone** sound the same but are spelt differently, such as **ly** and **lei**, and **pyl** and **peil**. **Paronieme** look or sound alike but mean different things: **personeel** (staff) and **persoonlik** (personal), **kollega** (colleague) and **kollege** (college), **kompliment** (praise) and **komplement** (something that completes). English can trick you here, because **personal** is **persoonlik**, never **personeel**.
g11u01l03.a: Tell homonyms, homophones and paronyms apart, and pick the right word in a sentence.
g11u01l03.n: When you’re not sure, check a dictionary instead of guessing. It takes ten seconds, and it can save you an embarrassing e-mail.

g11u01l04.h: Die derde keer: a short story about a young man, a hill, a test and a teacher he never expected to see. Pay attention to how he changes.
g11u01l04.c: At this level you’re expected to trace how a character changes across a story, with evidence from the text. This story is short, but it has a clear turning point, so it’s an ideal example.
g11u01l04.t: Sipho is sitting behind the wheel of the test car for the third time. The first time he drove through a stop street, and the second time he stalled twice on the hill by the post office. Then the examiner turns out to be Mrs Botha, his old maths teacher, who once caught him copying homework. She doesn’t say anything about it, but he has felt guilty ever since. Watch what Sipho feels at the start, what happens on the hill, and what he understands by the end. After the questions, you’ll answer in three sentences how Sipho changes.
g11u01l04.a: Read a short story, trace how a character changes, and find the turning point.

g11u01l05.h: Write a narrative essay called "Die dag toe ek nie moed opgegee het nie": the day I didn’t give up. Show how your main character changes.
g11u01l05.c: A narrative essay at Graad 11 is judged on structure, language and the way the character develops. A good turning point makes the difference between a story and a list of events.
g11u01l05.t: Write 200 to 250 words, not counting the title. Show your main character at the start, give a problem or fear, include a clear turning point, and show the change at the end. Use the past tense and a few precise details, like Sipho’s wet hands or the hill by the post office. Choose your words carefully, and check homonyms and paronyms such as **kollega** and **kollege**.
g11u01l05.a: Write a narrative essay with a clear turning point that shows a character changing.

g11u01l06.h: Story check! Let’s see if you got the turning point and the right words.
g11u01l06.c: A look back at the story and the confusable words before you read a classic poem.
g11u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Hy het geld by die bank geleen.** and **Ek wil haar persoonlik bedank.**, and choose between look-alike words.
g11u01l06.a: See which story words and confusable pairs are solid.

g11u02l01.h: A classic poem, written long ago. Before we read it, let’s learn how to talk about its shape and sound.
g11u02l01.c: At Graad 11 you read poems from different periods, and you need to talk about form as well as meaning. This unit takes you through a classic Afrikaans poem, and shows you how older poetic language and unusual word order work.
g11u02l01.t: **Die rymskema** (the rhyme scheme), **die ritme** (the rhythm), **die kontras** (the contrast), **die inversie** (inversion, or unusual word order) and **verouderd** (old-fashioned, archaic). The rhyme scheme is written with letters, such as a a b b, for lines that end alike. Inversion means a poet has changed the normal order of the words, for the rhythm, for the rhyme or for emphasis.
g11u02l01.a: Talk about the shape of a poem: rhyme scheme, rhythm, contrast and inversion.

g11u02l02.h: In the veld on a winter night: dew, frost, a sharp east wind and grass seed swaying. Let’s learn the words first.
g11u02l02.c: A winter night on the open veld is a very South African image, and the poem uses a rich vocabulary of weather and landscape. You’ll know these words before you meet them in the poem.
g11u02l02.t: **Skraal** (thin, meagre, or of wind sharp and cold), **die genade** (grace, mercy), **die dou** (dew), **die ryp** (frost) and **verbleek** (to turn pale). In sentences: **Daar is dou op die gras.**, **Vanoggend lê daar ryp op die veld.**, **Die grassaad wieg in die wind.** and **Die ooswind waai yskoud.** Notice how **dou** and **ryp** show the same water in two states, and how a drop can change from one to the other.
g11u02l02.a: Use the vocabulary of winter, dew and frost to describe a cold night on the veld.

g11u02l03.h: Poetry: inversion and older language. Poets bend word order and use old forms, and you can learn to straighten them out.
g11u02l03.c: Classic poems often sound unfamiliar, because their language is older and their word order is flexible. Once you know how to decode them, they become much easier to enjoy and to write about.
g11u02l03.t: Poets often change the normal word order, called **inversie**, for rhythm, rhyme or emphasis: **O koud is die windjie** means **Die windjie is koud.** Older poems use forms that sound old-fashioned now: **skade** meaning shadow, not damage, **elk'** meaning **elke**, and **aan roere** meaning in motion. In everyday modern Afrikaans, use the modern forms, **skaduwee** and **elke**. A diminutive such as **windjie** can show tenderness or smallness, not only size. To understand an old line, first rewrite it in normal modern word order, then ask why the poet chose the other order.
g11u02l03.a: Read older poetic language, straighten out inverted lines and name a rhyme scheme.
g11u02l03.n: Rewrite the line in modern prose first. Then compare the two versions, and the poet’s choice will show you the effect.

g11u02l04.h: Winternag, by Eugène N. Marais: a classic Afrikaans poem about a cold night on the veld. Read it aloud, because it was written to be heard.
g11u02l04.c: This poem is in the public domain and has been read in Afrikaans classrooms for generations. Its sound, its images and its old-fashioned wording are all worth close attention.
g11u02l04.t: Eugène N. Marais (1871 to 1936) describes the cold, thin wind, the bare fields lying in starlight and shadow, and the grass seed in the hills moving like beckoning hands. The sad tune on the east wind is compared to a girl’s song when her love has left her, and in the last lines a drop of dew in every blade of grass quickly turns pale into frost. Look for the inverted lines, the older words, the rhyme scheme and the contrast of beauty and cold. After the questions, you’ll describe what you see, hear and feel in the poem, in three sentences.
g11u02l04.a: Read a classic poem, decode its older language and word order, and describe what you see, hear and feel.

g11u02l05.h: Write a paragraph on how Winternag creates its mood. Two devices, correct quotations and a clear point of view.
g11u02l05.c: A paragraph on a poem is a standard Graad 11 literature task, and it’s marked on the quality of your argument and the accuracy of your evidence. Quoting correctly is part of the skill.
g11u02l05.t: Write one paragraph of 120 to 150 words about how the poet creates the mood. Refer to at least two devices or sound effects, such as rhyme, inversion, contrast, alliteration or the simile, and quote each one correctly, in quotation marks and with the exact words. For each quotation, say what effect it has on the mood. Organise your paragraph as point, evidence and effect, and end with a sentence that ties the examples together.
g11u02l05.a: Write a paragraph that explains how a poem creates its mood, with correct quotations.

g11u02l06.h: Poem check! Rhyme schemes, old words and inversions.
g11u02l06.c: A look back at the poem and its language before the next unit.
g11u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die velde lê in sterlig en skaduwee.** and **Die druppel verbleek vinnig tot ryp.**, and rewrite inverted lines in modern word order.
g11u02l06.a: See which poetry terms and older forms are solid.

g11u03l01.h: A survey about a cycle route, a committee and a report. This is the formal, factual Afrikaans you’ll need in a workplace or a community group.
g11u03l01.c: Reports are written at work, at school and in community groups, and they follow a clear format: who it’s for, what was asked, how, what was found and what to do next. This unit follows a short formal report from a survey of residents about a cycle route. The survey and the town are made up for the lesson.
g11u03l01.t: **Die verslag** (the report), **die opname** (the survey), **die respondent** (the respondent), **die bevinding** (the finding) and **die aanbeveling** (the recommendation). A finding is a fact the survey turned up, while a recommendation is what the writers suggest should be done about it. Keeping the two apart is the heart of good report writing.
g11u03l01.a: Talk about a survey report, using words for respondent, finding and recommendation.

g11u03l02.h: Method and recommendations: how the committee asked, what worried people and what it suggests. The words are formal, and they’re useful.
g11u03l02.c: The method section tells readers how you collected your information, and the recommendations tell them what to do. Both use a formal register that you’ll meet in any official document.
g11u03l02.t: **Die vraelys** (the questionnaire), **die metode** (the method), **haalbaar** (feasible) and **die bekommernis** (the concern, worry). In sentences: **Voltooi asseblief die vraelys.**, **Ons moet hul kommer ernstig opneem.**, **Die komitee beveel 'n tweede opname aan.** and **Die roete moet van die hoofweg geskei wees.** Note that **aanbeveel** is separable, so you’ll see **beveel … aan** with the particle at the end. Each sentence is something a committee would really write, so try changing one detail in each and reading it aloud in a formal voice.
g11u03l02.a: Describe a survey’s method and recommendations in formal sentences.

g11u03l03.h: Grammar: fractions, percentages and decimals. Drie kwart and vier komma vyf: numbers that you read out loud need their own Afrikaans.
g11u03l03.c: Reports, news and school work are full of numbers, and you need to read and write them properly, since Afrikaans uses a decimal comma, a spoken persent and a few word forms you can’t guess from English.
g11u03l03.t: Fractions: **die helfte van die personeel**, **een derde**, **'n kwart** and **drie kwart**, and it’s **die helfte van**, not *die half van*. Percentages: **agt-en-vyftig persent** is read in full, and **persentasie** is the noun. Afrikaans uses a decimal comma, so the route is **vier komma vyf kilometer** lank, and large numbers are grouped in threes with a space. **Die meeste** (most) takes a plural noun: **Die meeste inwoners verkies die rivierroete.**
g11u03l03.a: Read and write fractions, percentages and decimals correctly, using the Afrikaans forms.
g11u03l03.n: Remember the decimal comma. If you write a point where Afrikaans expects a comma, a reader will notice straight away.

g11u03l04.h: A formal report on a cycle-route survey: headings, numbered findings and a clear conclusion. Read it like an official.
g11u03l04.c: A formal report has a fixed layout, and reading one closely teaches you where to look for each piece of information. It’s also the model for the short report you’ll write.
g11u03l04.t: The report is addressed to the management of the Bergsig community forum, from the secretary of the transport committee. It’s divided into numbered headings: the assignment, the method, the findings and the conclusion. Altogether 640 residents completed the questionnaire. Nearly three quarters support a cycle route, a third say they would use it at least three times a week, safety is the biggest concern, about one in ten are against it because they fear parking will vanish, and most prefer a route along the river. Notice how the findings are numbered and use fractions and percentages. After the questions, give three findings using fractions or percentages.
g11u03l04.a: Read a formal report, find the numbered findings, and report three of them with fractions or percentages.

g11u03l05.h: Write a short report to your manager about a staff survey on the office kitchen. Headings, numbering and at least two fractions or percentages.
g11u03l05.c: Writing a short formal report is a practical skill for school, community groups and nearly every office job, and it makes you organise your thoughts into a clear order.
g11u03l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words to your manager about a staff survey on the office kitchen. Use headings and numbering, such as **1. Opdrag**, **2. Metode**, **3. Bevindinge** and **4. Aanbevelings**, and include at least two fractions or percentages, written correctly with **die helfte van**, **drie kwart** or **persent**. Keep the findings separate from the recommendations, and use a formal tone throughout.
g11u03l05.a: Write a short formal report with headings, numbered findings and correct use of fractions or percentages.

g11u03l06.h: Report check! Numbers, findings and formal language.
g11u03l06.c: A look back at reports and numbers before a dialogue unit.
g11u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Drie kwart van die inwoners steun die plan.** and **Die roete is vier komma vyf kilometer lank.**, and read numbers aloud correctly.
g11u03l06.a: See which report words and number forms are solid.

g11u04l01.h: A leaking geyser at seven on a Saturday morning: a tenant, a landlord and a very wet bathroom. Real-life Afrikaans, and a very useful dialogue.
g11u04l01.c: Phoning a landlord, a plumber or a service provider about a problem at home is something nearly everyone has to do, and it takes a particular tone: polite, clear and calm. This unit’s dialogue is written like a script, and you’ll learn to write one yourself.
g11u04l01.t: **Die geiser** (the geyser, the hot-water cylinder), **die loodgieter** (the plumber), **die verhuurder** (the landlord), **die huurder** (the tenant) and **die plafon** (the ceiling). **Geiser** is a word that every South African household knows, since it’s the cylinder that heats the water, and it’s the same in Afrikaans.
g11u04l01.a: Talk about a problem in a rented flat, using words for geyser, plumber, landlord, tenant and ceiling.

g11u04l02.h: An emergency: first turn the water off, then phone. Here are the words and phrases for acting calmly.
g11u04l02.c: In an emergency at home, you need short, clear instructions and polite phrases for asking for help. These are the ones the dialogue uses. (They’re for language practice, not safety instructions.)
g11u04l02.t: **Die noodgeval** (the emergency), **die hoofkraan** (the main tap, stopcock), **die kragkas** (the distribution board, fuse box) and **optree** (to act, take action). In sentences: **Draai die water by die hoofkraan af.**, **Ek sal my bes doen.**, **Ek bel jou binne 'n halfuur terug.** and **Dit is gaaf van u.** Notice that **u** is used when speaking to someone formally, while a landlord may use **jy** with a younger tenant.
g11u04l02.a: Use polite and clear phrases to report an emergency and promise to follow up.

g11u04l03.h: Grammar: punctuating speech. Quotation marks, commas and dashes: the little marks that make a dialogue easy to read.
g11u04l03.c: In stories, scripts and even messages, punctuating speech correctly lets the reader hear who is talking. It’s tested often, and it’s easy to get right once you know the few rules.
g11u04l03.t: Direct speech goes in quotation marks, and the comma, question mark or exclamation mark goes inside them: **"Die geiser lek," sê Marlize.** and **"Wanneer kan u kom?" vra sy.** Start a new line each time a different person speaks. In a script, use the speaker’s name and a colon, with no quotation marks, and put stage directions in brackets. The **beletselteken** (…) shows hesitation, a pair of **aandagstrepe** (–) sets off an aside, and the **apostrof** marks plurals such as **foto’s** and **ma’s**.
g11u04l03.a: Punctuate direct speech and write a script dialogue correctly.
g11u04l03.n: If a different person starts talking, start a new line. That single habit makes a dialogue much easier to follow.

g11u04l04.h: Die geiser: a phone call between a tenant and a landlord, written as a script. Listen for the tone, polite but worried.
g11u04l04.c: A dialogue in script form is a good way to see register and tone, since each speaker reveals who they are in a few words. It’s also the format you’ll use for your own dialogue.
g11u04l04.t: Marlize Kruger rents flat number four from Mr Pillay. It’s early on a Saturday morning, and she phones to say the geyser is leaking: the bathroom floor was full of water when she woke, and now it’s dripping through the ceiling in the passage. Mr Pillay asks whether she has turned the water off at the main tap, and she has, and she’s also switched the geyser off at the distribution board. He asks for photos for the insurance company and says he’ll ask the plumber to come the same day, even though Saturday is his busiest. Notice how both speakers stay polite and exact, and how the script uses names and colons. After the questions, you’ll phone your own landlord in three sentences.
g11u04l04.a: Read a dialogue in script form, notice register and tone, and report a problem to a landlord.

g11u04l05.h: Write a dialogue with a neighbour about noise, in script form, and in the right register. Polite but firm, and a solution at the end.
g11u04l05.c: Talking through a problem with a neighbour is something people dread, but a clear and friendly approach usually works. Writing the conversation first is a good way to prepare.
g11u04l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words, not counting the title, as a script: the speaker’s name, a colon and the words, with stage directions in brackets. Choose the register carefully, such as **jy** for a neighbour you know well or **u** for someone older or more formal. Show the problem, a polite request and an agreed solution. Include at least one **beletselteken** and one pair of **aandagstrepe**, and use the apostrophe correctly.
g11u04l05.a: Write a script dialogue that solves a problem, in the right register and with correct punctuation.

g11u04l06.h: Dialogue check! Quotation marks, commas and a leaking geyser.
g11u04l06.c: A look back at dialogue punctuation before the last unit of Graad 11 part one.
g11u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **"Wanneer kan u kom?" vra sy.** and **"Die water loop oral!" roep sy uit.**, and place the punctuation correctly.
g11u04l06.a: See which punctuation and dialogue patterns are solid.

g11u05l01.h: Smart programs that write, translate and summarise: friend or foe at work? A very current topic, and a great one for practising balanced argument.
g11u05l01.c: Discussing new technology comes up at work, at school and at home, and a discursive essay is the way to weigh it up fairly. In this unit you’ll read an essay about artificial intelligence at work, learn the formal words for balancing two sides and write a balanced essay of your own. The unit doesn’t tell you what to think.
g11u05l01.t: **Kunsmatig** (artificial), **die hulpmiddel** (the aid, tool), **outomaties** (automatically), **vertroulik** (confidential) and **die privaatheid** (privacy). **Kunsmatige intelligensie** is often shortened to **KI**, and you’ll see it in the text. **Vertroulik** and **privaatheid** are the words that tell you why some people worry about typing private information into a program.
g11u05l01.a: Talk about artificial intelligence at work, using words for tool, automatic, confidential and privacy.

g11u05l02.h: Thinking critically: judge every answer, spot the advantage and ask who it helps. The words here are the ones a thoughtful writer uses.
