g11u05l02.c: A discursive essay asks you to assess both sides, and these words help you do it. They also appear in news and workplace talk about technology and change.
g11u05l02.t: **Beoordeel** (to judge, assess), **die voorsprong** (the advantage, head start), **ontstaan** (to arise, come into being) and **indrukwekkend** (impressive). In sentences: **Die program skryf 'n eerste konsep.**, **Beoordeel elke antwoord krities.**, **Dit hang af van hoe ons dit gebruik.** and **Die kenners is dit eens.** Notice how **dit hang af van** is a very handy way to avoid giving a flat yes or no.
g11u05l02.a: Use the vocabulary of judging and weighing up, to talk about technology and its effects.

g11u05l03.h: Grammar: formal linking words. Enersyds, andersyds, weliswaar, nietemin: the words that make an essay sound balanced and educated.
g11u05l03.c: In a discursive essay, an argument, a report or a formal letter, these linking words show how your points connect. They’re formal, so you’ll use them on paper more than in speech, and they’re tested in Graad 11.
g11u05l03.t: **Enersyds … andersyds** (on the one hand … on the other) set two sides against each other. **Weliswaar … maar** admits a point before limiting it: **Dit is weliswaar vinnig, maar nie altyd korrek nie.** **Bowendien** (moreover) adds a point, and **derhalwe** (therefore) gives a result. **Desondanks** and **nietemin** (nevertheless) introduce something that is true in spite of what you’ve just said. When one of these starts a sentence, the verb comes straight after it: **Desondanks wil baie mense dit gebruik.**
g11u05l03.a: Use formal linking words to balance and connect arguments, with the verb in the right place.
g11u05l03.n: In speech you’d say **ook** and **daarom**. In a formal essay, **bowendien** and **derhalwe** sound more polished.

g11u05l04.h: Kunsmatige intelligensie by die werk: vriend of vyand? A discursive essay that gives both sides before it makes up its mind.
g11u05l04.c: A discursive essay has a clear shape: an introduction, one side, the other side and a balanced conclusion. This one is a good model for your own, and a good place to see the formal linking words at work. It’s a language-learning text, not a verdict on the topic.
g11u05l04.t: The essay begins with programs that write text, answer questions and create pictures, and workers wondering whether AI will make their work easier or take it away. On the one hand, it can save time, for example by summarising a long document, translating an e-mail or writing a first draft, and it can spot errors a tired person might miss. On the other, the programs make mistakes, often sound very sure even when they’re wrong, and raise questions about privacy. The biggest fear is that it will take work away, though many new jobs have also come into being. The conclusion is that AI is a tool, and whether it’s a friend or a foe depends largely on how we use it. After the questions, you’ll give one advantage and one disadvantage using enersyds and andersyds.
g11u05l04.a: Read a discursive essay, find each side’s points and the conclusion, and balance one advantage against one disadvantage.

g11u05l05.h: Write a discursive essay, either on a topic of your choice or on working from home: blessing or curse? Both sides, fairly, with at least four formal linking words.
g11u05l05.c: A balanced discursive essay is a Graad 11 staple, and it shows you can see more than one side of a question, a skill that matters outside school too.
g11u05l05.t: Write 200 to 250 words, not counting the title. Choose your own topic, or write about working from home. Give both sides fairly, using **enersyds** and **andersyds**, and use at least four formal linking words, such as **weliswaar**, **bowendien**, **nietemin** and **derhalwe**. Remember that the verb comes right after a linking word at the start of a sentence. End with a conclusion that weighs the two sides, rather than one that simply repeats them.
g11u05l05.a: Write a balanced discursive essay that uses formal linking words correctly.

g11u05l06.h: Discursive-essay check! Enersyds, andersyds and a lot of balance.
g11u05l06.c: A look back at formal linking words and the language of weighing up before the last unit.
g11u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Enersyds spaar dit tyd; andersyds maak dit foute.** and **Desondanks wil baie mense dit gebruik.**, and place the verb correctly after each linking word.
g11u05l06.a: See which linking words and word-order patterns are solid.

g11u06l01.h: "Congratulations! You’ve won R50 000!" Almost everyone has had a message like that, and this unit gives you the Afrikaans to talk about it. (Language practice, not security advice.)
g11u06l01.c: Scams arrive by SMS, e-mail and WhatsApp, and they’re a part of modern life that people discuss at home, at work and in the news. This unit’s information text explains how scams work and what to watch for, and it’s for language practice, not security advice. Always follow your own bank’s guidance for anything about your money.
g11u06l01.t: **Die bedrieër** (the fraudster), **die swendelary** (the scam), **agterdogtig** (suspicious), **amptelik** (official) and **die waarskuwing** (the warning). **Agterdogtig** is the word for the healthy doubt you feel when a message rushes you, and it’s the attitude the whole text recommends. **Amptelik** is a word you’ll want for official apps, official websites and official letters.
g11u06l01.a: Talk about scams, with words for fraudster, suspicious, official and warning.

g11u06l02.h: Stay calm and check first. The words here are short, and they’re the advice that scam texts hope you’ll forget. (Language practice, not security advice.)
g11u06l02.c: A good information text on scams uses short, direct advice and a few strong images, such as a trap. These are the phrases the text uses, and they’re useful far beyond scams.
g11u06l02.t: **Oorbetaal** (to transfer money), **blokkeer** (to block), **die hebsug** (greed) and **rapporteer** (to report). In sentences: **Dit klink te goed om waar te wees.**, **Moenie in die strik trap nie.**, **Bly kalm en gaan eers na.** and **Hulle maak staat op skrik.** **Nagaan** is separable, so the particle goes to the end: **Gaan eers na.** These phrases are for language practice. For real money matters, follow your own bank’s advice.
g11u06l02.a: Use short, firm phrases to give warnings and advice about scams.

g11u06l03.h: Grammar: verbs at the end. After dat, omdat, as and sodat, all the verbs march to the end of the clause, and in order.
g11u06l03.c: Longer sentences with two or three verbs trip up many writers, and a good command of verb order is one of the clearest signs of fluent Afrikaans. You’ll need it for the summary at the end of the unit.
g11u06l03.t: After **dat**, **omdat**, **as**, **wat**, **sodat**, **voordat** and similar words, all the verbs of that clause go to the end. With a modal and an infinitive, the modal comes first: **… dat jy dadelik moet betaal.** In the past tense, the past participle comes before **het**: **… as jy op die skakel geklik het.** Separable verbs stay joined at the end: **… sodat hulle jou rekening kan leegmaak.** With three verbs, keep the order: **… dat hy die geld sou kon terugkry.**
g11u06l03.a: Put two or three verbs in the right order at the end of a subordinate clause.
g11u06l03.n: Count the verbs in your clause, and write them in the order: modal, then main verb, then **het** or **sou** where needed, as in the examples.

g11u06l04.h: Moenie in die strik trap nie: an information text on online scams, with tips in a clear order. (Language practice, not security advice.)
g11u06l04.c: Practical information texts about modern life are a common reading task at this level, and they’re good for summarising. This one opens with messages you’ve probably seen yourself. It’s a language-learning text only.
g11u06l04.t: The text begins with messages that sound too good, or too frightening, to be true, such as a prize of R50 000 or a bank account that has been closed. It says scammers are getting smarter, but that a few simple rules help: be suspicious of anything that rushes you, look closely at the sender, don’t click on links in unexpected messages and never give anyone your password or one-time PIN, not even someone who says they’re from the bank. It also says that if it happens, you shouldn’t feel ashamed, and you should phone your bank straight away. Look for the verbs at the end after **dat**, **omdat** and **sodat**. After the questions, you’ll give your grandfather three pieces of advice. Always follow your own bank’s guidance for real situations.
g11u06l04.a: Read an information text on scams, find its tips in order, and give three pieces of advice.

g11u06l05.h: Summarise the text: seven tips, one paragraph, seventy to eighty words, in your own words. This is the longest summary yet. (Language practice, not security advice.)
g11u06l05.c: A summary of 70 to 80 words needs more detail than the earlier ones, so you’ll need to join ideas in longer sentences. That’s where verb order really counts.
g11u06l05.t: Choose seven tips from the scams text, and leave out the introduction and the examples. Write one paragraph of 70 to 80 words in full sentences and in your own words, not copied. Join ideas with **omdat**, **sodat**, **as** and **voordat**, and check that the verbs are in the right order at the end of each clause. This is language practice. For real situations, follow your bank’s own guidance.
g11u06l05.a: Pick out the main tips from an information text and summarise them in 70 to 80 words.

g11u06l06.h: The last check of Graad 11! Verbs at the end and a year of formal language.
g11u06l06.c: A final look at verb order and the language of warnings before the final level.
g11u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Hulle sê dat jy dadelik moet betaal.** and **Hy het gedink dat hy die geld sou kon terugkry.**, and put every verb in the right place.
g11u06l06.a: See which verb-order patterns are solid.

g12u01l01.h: Welcome to Graad 12! We start with a story about two brothers, an old farmhouse and twelve years of not speaking.
g12u01l01.c: Matric is the year of long, thoughtful reading and writing, and literary short stories ask you to look beneath the surface at what a character feels and what a symbol means. This unit takes you through a story of regret and reconciliation, and shows you how to talk about things that didn’t happen.
g12u01l01.t: **Die verwyt** (the reproach), **die versoening** (the reconciliation), **die spyt** (regret), **die koppigheid** (stubbornness) and **die terugflits** (the flashback). Many stories have both an outer conflict, such as an argument about money, and an inner one, such as pride fighting with love, and these words let you name both. A **terugflits** is a scene that goes back to an earlier time.
g12u01l01.a: Talk about regret and reconciliation, with words for reproach, stubbornness and flashback.

g12u01l02.h: Back on the farm: a lawyer, a funeral and a door that was never locked. The words in this lesson set the scene, and a few of them set the mood.
g12u01l02.c: In a literary story, small physical details carry a lot of feeling, such as grey temples or a loosening chest. These words and sentences are the ones you’ll meet in the story, so you can read it without stopping.
g12u01l02.t: **Die prokureur** (the attorney), **die begrafnis** (the funeral), **die slape** (the temples of the head) and **vasgeknoop** (knotted, tied up). In sentences: **Hy het grys geword by die slape.**, **Die deur was nooit gesluit nie.**, **Hy het 'n tree nader gegee.** and **Iets in sy bors het begin losraak.** Notice how a step and a feeling in the chest show a change in a character without the writer saying so.
g12u01l02.a: Use the vocabulary of a funeral and a farm, and understand how physical details show feeling.

g12u01l03.h: Grammar: the past unreal. If I had stayed, I would have said something. The grammar of regret.
g12u01l03.c: Talking about things that didn’t happen, such as a missed phone call, a lost chance or a better decision, is an essential part of reflective writing and of conversation about regret. It’s also a Graad 12 exam favourite.
g12u01l03.t: For something that didn’t happen and its imagined result, use **as** plus **het … ge-** in the if-part, and **sou … ge- … het** in the result: **As ek gebly het, sou ek iets gesê het.** When the if-part comes first, the result starts with **sou**, with the verb first after the comma. **Moes … het** means should have: **Ek moes lankal gekom het.** **Kon … het** means could have: **Dit kon erger gewees het.** **Wees** becomes **gewees** in these structures. **Ek wens ek het vroeër gebel.** expresses regret about the past.
g12u01l03.a: Talk about things that did not happen, with as … het, sou … het, moes … het and kon … het.
g12u01l03.n: Count the **het**s. In the full pattern, there’s one in the if-part and one at the end of the result, and that second **het** is the one people forget.

g12u01l04.h: Twaalf jaar: a literary short story about a man in a car outside the farm he hasn’t seen for twelve years. Read slowly. Every detail counts.
g12u01l04.c: A literary short story rewards close reading: the setting, the small objects and the silences all carry meaning. In the exam you’ll be asked to discuss conflict and symbols with evidence, and this story is built for that.
g12u01l04.t: Johan parks under the pepper tree by the farm gate but doesn’t get out. The house looks smaller than he remembers, the red stoep where he and his brother Willem once played marbles has peeling paint, and someone has put in a new sliding door. For twelve years the brothers haven’t spoken, since an argument about money after their mother’s death. Willem stayed on the farm and looked after their father, and Johan moved to the city. Last week their father died, and Johan sat at the back of the church and slipped out as soon as the last hymn ended. Now he’s turning an envelope over in his hand, addressed to him in his father’s slanting handwriting. Look for the inner and the outer conflict, and the symbols. After the questions, you’ll say what would have been different if Johan had phoned every Sunday.
g12u01l04.a: Read a literary short story, identify inner and outer conflict and symbols, and say what would have been different.

g12u01l05.h: Write a reflective essay called "As ek kon teruggaan": if I could go back. Use the past unreal at least three times, and be honest.
g12u01l05.c: A reflective essay is a quiet, personal kind of writing, and it’s a natural place for **sou … het** and **moes … het**. Matric exams include a long piece like this one, so practise it carefully.
g12u01l05.t: Write 250 to 300 words, not counting the title. Think of one moment, such as a decision, a chat or a missed chance, and describe what happened, what you wish had happened and what you’ve learned. Use the past unreal at least three times, with structures such as **As ek gebly het, sou ek …**, **Ek moes … het** and **Ek wens ek het …** Keep a thoughtful tone, and end on what you understand now.
g12u01l05.a: Write a reflective essay that uses the past unreal correctly and ends on what you have learned.

g12u01l06.h: Twelve-years check! What would have happened if you had revised?
g12u01l06.c: A look back at the story vocabulary and the past unreal before the next unit.
g12u01l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **As ek gebly het, sou ek iets gesê het.** and **Ek moes lankal gekom het.**, and put every **het** in the right place.
g12u01l06.a: See which past-unreal patterns and story words are solid.

g12u02l01.h: Tone and irony: how what is said and what is meant can be two different things. Welcome to the stage.
g12u02l01.c: Drama is written to be performed, so the writer’s clues are in the words, the stage directions and what the audience knows. In this unit you’ll read a short extract and learn to read tone and irony, which is essential in Graad 12 literature.
g12u02l01.t: **Die toneelaanwysing** (the stage direction), **die ironie** (irony), **die toon** (the tone), **sarkasties** (sarcastic) and **die monoloog** (the monologue). Stage directions, usually in brackets, tell actors how to speak and move, and they tell you a great deal about tone. Irony is when the surface and the real meaning differ.
g12u02l01.a: Talk about drama, with words for stage direction, tone, irony, sarcasm and monologue.

g12u02l02.h: The birthday: a crooked cake, a gift voucher and a family that hasn’t quite said what it means. Let’s learn the words before the curtain goes up.
g12u02l02.c: A family gathering is a perfect setting for drama, because everyone has something to say and something to hide. These words and phrases are the ones in the extract.
g12u02l02.t: **Die geskenkbewys** (the gift voucher), **bedagsaam** (thoughtful), **die nagmerrie** (the nightmare) and **verdof** (to dim). In sentences: **Die koek is effens skeef.**, **Hier gaan ons weer.**, **Ten minste is ek hier.** and **Wanneer was jy laas hier?** Notice how short lines like **Hier gaan ons weer.** carry a whole history of old arguments. Try saying it once warmly and once sharply, and hear how the meaning shifts.
g12u02l02.a: Use the vocabulary of a family birthday, and notice how short lines carry feeling.

g12u02l03.h: Drama: register, tone and irony. "Die verkeer. Natuurlik.": two words that mean the opposite of what they say.
g12u02l03.c: Reading a play means hearing the voices behind the words: who’s polite, who’s bitter and who knows more than they let on. You’ll be asked about this in the exam, and it makes drama far more enjoyable.
g12u02l03.t: **Register**: many adults address their parents as **Ma** and **Pa** instead of **jy**, to show respect: **Ma moet rus.** Formal writing uses **u**. **Toon** is the attitude behind the words: **sarkasties**, **droog**, **bitter**, **teer** and **speels**, and stage directions often tell you. **Verbale ironie** is saying the opposite of what you mean: **Die verkeer. Natuurlik.** **Dramatiese ironie** is when the audience knows something the characters don’t: **Die gehoor weet meer as die karakters.** Adjectives take **-e** before a noun but not after **is**: **'n sarkastiese toon**, but **dit is ironies**.
g12u02l03.a: Read tone and register in a script, and tell verbal irony from dramatic irony.
g12u02l03.n: For dramatic irony, ask: what does the audience know that the characters don’t? That gap is where the effect comes from.

g12u02l04.h: Die huis in Kerkstraat: a drama extract set in a sitting room in the Paarl, with a crooked cake, a late daughter and a letter in Elsa’s handbag.
g12u02l04.c: A drama extract is short enough to read twice: once for the words and once for the stage directions and what they reveal. This one is built so that the audience knows something the characters don’t.
g12u02l04.t: Elsa, sixty, sits alone on a Saturday afternoon reading a letter that confirms the sale contract for Kerkstraat 14 has been signed. She smiles, folds it away and puts it in her handbag. Her son Ruben comes in with a slightly crooked cake, jokes that it looks like the Tower of Pisa, and her daughter Carla arrives on the phone to a colleague, apologising that she’s late because of the traffic. Watch the stage directions in brackets, the tone of each speaker and what the audience knows about the letter. After the questions, you’ll describe Carla and Ruben in one sentence each, and explain the dramatic irony.
g12u02l04.a: Read a drama extract, use the stage directions to read tone, and explain the dramatic irony.

g12u02l05.h: Write a diary entry as Carla or Ruben on the evening after the birthday. Show how your character feels, in a tone that fits.
g12u02l05.c: Writing as a character is a good test of whether you’ve really understood them: their voice, their worries and what they’d say only to a diary.
g12u02l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words as Carla or Ruben on the evening after the birthday. Show how the character feels, using a tone that fits them, such as dry and hurried for Carla or warm and joking for Ruben, and refer to something that actually happened in the extract, such as the cake or the traffic. Use the register of a private diary, and let the feelings come through the details rather than being named.
g12u02l05.a: Write a diary entry as a character, with a tone that fits and details from the extract.

g12u02l06.h: Drama check! Tone, irony and a very crooked cake.
g12u02l06.c: A look back at drama language and irony before the next unit.
g12u02l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die verkeer. Natuurlik.** and **Die gehoor weet meer as die karakters.**, and decide whether each line is verbal or dramatic irony.
g12u02l06.a: See which drama terms and irony types are solid.

g12u03l01.h: A poem about a video call with Mom, where the screen freezes and the line breaks. We’ll start with the poet’s toolkit.
g12u03l01.c: A modern poem in free verse relies on repetition, line breaks and contrast more than on rhyme, and Graad 12 expects you to discuss these techniques with close reference to the text. This unit is about one poem, and how it makes distance feel real.
g12u03l01.t: **Die refrein** (the refrain), **die paradoks** (the paradox), **die simbool** (the symbol), **die slotreël** (the closing line) and **die vrye vers** (free verse). A refrain is a line that returns, and each time it comes back it can mean something different. A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself and yet makes a deeper point. Free verse has no fixed rhyme or rhythm, so the line breaks do much of the work.
g12u03l01.a: Talk about a modern poem’s refrain, paradox, symbol, closing line and free verse.

g12u03l02.h: Far away: a poor connection, a warm stoep and a little mark on the kitchen wall. These words come from a poem about missing home.
g12u03l02.c: Calls between family members in different countries are a daily reality for many people, and they make strong material for poetry. Here you’ll learn the vocabulary of a video call and of missing someone.
g12u03l02.t: **Vries** (to freeze), **die plooi** (the wrinkle, fold), **die verlange** (longing) and **die verbinding** (the connection). In sentences: **Die verbinding is swak.**, **Die stoep is nog warm.**, **Daar is 'n vlekkie op die kombuismuur.** and **Die koffie is duur en dun.** Notice how ordinary details, such as weak coffee and a warm stoep, give a feeling of place and loss.
g12u03l02.a: Use the vocabulary of a video call and longing, with the small details that make a poem concrete.

g12u03l03.h: Poetry: refrain, enjambment, contrast and irony. "Kan Ma my hoor?": a question that changes every time it comes back.
g12u03l03.c: In Graad 12, you’re expected to say not only which technique a poet uses, but what it does to the meaning. This lesson gives you the four techniques for the poem, with the effect of each.
g12u03l03.t: A **refrein** is a line that comes back, and each time it can gain meaning: first a practical question, at the end a cry of longing. **Enjambement** is when a sentence runs on into the next line, so the reader has to wait: **soos 'n deur / wat nie besluit het nie**. **Kontras** sets two things against each other: **hier is dit winter / daar is dit Desember**. **Ironie** is when the words say one thing and the situation shows another: **Ons is nader as ooit**, while they’re far apart. In **vrye vers**, look at line breaks, repetition and the closing lines instead of rhyme.
g12u03l03.a: Spot a refrain, enjambment, contrast and irony in a poem, and say what each one does.
g12u03l03.n: For every technique, finish the sentence "this makes the reader feel …". That one phrase turns naming into analysis.

g12u03l04.h: Videoskakel: a poem about a video call with a mother, in a different season and a different hemisphere. Read it aloud, and notice what changes.
g12u03l04.c: A short free-verse poem lets you look at every line break and every repeated word, and it’s the sort of poem you’ll be asked to discuss in the exam.
g12u03l04.t: The poem opens with the question **Kan Ma my hoor?**, as the screen freezes on Mom’s smile, half open like a door that hasn’t decided. Here it is winter and the coffee is dear and weak, while there it’s December and the stoep is still warm at ten at night. Mom talks about the neighbours, the rain that won’t come and Dad’s knee, and the speaker nods while the internet takes every third word. They’re closer than ever, the speaker says, and can count the wrinkles around her eyes. Then the line breaks, and the speaker is left looking at their own face in a black screen. Watch how the refrain returns, and what it means each time. After the questions, you’ll explain in three sentences how its meaning changes.
g12u03l04.a: Read a modern poem closely and trace how its refrain changes meaning from start to end.

g12u03l05.h: Write a literary paragraph on Videoskakel: how does the poet use refrain, contrast and irony to show distance? Quote correctly.
g12u03l05.c: A literary paragraph is the building block of every poetry essay, and a good one has a clear point, accurate quotations and an explanation of effect.
g12u03l05.t: Write one paragraph of 150 to 180 words. Begin with a clear statement about the theme of distance, then discuss the refrain **Kan Ma my hoor?**, the contrast between winter and December, and the irony of **Ons is nader as ooit**. Quote each one correctly, with quotation marks and the exact words, and say what effect each has. Finish with a sentence that links all three to the final image of the black screen.
g12u03l05.a: Write a literary paragraph that analyses refrain, contrast and irony, with correct quotations.

g12u03l06.h: Video-call check! Can you hear what the refrain is doing?
g12u03l06.c: A look back at the poem’s techniques and vocabulary before the next unit.
g12u03l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild lines such as **Die skerm vries op Ma se glimlag.** and **Ma se oë, net verder weg.**, and name the technique in each.
g12u03l06.a: See which poetry techniques and poem vocabulary are solid.

g12u04l01.h: Meetings: somebody chairs, somebody takes notes and somebody always asks for any other business. Let’s learn the roles.
g12u04l01.c: Committees, clubs, school governing bodies and workplaces all hold meetings, and the minutes are the official record of what was decided. Being able to read and write them is a practical skill for adult life. This unit follows the minutes of a small athletics club.
g12u04l01.t: **Die notule** (the minutes), **die sakelys** (the agenda), **die voorsitter** (the chairperson), **die sekretaris** (the secretary) and **die penningmeester** (the treasurer). The **sekretaris** writes the minutes, and the **voorsitter** leads the meeting, so you’ll see their names in the text. Notice that **notule** is used with a singular verb, as in **Die notule is sonder veranderinge goedgekeur.** in the next lesson. Try saying who does what in your own club or committee, using these five words.
g12u04l01.a: Talk about a committee meeting, using words for minutes, agenda, chairperson, secretary and treasurer.

g12u04l02.h: Proposed and seconded: the little formal phrases that make a meeting official. A bit like a ritual, and just as useful.
g12u04l02.c: Formal meetings use a set vocabulary for proposing, agreeing and postponing decisions, and minutes record each step in a standard way. These are the phrases you’ll read in the next lesson.
g12u04l02.t: **Goedkeur** (to approve), **sekondeer** (to second a motion), **die borg** (the sponsor) and **die ledegeld** (membership fees). In sentences: **Die notule is sonder veranderinge goedgekeur.**, **Die voorsitter het almal welkom geheet.**, **Die besluit word tot die volgende vergadering uitgestel.** and **Die vergadering is om twintig voor agt afgesluit.** Notice the passive in the minutes: they record what was done and not who did it.
g12u04l02.a: Use the formal phrases of a meeting to propose, approve, postpone and close.

g12u04l03.h: Grammar: capital letters. After 'n, the next word takes the capital. Dinsdag has one, somer doesn’t. The details matter.
g12u04l03.c: Capital letters look small, but they’re a clear sign of careful writing, and they’re tested in Graad 12 spelling and editing questions. Minutes, letters and reports are where you most need them.
g12u04l03.t: When a sentence starts with **'n**, the next word gets the capital, not **'n**: **'n Vergadering vind op Dinsdag plaas.** Use capitals for names of people, places, organisations and languages, and for adjectives made from names: **Afrikaans**, **Engels**, **Kaapse**, **Suid-Afrikaanse**. Days, months and festivals take capitals in Afrikaans, as in **Dinsdag**, **Maart** and **Kersfees**, but seasons don’t, so it’s **somer** and **winter**. Abbreviated titles inside a sentence stay lowercase: **mnr. Naidoo**. Minutes also use abbreviations such as **i.p.v.**, **m.b.t.**, **t.o.v.**, **i.v.m.** and **vgl.**, and you should be able to read them aloud in full.
g12u04l03.a: Use capital letters correctly, and read and write the common meeting abbreviations.
g12u04l03.n: Days, months and festivals get capitals, but seasons never do. Memorise that one contrast and you’ll avoid the most common slip.

g12u04l04.h: The minutes of the Rivierdal Athletics Club committee meeting: numbered items, formal phrases and a decision that gets postponed.
g12u04l04.c: Minutes follow a strict layout, and reading a real-looking set is the best way to learn it. It’s also the model for the minutes you’ll write.
g12u04l04.t: The meeting opens at 18:35 on a Tuesday in the clubhouse, and the chairperson welcomes everyone. The minutes record who’s present and who sent apologies, and the previous minutes are approved without changes, proposed by one member and seconded by another. The treasurer reports the club’s bank balance and says that not all members have paid their fees. Under new business a fun run is discussed, and one member proposes appointing a coach for the juniors, but the committee decides to look into the cost first, so the decision is postponed. The next meeting is set, and the chairperson closes the meeting at 19:40. Look for the numbered headings, the passive and abbreviations such as **i.p.v.** and **m.b.t.** After the questions, you’ll tell an absent member the three most important decisions.
g12u04l04.a: Read the minutes of a meeting, find the decisions, and report back to someone who was absent.

g12u04l05.h: Write the minutes of a short meeting of a street committee, club or team. Correct format, correct capitals and at least one abbreviation.
g12u04l05.c: Writing minutes means turning a conversation into a clear, accurate record, and it’s a task that many people take on at work or in a community group.
g12u04l05.t: Write 120 to 150 words. Use the format from the model: a title with the date, time and place, numbered items, who was present and who sent apologies, decisions with the person who proposed and seconded, the next meeting and the closing time. Use capitals correctly, with days and months capitalised and seasons not, and include at least one abbreviation such as **i.p.v.** or **m.b.t.** Keep to facts, and write decisions in the passive where it fits.
g12u04l05.a: Write the minutes of a short meeting in the correct format with capitals and abbreviations.

g12u04l06.c: A look back at meeting language and capitals before the next unit.
g12u04l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **'n Vergadering vind op Dinsdag plaas.** and **Die notule is sonder veranderinge goedgekeur.**, and fix capitals and abbreviations.
g12u04l06.a: See which meeting words and capital-letter rules are solid.

g12u05l01.h: It’s ten at night, your phone beeps and it’s your manager. This unit is about the right to switch off, and the words that argue for and against it.
g12u05l01.c: Whether work should be able to reach you after hours is a debate happening in workplaces and newspapers, and it makes a rich topic for an argumentative essay. You’ll read one writer’s position, learn how to spot position, arguments and rebuttals, and write your own. The unit doesn’t ask you to share the writer’s view.
g12u05l01.t: **Die uitbranding** (burnout), **die welstand** (well-being), **op bystand** (on call), **vergoed** (to compensate) and **aanvoer** (to argue, contend). **Aanvoer** is separable, so you’ll meet **Hy voer aan dat …** with the particle at the end. A good argumentative essay states a position, backs it up with arguments, and answers the other side’s strongest points.
g12u05l01.a: Talk about work, rest and well-being, with words for burnout, on call, compensate and argue.

g12u05l02.h: Always reachable: a beeping phone, a blurred line between work and home and an employer’s own interest. The vocabulary of a modern problem.
g12u05l02.c: Arguments about work and technology draw on a precise vocabulary, and the same words appear in news and workplace talk. They’re also the words that make your own essay sound convincing.
g12u05l02.t: **Bereikbaar** (reachable), **tydelik** (temporary), **vervaag** (to blur, fade) and **die produktiwiteit** (productivity). In sentences: **My foon gee 'n piep.**, **Ek skakel my foon saans af.**, **Dit is in die werkgewer se belang.** and **Ons behoort hul voorbeeld te volg.** Notice **behoort … te**, which means ought to and takes **te** without **om**. Try turning each sentence into a claim you could argue for, such as that employers ought to follow another company’s example.
g12u05l02.a: Use the vocabulary of work, technology and productivity to make a point in an argument.

g12u05l03.h: Grammar: making nouns. Verbeter becomes verbetering, beskikbaar becomes beskikbaarheid. Formal Afrikaans loves them, but use them wisely.
g12u05l03.c: Formal and academic writing turns actions and qualities into nouns, which makes it more compact and precise. It’s a hallmark of Graad 12 writing, and it’s the best way to sound formal without sounding stuffy, if you’re careful.
g12u05l03.t: **-ing** comes from verbs: **verbeter** becomes **die verbetering**, **ontwikkel** becomes **die ontwikkeling** and **beplan** becomes **die beplanning**. **-heid** comes from adjectives: **beskikbaar** becomes **die beskikbaarheid** and **noodsaaklik** becomes **die noodsaaklikheid**. Also **-skap**, as in **vriend** and **die vriendskap**, and **-nis**, as in **gebeur** and **die gebeurtenis**. Some verbs are their own noun, such as **besluit** and **gebruik**. Too many nouns make writing heavy, so use them where they make you more precise, not to sound important.
g12u05l03.a: Form nouns with -ing, -heid, -skap and -nis, and know when a verb reads better.
g12u05l03.n: If a sentence has three nouns in a row joined by **van**, try rewriting it with a verb. It’s usually clearer, and it still sounds formal.

g12u05l04.h: Die reg om af te skakel: an argumentative essay with a clear position, three arguments and a counter-argument that gets answered.
g12u05l04.c: At Graad 12 you need to see how an argument is built: a position, arguments in order, a rebuttal and a conclusion. This essay is a good model, and you can compare its structure with what you’ll write. The essay is a language-learning text, and it doesn’t claim to settle the question.
g12u05l04.t: The essay opens at ten at night: you’ve just put the children to bed, your phone beeps and it’s your manager asking you to look at a report. The writer believes employees should have a legal right not to respond to work calls and e-mails after hours. In the first place, rest is a necessity and not a luxury, because people who never get away from work risk burnout. Second, since smartphones became common, the line between work and home has blurred. Third, the writer says, such a right protects the weakest workers. Notice the nominalisations such as **die verbetering** and **die beskikbaarheid**. After the questions, you’ll give the writer’s position, one argument and one counter-argument in three sentences.
g12u05l04.a: Read an argumentative essay, find the position, arguments and rebuttals, and summarise them in three sentences.

g12u05l05.h: Write your own argumentative essay: choose a topic, or ask whether plastic shopping bags should be banned. Take a clear position and answer the other side.
g12u05l05.c: This is the longest argumentative essay of the course, and it brings together everything about linking words, negatives and now nouns. It’s the sort of piece you’ll write in the final exam.
g12u05l05.t: Write 250 to 300 words, not counting the title. Take a clear position, support it with at least three arguments in order, and rebut at least one counter-argument fairly. Use at least three nouns ending in **-ing**, **-heid**, **-skap** or **-nis**, such as **die verbetering** or **die noodsaaklikheid**, and use formal linking words such as **bowendien** and **nietemin**. Finish with a conclusion that follows from your arguments.
g12u05l05.a: Write an argumentative essay with a clear position, a rebuttal and formal nouns.

g12u05l06.h: Argument check! Position, rebuttal and a lot of nouns.
g12u05l06.c: A look back at the argument vocabulary and noun-forming endings before the last unit.
g12u05l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Die verbetering van welstand help almal.** and **Rus is 'n noodsaaklikheid.**, and form the noun from each verb or adjective.
g12u05l06.a: See which noun-forming endings are solid.

g12u06l01.h: The very last unit of the course, and the right one to finish with: how to actually learn a language, and keep learning it.
g12u06l01.c: After twelve levels, you know how much practice, patience and courage a language takes, and this unit’s advice article says so in its own words. It also teaches you the idioms and proverbs that make speech sound like a real Afrikaans speaker’s. The advice is for language learning, not a guarantee of results.
g12u06l01.t: **Die selfvertroue** (confidence), **die uitspraak** (pronunciation), **die herhaling** (repetition), **die aksent** (accent) and **die leerkurwe** (the learning curve). **Herhaling** is the main idea of the article, and **selfvertroue** is the thing that comes from it. **Leerkurwe** is a compound of learn and curve, and it describes how learning feels steep at first.
g12u06l01.a: Talk about learning a language, using words for confidence, pronunciation, repetition and accent.

g12u06l02.h: A little every day: progress, routine and a gentle reminder that mistakes are part of the process.
g12u06l02.c: Advice about learning is full of short, practical sentences and encouraging phrases, and they’re sentences you can use when you encourage someone else who’s learning. They also work for yourself.
g12u06l02.t: **Die vordering** (progress), **vlot** (fluent), **die roetine** (routine), **volhard** (to persevere) and **onbeholpe** (awkward, clumsy). In sentences: **Foute is deel van die leerproses.**, **Tien minute elke dag is beter as drie uur op 'n Sondag.**, **Praat hardop, ook as jy alleen is.** and **Ek verstaan meer as wat ek kan sê.** That last sentence is true for almost every learner, and it’s nothing to be ashamed of.
g12u06l02.a: Give encouraging, practical advice about learning, and describe your own progress.

g12u06l03.h: Idioms and proverbs: die kat uit die boom kyk, onder die knie kry. Not about cats or knees, and very much about how Afrikaans speakers talk.
g12u06l03.c: Idioms and proverbs are one of the clearest marks of a fluent speaker, and one of the hardest things to learn from a textbook. They’re also tested in Graad 12, and they make your writing feel alive.
g12u06l03.t: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning isn’t the sum of its words: **die kat uit die boom kyk** means to wait and see before you act. Don’t translate idioms word for word, and don’t change their words: **onder die knie kry**, **twee vlieë met een klap slaan**, **die spyker op die kop slaan**, **jou kop in die sand steek** and **jou hande vol hê**. The verb can change for tense and person: **Sy het die taal onder die knie gekry.** A proverb is a short saying that gives advice: **Oefening maak meester.** and **Aanhouer wen.** Use idioms sparingly, because one well-chosen idiom lifts a text and five in a paragraph read like a list.
g12u06l03.a: Use common idioms and proverbs correctly, tell literal from figurative meaning, and spot them in a text.
g12u06l03.n: Keep the idiom’s words fixed and let only the verb change. If you change the animal, or the body part, an Afrikaans speaker will hear it.

g12u06l04.h: Onder die knie: an advice article about how people really learn a language, with idioms in nearly every paragraph. Spot them all.
g12u06l04.c: An advice article is friendly, practical and a little humorous, and this one is also a showcase of idioms and proverbs in use. It’s the text you’ll summarise in the next lesson.
g12u06l04.t: The article begins by saying that nobody becomes fluent overnight, and that the secret is seldom talent and usually a good routine. Many people watch the cat out of the tree for years, waiting for the right time to start, and the right time never comes. It advises starting with repetition, ten minutes every day instead of three hours on a Sunday, and it says that even with your hands full of work and children, ten minutes is usually possible. It also tells you to use the language, speaking aloud even when you’re alone and describing what you see while you brush your teeth. Count the idioms and proverbs as you read. After the questions, you’ll give a colleague three tips for learning Afrikaans.
g12u06l04.a: Read an advice article, spot its idioms and proverbs, and give a colleague three tips for learning a language.

g12u06l05.h: The last summary of the course: seven tips, one paragraph, eighty to ninety words, in your own words. Make it count.
g12u06l05.c: This is the longest summary in the course, and it uses everything you’ve practised: reading for the main points, choosing your words and joining ideas in correct sentences. It’s also a good way to take the article’s advice with you.
g12u06l05.t: Choose seven of the writer’s tips from the article, and leave out the introduction and the examples. Write one paragraph of 80 to 90 words in full sentences and in your own words, not copied. Use linking words such as **eerstens**, **verder**, **bowendien** and **laastens**, keep each verb in the right place, and use no more than one idiom. Read it aloud when you finish, and see if it sounds like you.
g12u06l05.a: Pick out seven tips from an advice article and summarise them in 80 to 90 words.

g12u06l06.h: The final check of the whole course! Idioms, proverbs and twelve levels of Afrikaans behind you.
g12u06l06.c: A last look at idioms and proverbs, and at everything you’ve learned along the way.
g12u06l06.t: You’ll hear and rebuild sentences such as **Ek het die werkwoorde nou onder die knie.** and **Jy het die spyker op die kop geslaan.**, and match each idiom to its meaning.
g12u06l06.a: See which idioms and proverbs are solid, and be proud of how far you’ve come.
